The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is subsumed within the single character "existence" (*sat*) of the term "dependent existence. If this existence is regarded as a false existence, it is the dependent nature;

if one clings to this existence as a real existence, it is the imagined nature. Therefore, even in this brief explanation of contemplation, all three natures are encompassed. One should understand these three natures.

Regarding the discussion on the contemplation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): *parikalpita* (the imagined) takes "existence as a real entity" as its essence; *paratantra* (the dependent) takes "existence as an illusion" as its essence;

and *pariniṣpanna* (the perfected) takes "the absence of the former two natures" as its essence. This concludes the discourse on the three natures. Regarding the cessation (*śamatha*) of these three natures:

*parikalpita* ceases with "existence as a real entity" as its essence; *paratantra* ceases with "existence as an illusion" as its essence; and *pariniṣpanna* ceases with "the absence of nature" as its essence. Such are the general positions; the detailed exposition follows in the subsequent text.

Second, the external opponent’s [objection] below. This is explained in detail in two parts. First, the request for an explanation: Because the arising of understanding from consciousness must necessarily depend on the subtlety of that consciousness, one cannot achieve awakening through hearing only a brief summary;
thus, he requests further skillful means for a detailed and thorough exposition.
[The section] "The Śramaṇa" concludes. Regarding the second part, which promises an extensive explanation, there are two sections. First is the presentation of the headings.

As for the establishment in five parts, it is not without its rationale. First, to clarify the basis (*āśraya*): this refers to the single nature of equality as the basis upon which all phenomena depend.
Because sentient beings are deluded regarding this single nature and give rise to false imaginings, there exists the discriminated and dependent realm.
To counteract this delusion and reveal the true nature, the realm of reality is shown. Once these realms have arisen, they are designated as the object of contemplation.

Based on this object of contemplation, one must discern the essential characteristics of the contemplating subject—calm abiding and insight. Having cultivated calm abiding and insight, the cause is perfected.

Because the fruit is accomplished, there is the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*). Since the fruit has been realized, one ought accordingly to benefit sentient beings; thus, there is the function (*kāritra*).

If these five are correlated with the ten chapters of the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation): the function corresponds to the "Exhorting to Teach" chapter; the virtue of cessation corresponds to the "Fruit and Retribution" chapter;
the essential nature corresponds to the "Calming and Contemplation" chapter; and the objective realm and the basis correspond to the preceding six chapters.

Second, regarding the first [section], the explanation is divided into five parts. First, the basis for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This is further divided into three sections. First, the heading and enumeration.

Regarding the phrase "further establishing three gates": the first concerns the essence of concentration (*samādhi*). "Essence" refers to the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*). Second, this discusses its function;

because this single nature is the foundation of all phenomena, and moreover possesses both the virtues of quiescence (*śama*) and activity (*vyāpāra*), one must rely upon it. Third, this distinguishes...
Regarding cultivation: when one wishes to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, by what dharma does one rely to practice them? It is as stated in the text below:

"One practices *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by relying on this mind with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Here, the mental consciousness is the initial mind that gives rise to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, upon what does it rely? This precisely indicates the inconceivable object of contemplation (*ālambana*). Why does it rely [upon this]?

Regarding "stopping" (*śamatha*): it reveals that the observing mind takes the object itself as the observation; therefore, one relies upon this mind. Why? Because this pure mind is the source of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Since there are no phenomena apart from the mind, the object is taken as the observation itself, unlike ordinary objects which possess a distinction between subject and object.
As for what is relied upon: the mind that gives rise to observation is the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Although the object and the observation are fused, [the mind remains] coarse...

Alternatively, it may still exist; therefore, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is designated as the support. The perfectly expressive consciousness is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
This can also be said to mean that the observing wisdom is itself ignorance (*avidyā*).

Second, first providing a preliminary clarification and then correctly explaining the text itself, which is divided into three parts. First, "What is it that serves as the basis? Second, first the heading, and second, the explanation beginning with "That is, based on...
which contains both a general and a specific exposition. Within the general exposition, it says: "That is, based on the one mind" refers to the single nature of equality.
Furthermore, this single nature is precisely the nature of the three thousand [realms]. This nature of the three thousand is not to be sought afar; rather, it is...
The practitioner’s present single thought-moment—pointing to this very thought-moment as being identical to the one nature—is taken as the basis for practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Next, the two [aspects] are explained individually. First, the outline is presented. Regarding "the emergence of various names," etc.:

because this one nature fully contains its essential substance and attributes, the sūtras and śāstras employ various different names for it. By relying on these names to explain their meanings, and by examining these meanings to discern the essence, [one arrives at the following]:

There are three sections. The second [section] begins with "Next, the following" and constitutes the formal explanation. This text itself is divided into three parts: first, the presentation of various names; second, the discussion [of these names];

third, the explanation of the meanings of the names. The first [of these three] has two parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation beginning with the question. This text itself is further divided into seven parts.

First, the explanation of the intrinsically pure mind has two parts. First, the question: "The intrinsic nature is not ignorance; the purity of the other-nature is distinct from the defilement of ignorance.
This mind differs from ignorance and its lack of awakening; one should know that this mind is originally nameless. Because ignorance exists, this name arises.
Second, the answer has two parts. First, the explanation has two parts. First, the explanation of purity has two parts. First, the general indication.
Regarding the statement, "Because this mind reaches [purity], it is called 'pure'": defiled phenomena obscure its nature, yet its nature is eternally pure. Question:

Some claim that in the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), the essence of nature is eternally pure because it is not identical to defilement; whereas in the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), the essence of nature is not said to be eternally pure because it is identical to defilement.

Should this not indicate that the present text belongs to the Separate Teaching and not the Perfect Teaching? Answer: One must understand that within the Perfect Teaching there is both identity and separation. With respect to...

When speaking of ignorance in terms of the nature of the mind, it cannot be said that they are separate; when speaking of the nature of the mind in terms of ignorance, it cannot be said that they are identical.

However, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) discusses their separation based on their identity, whereas other schools maintain a fixed separation where the beginning and end are eternally pure. The phrase "How can these two...
explains the reason for this: it means that because the essence (*tǐ*) of ignorance is a non-existent dharma, what is called "essence" here refers to its [conventional] presence.

This explains the essence by means of its name. To discuss the essence according to its reality: if one identifies the essence following the name, since the name "ignorance" (avidyā) exists, there must necessarily be an essential substance corresponding to that name;

thus, one would take false delusion (*mṛṣā*) as its essence. However, if one discusses the essence according to its actual reality, ignorance has only a dependent nature as its essence and possesses no substantial reality of its own; it is merely a designation (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) called "ignorance."
Why is this so? Because ignorance is entirely identical in essence with the *dharmatā*, it lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is like a stream, which has water as its essence;
there is only its appearance, which we call a "stream. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The two kinds of ignorance are fundamentally without substance;
they have only the pure mind as their essence. The *Fuxing* commentary says: "Therefore, the names 'dullness' and 'scattering' do not possess any real substance."
It is further taken to have quiescent illumination as its nature. Question: Can it be said that the dharma-nature (dharmatā) has no substance? Answer: The meanings do not follow a single path.

If one considers the substance of the nature of equality, it is neither the dharma-nature nor ignorance; therefore, ignorance and the dharma-nature possess only two names, yet both are without substance.
As the *Fǔxíng* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) says: "The two dharmas have no substance and possess only provisional names. This is truly because...
The dharma-nature of ignorance is fundamentally without name; it is only out of response to conditions that two names are provisionally established. In reality, it has no self-substance.
If one takes the single nature of equality as the truth, then the entirety of that truth becomes the substance of delusion; thus, ignorance has no substance, as in the present text.
If one holds that there is no principle remaining and that this is entirely the phenomenal event, then the dharma-nature has no substance, as in [the following].
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says: "Seeing depends on ignorance; ignorance depends on the Dharma-nature; the Dharma-nature has nothing upon which it depends.

Why? Because the Dharma-nature has no substance; it is entirely ignorance. Nevertheless, one must understand this: if one were to discuss the ultimate reality, that the Dharma-nature has no substance does not mean it lacks its own essential nature;
it simply means that there is nothing upon which the Dharma-nature depends outside of itself. Therefore, the text below says:"

This does not mean that the substance of the mind is empty and non-existent. When it is said that ignorance has no substance, it does not mean it lacks a basis; rather, it simply means its substance is unreal and non-substantial. Some say:
"If ignorance has no basis, this is an exhaustive analysis from the perspective of delusion; however, from the perspective of the perfect [teaching], it is identical with the nature."
Second, the explanation of *tathatā* (true suchness) has two parts. First, the question; second, the answer, which has three parts. First, the actual explanation, which has two parts.

First, explaining each of the two characters (*zhen* and *ru*) according to the meaning of "leaving" (*li*). First, *zhen* (real); second, *ru* (such). Within *zhen*, there are two points. First, it is called "real" in contrast to the "false.
Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they take the pure mind as their essence. Since they lack intrinsic nature, they are all entirely false.

By this, it is shown that the mind itself is what is called "true. Second, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, below" establishes that the essence of the pure mind itself is what is called "true.
Because this pure mind is neither subject to arising nor ceasing, it is without increase or decrease; therefore, it is called "true. Furthermore, it says:
"All phenomena possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing due to false causes and conditions. Thus, we know that ignorance possesses only its phenomenal marks.
Yet in reality, it has no essence. From "The Buddhas of the past, present, and future" onwards, [the text] explains *tathatā* (suchness) by way of *pṛthaktva-vimukti* (separation).

Because it is free from the distinct characteristics of the differences between ordinary beings and sages, there is no difference; this is called *tathatā*. *Tathatā* means "sameness. It is the same because its essence is one; it is not the same in the sense of being parallel.

It is called *tathatā* because it is without marks. *Tathatā* means "emptiness. It is primordially subtle, and thus empty; it is not empty in the sense of being a state of annihilation. Second, from "Furthermore, the True... onwards, [the text] explains by way of *tādātmya* (identity).

The meaning of the two characters "True Suchness" (tathatā) is shown as follows. First, to reveal what it is: it indicates that all phenomena, in their very place, are True Suchness, which is nothing other than the One Mind.

Second, from the words "If the mind... onwards, it distinguishes what it is not; this distinguishes the partial and the deviant. Because they are outside the mind, they are different and not the same;
because they possess [independent] dharmas, they are characterized and not empty. Since one loses the true reality, divergent characteristics arise; therefore, they are not [True Suchness].
*Tathatā* (Suchness).
Second, the following citation provides scriptural evidence specifically to prove the meaning of "separation. Therefore, it is beyond verbal expression; names and mental objects [cannot reach it].
If its realization were itself the object, one should cite the treatise as follows: "The essence of this *tathatā* cannot be discarded, because all phenomena are entirely..."

Because they are real, there is likewise nothing that can be established; for all dharmas are identical with suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, this passage may also serve as a general proof for the meaning of "identity" (*jia-yi*):

since all dharmas are identical with the one mind (*ekacitta*), and there are no dharmas external to the mind, they cannot be conceptualized or expressed through the three—words, letters, and the mind.
While the mind’s conditions are directed specifically toward the mind and speech, names and words may apply generally to either the mind or [its objects].
One contemplates names, or speaks them aloud; furthermore, it is said that these spoken words are the names of real dharmas because they belong to conventional designations (*prajñapti*).
The Wise One says: "That which is free from the conceptual proliferation of speech is inconceivable.

That which is free from letters, though it is a conventional designation, is ultimately equal and reaches the state of being indestructible. The Master of the *Piṭaka* [Jñānaprabha] explains these three phrases as successive stages.
Explanation of the characteristics: "It is solely this one mind" concludes by returning to the essence of the Dharma. Now, for the time being, "ultimate equality" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
"the absence of change or variation" refers to the conventional (*prajñapti*); and "that which cannot be destroyed" refers to the middle (*madhyama*). These three are identical;

therefore, it is said that "it is solely this one mind," which is named True Suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, these four phrases may be correlated with the four virtues (*catvāri guṇāni*). Question: One—
Are the mind and suchness identical or different? If one says they are identical, the *Awakening of Faith* distinguishes two gates based on the one mind;
within these two gates, there are both suchness and the gate of arising-and-ceasing. The one mind is the general [principle], while suchness is the specific [aspect].

If it is asked, "If they are different, why does the present text state that 'it is solely this one mind, therefore it is named True Suchness'? The answer is: their substance is identical, yet their meanings differ.

Because True Suchness is singular, it is said that their substance is identical; yet because there are both the "differentiated True Suchness" and the "equal True Suchness," it is said that their meanings differ.
Furthermore, the equal True Suchness is precisely the same as the one mind; since the differentiated True Suchness stands in contrast to arising and ceasing, [the meanings differ].
Therefore, "one mind" is the general [term], while "true thusness" (tathatā) is the specific. Why is this? The natural, singular nature is neither true nor false;
it cannot be named. This is equality. Because sentient beings are deluded, they perceive arising and ceasing.

In response to this arising and ceasing, one points to that singular nature and calls it "true thusness. This is differentiation. Since this differentiated true thusness has already been pointed out...
The single nature serves as its name; therefore, this equality is also called *tathatā* (suchness).
Thus, while the name is derived from differentiation, the essence manifests as inherently equal. Because equality is named by means of differentiation, equality is also termed *tathatā*.
Therefore, the present text takes the single mind as *tathatā* (suchness). Because equality is itself differentiation, differentiation is also termed the "universal unity.
Consequently, in the section on the two gates within the *Awakening of Faith*, it states regarding the gate of *tathatā*:

"The suchness of mind is the very substance of the great universal characteristic dharma-gate of the one dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, when the *Awakening of Faith* distinguishes *tathatā*, it is precisely...

This was explained within the two gates of distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); the present text, however, clarifies True Suchness (*tathatā*) by specifically addressing it within the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the basis for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

This constitutes a difference in meaning. Because their essence is one, the present text invokes the specific [teachings] of the *Awakening of Faith* to corroborate the general [principle] of the basis.

The third section explains Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). First is the question; second is the answer, which has two parts. The first part is the formal explanation, which has two sub-sections: first, an explanation based on essence (*tattva*); second, an explanation based on function (*vṛtti*).

Furthermore, there are five general meanings of essence and function: first, the three delusions (*kleśa*) and their latent tendencies constitute the function, while the three truths (*satya*) constitute the essence.

Second, regarding the fact that each of the three truths possesses its own essence and function: the three truths are all essence, and the three truths are all function. Third, regarding phenomena and principle:

the conventional truth is the function, while emptiness and the middle way are the essence. Fourth, regarding the center and the extremes: emptiness and the provisional are the function, while the Middle Way is the essence.
Fifth, regarding non-attainment and illumination: the three truths are the function, while the single nature is the essence. Thus says the Wise One (Jizhi).
It is said that there are five functions based upon a single eye. Is this single eye not the essence of the one, perfect, eternal, and equal nature?
Are these five functions not the activity of illuminating the three truths simultaneously? The present text encompasses both: first, the center and the periphery.
Taking the Buddha-nature of the Dharma-body as its essence and the Buddha-natures of conditions and fulfillment as its function;
taking the two aspects of non-existence and illumination as its essence and the three kinds of Buddha-nature as its function. Therefore, the subsequent text states:

"If one clarifies awakening by way of the meaning of the mind-essence as the Dharma-realm's function, this mind-essence possesses the three kinds of great wisdom; how much more so the three kinds of wisdom [themselves]!"

The nature consists of the three Buddha-natures. Furthermore, it is said that the meaning of original enlightenment (benjue) is its function; therefore, it reveals the aforementioned essence, which is solely the general characteristic of the single, equal nature.

In the explanation by way of the essence (*tattva*), there are three parts. First is the general response: because the essence of the mind is neither awakening nor non-awakening, and because one wishes to discern the meaning of "Buddha," it is therefore called "awakening" due to its non-awakening.
Second is the investigation, which has two parts. First is the investigation that the nature is not non-awakening.

This has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Within the answer, there are two parts. First is the explanation based on the purity being different from defilement: if purity were identical to defilement, then at the time of extinguishing defilement, purity— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
It must also be extinguished. Since defilement is extinguished while purity remains, we know that this purity is not the same as defilement;
this demonstrates that the pure mind is not non-awakening (*abodhi*). As the current text states: "Since ignorance (*avidyā*) extinguishes itself, the pure mind remains of its own accord.

Furthermore, the *Zhizhe lun* says: "When ignorance is destroyed, there is no longer ignorance. Against what, then, could one further discuss the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)? If this is so, then when ignorance is extinguished...
Question: Since there is no pure mind [independent of ignorance], why does this text state that "ignorance is extinguished of itself and the pure mind exists of itself"?

Answer: The *Zhìzhě* (The Wise One) explains exclusively from the perspective of identity (*ji*). In this text, identity does not preclude separation (*lí*). Although the pure mind is identical to ignorance, this does not prevent ignorance from being extinguished of itself while the pure mind exists of itself.
Second, the subsequent section explains by way of the difference between defilement and purity; if defilement were identical to purity, [the distinction would collapse].
When one was in the state of defilement, one had already realized the pure mind; now, by means of the cessation of defilement, one realizes the pure mind.

Therefore, we know that this defilement is not identical to purity, and thus we see that the pure mind is not non-awakening (*abodha*). Second, investigating the source from which the names are derived.
First, regarding the intent of the question: why is the self-substance of the pure mind not itself named "awakening" (*bodhi*), but instead is named in contrast to "non-awakening"?

"Is it awakening? He replied: "There are two aspects. First, the direct answer: The essence of the nature of equality is fundamentally inexpressible; it is only by contrast with non-awakening that it is forcibly designated as 'awakening.
Thus, the name is derived from its opposite, yet the essence reveals itself through its own nature. By following the name back to the essence, the essence itself is also called 'awakening.'"
Since names follow from substance, what name could there even be for a "name"? For this reason, the following citation provides scriptural proof; it is from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
"There is no nirvāṇa in all things" refers to the teaching solely in terms of phenomena (*dharma*). "There is no Buddha in nirvāṇa" means that there is awakening without a causal phenomenon.
"There is no nirvāṇa in the Buddha" means that there is a phenomenon without a causal awakening. Since neither exists...

Awakening is such that there is nothing that is not awakened to. Why? Because it is said that awakening awakens to non-awakening; now, since awakening itself does not exist, there is no non-awakening. Therefore, the conclusion is stated:
"One remains far removed from both the awakener and that which is awakened to. That which is awakened to is precisely non-awakening.
Regarding "whether existent or non-existent": if it exists, this is the existence of awakening; if it does not exist, this is the non-existence of awakening. Thus, it belongs to non-awakening.
Enlightenment—both of these are entirely transcended. Thus, both enlightenment and non-enlightenment are neither existent nor non-existent.

Furthermore, that which is far removed from both the enlightened subject and the enlightened object is the person who enlightens and the phenomena that are enlightened; the existence or non-existence of both person and phenomenon cannot be apprehended.
These enlightened phenomena are also termed "non-enlightenment," though this differs from the initial explanation where ignorance was defined as non-enlightenment.

Second, this section explains [the nature of the mind] by way of its function. It consists of two parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, the actual explanation of "this mind" and so forth.

Regarding the first, there are four sections concerning the Buddha-nature as the wisdom of the *parijñā-hetu* (cause of comprehension). First, a general indication: "This mind-body is endowed with the three kinds of great wisdom.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom; it is only because of delusion..."

Through attachment, one fails to realize [enlightenment]. If one is free from deluded conceptualization, all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*), teacherless wisdom (*aśaikṣajñāna*), spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhūjñāna*), and unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) will immediately manifest before one.
The scriptural passage mentions "all-encompassing wisdom" as a general indication; the "teacherless" and subsequent terms refer specifically to these three types of wisdom.
Because the essence of the mind is of a single nature, this single nature serves as the capacity to possess the three kinds of greatness.
Wisdom is that which is possessed. If these three great wisdoms are correlated in sequence with their opposites: innate wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is omniscience (*sarvajña*);
spontaneous wisdom (*prakṛti-jñāna*) is the knowledge of the paths and their modes (*mārgajñatā*); and unimpeded wisdom (*asaṅga-jñāna*) is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
According to the *Fahua wenju*, since spontaneous wisdom is already identified as omniscience, the present "teacherless wisdom" (*aśikṣita-jñāna*) is likewise the wisdom of the Buddha.

The knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) and the unimpeded knowledge (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) are identical to the wisdom of the Tathāgata; this is the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (*mārgākārajñatā*).
The single nature of the Middle Way is so by its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). Since the fruit of Buddhahood is ultimate, it is without a teacher;

as it is also ultimately empty and quiescent, how could there be anyone to serve as a teacher? Because it is unimpeded, it may be said to "come. Although there are these three types of knowledge, they do not transcend the cultivation of the paths and their varieties for oneself and others.
The other two are his own practices; "original" refers to the single nature that is fully endowed with both self and others—this is what is meant.

Therefore, taking this mind as the awakened nature (bodhi-svabhāva) means it possesses both substance and function: the single nature of awakening is the substance, and the three types of awakening are the function.
These three awakenings are also called the Three Truths and are also called the Three Natures. Because these three are thoroughly examined and verified...

Therefore, they are called *satya* (truths). Because these three illuminate, they are called *bodhi* (awakening). Because these three are unchanging, they are called *prakṛti* (nature). These are thus different names for a single dharma.
Second, below this, in contrast to the aforementioned equality of one nature, the similarities and differences are distinguished. First, the heading; next, "How so? [is asked].
The following section distinguishes two aspects. First, it distinguishes their identity. Regarding the phrase "the essence of mind is equal," this means that the three wisdoms share a single nature;

while their substance is one, their meanings differ. Here, because we take their substance to be one, they are said to be identical. Why is this? It is because this single nature is neither delusion nor awakening;
it is suchness (tathatā) beyond naming, yet it may be forcibly designated as "awakening" (bodhi). Because sentient beings are deluded, there are the three afflictions (kleśa). In contrast to these...
Because awakening is spoken of in relation to delusion, this single awakening constitutes three wisdoms due to the difference in their meanings.
Unity is the essence (*svabhāva*), while the three wisdoms are the functions (*karitra*). Since awakening is spoken of in relation to delusion, wisdom becomes the function;

yet because the essence is one, these three wisdoms are that same unity which manifests as three, and thus they are said to be identical. Second, the passage beginning "Furthermore, how... below distinguishes them. [End of] Original Text.
Awakening is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Therefore, it is said that while in the state of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), it is called "Buddha-nature" (*tathāgatagarbha*).

When emerging from obstructions, it is called the "Wisdom Buddha," which refers to initial awakening (*ādikṣayabodhi*); this encompasses the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) as well as the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*).

Furthermore, original awakening (*mūlabodhi*) consists of the three wisdoms of the nature-qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*). Thus, it is also called the "threefold wisdom. When the nature emerges from obstructions, it is called the "Wisdom Buddha," which is initial awakening.

These are the three wisdoms. "Original" refers to the virtue of nature (*xing-de*), while "initial" refers to the virtue of cultivation (*xiu-de*). Although cultivation and nature differ, both are employed in their function.

This further demonstrates that the three dharmas all employ the single nature as their essence. Furthermore, it is said that "the essence of mind is equal": first, because the three dharmas are one, they are equal;
second, because the virtues of cultivation and nature are one, they are equal.
Third, the extensive explanation. First, one must understand the meaning of the two natures: equality and differentiation.

Only then will one thoroughly penetrate the intent of what Nanyue taught from beginning to end. First is the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding "differentiation," its essence consists of phenomenal events (*dharmas*).

Regarding "equality," its essence consists of the principle of nature (*dharmatā*). Second is their mutual identity: because phenomena are identical to the nature, phenomena are also equal. Because...

The nature is itself the phenomenal nature, and these are also differentiated. Thus, there is both the nature of equality and the nature of differentiation; the phenomenon of equality and the phenomenon of differentiation.

Regarding the first [the nature of differentiation], when discussing differentiation in terms of essence and function, there is furthermore the nature of the phenomenal nature that constitutes the nature of differentiation.
Just as fire is hot and water is cold, or as hatred is evil and joy is good—such things constitute the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Therefore, the Great Master, citing the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, states: "The nature of phenomena is such because their natures are differentiated. Within emptiness, the nature of principle belongs to equality;

this takes the single essence of emptiness as its nature. If one regards phenomena as being identical to that nature, then the aforementioned differentiations are likewise equal, just as [all things are]...

Because sentient beings possess distinctions, entering fire inevitably leads to being burned, and entering water inevitably leads to drowning. The Buddha perceives that within these very distinctions lies their inherent nature;

therefore, fire cannot burn him and water cannot drown him. Even regarding anger and joy, he constantly perceives them as having a single nature, and for this reason, these matters are also termed "equality.
If one understands that the nature is identical to the phenomena, one should know that this very nature is also termed "distinction."
These are the nature of fire, the nature of water, the nature of anger, and the nature of joy. These natures differ from the "phenomenal natures" (*vastu-svabhāva*) mentioned previously;

therefore, among the virtues of nature (*svabhāva-guṇa*), that which possesses the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is also called "differentiated nature" (*viśeṣa-svabhāva*). Alternatively, the character *xing* (nature) may be taken as the possessor of the differentiated nature.
Now it is said: the differentiation is that which is possessed, while nature is the possessor. Because the possessed is identical to the possessor, [the two are non-dual].

This refers to the differentiation of nature (*prakṛti-viśeṣa*). Alternatively, it may mean that the nature itself possesses differentiated phenomena; thus, it is said that these phenomena are non-sentient (*acetana*). Now, we respond:

the term "differentiation" fundamentally refers to sentient matters (*sattva-vastu*). Because [the nature] is able to possess them, it is called the "differentiation of the nature's virtues" (*prakṛti-guṇa-viśe�șa*).

This does not mean that within the nature's virtues there are differentiated phenomena and non-differentiated sentient beings. The above constitutes the discussion of the two—essence and function—and the middle and extremes. Thus says the commentator.

The conditions (*pratyaya*) and the aids (*upaniṣad*) constitute differentiation, while the primary cause (*hetu*) constitutes equality. Among these three—conditions, aids, and the primary cause—all three are differentiated.
Herein, the primary cause receives the designation of "differentiation" because it is set forth in contrast to the conditions and aids;
thus, the primary cause is made distinct from the conditions and aids. That the three factors are not identical is what is termed "differentiation. If, by means of the primary...
Therefore, the conditions (pratyaya) and the causes (hetu) are identical to the true cause (samyag-hetu). Thus, these conditions and causes are the same as the true cause.
The essence of the true cause is an equal, singular nature without differentiation. For this reason, the three dharmas are one body without distinction, all being entirely equal. Question:

Why is it stated specifically that "if by means of the true cause, it is identical to the conditions and causes"? Could it not also be explained conversely that "the conditions and causes are identical to the true cause"?

"No. He replied: "The primary cause (正因) accords with the essence of the Dharma (法體) and belongs to principle (理); it is the essence of 'identity' (即). The conditions (緣) and the aids (了) belong to phenomena (事); they are the essence of 'separation' (離).
Because the primary cause is identical [to the essence], the conditions and aids are also identical. Because the conditions and aids are separate, the primary cause is also separate.
As Jingxi said: 'The fundamental substance is not separate,' yet now we add 'not identical. That the fundamental substance is not separate is because..."
Because the substance of the true cause is fundamentally identical [to the other two], it reveals that the conditions and the understanding are not fundamentally identical;

now, by adding "not separate," some might say this is not so. To further clarify this by analogy with the categories of permanence and impermanence, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: Question:
"Seed" (*bīja*) has the meaning of "that which can produce"; its meaning accords with impermanence. "Nature" (*prakṛti*) has the meaning of "that which does not change";

its meaning accords with permanence. These two meanings are distinct; how can it be said that they accord? Answer: It is not surprising that the "contributory cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*) and the "efficient cause" (*hetu-hetu*) accord with the seed.

However, as for the "direct cause" (*samyag-hetu*) acceding with the seed, the meaning seems to be inconsistent. This passage precisely proceeds from the perspective of the essential nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), addressing both principle (*li*) and phenomenon (*shi*).
Regarding the distinctions within equality, how much more so when this very equality still possesses differentiation? One should understand both the phenomena (事) and the principle (理).

Whether they are identical or not identical, all are equal and cannot be conceptually distinguished. Furthermore, for the time being, let us establish a formal framework based on the distinction between equality and differentiation:
whether it be "both" or "neither," these do not exhaustively encompass all possibilities.

Regarding the text, there are two parts. First, concerning the question regarding "wisdom, the Buddha," and so forth: if the dharma of wisdom exists as awakening in contrast to non-awakening, this would belong to cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
However, since this cultivation refers to the essence of the mind of equality as the object of cultivation, it also belongs to the nature (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, when asked in terms of cultivation, it says "that which can awaken the pure mind"; when asked in terms of nature, it says...
"Pure mind is self-awakening" is the answer provided below that applies to both questions. Therefore, both cultivation (*xiu*) and nature (*xing*) can be termed "awakening.

The answer has three parts. First, the indication: although it is said that the two meanings are non-different in essence, "awakening pure mind" refers to contemplative wisdom (*guan-zhi*), while "pure mind is self-awakening" refers to the principle of truth (*di-li*). While the meanings of "truth" and "contemplation" are distinct, their essence is the same. Second, this...
The second section, the formal explanation of the meaning, has two parts. First, the delusion of truth giving rise to falsehood. This first part has two sub-sections.

First, the explanation based on the fundamental [cause], which refers to the three subtle states outside the realm (*dhātu*). Regarding "the mind transforms in dependence upon perfuming": this refers to the true mind of the ninth consciousness transforming through the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding "unawakened spontaneous movement":

this corresponds to the first (karma), second (transformation), and third (manifestation) [stages] in the *Awakening of Faith*; in the present text, it refers to the first (ignorance) and the second (delusion).

One contemplates three realms. Because it takes up objects (*artha*), its progression neither opens nor closes; this differs from the *Awakening of Faith*, which takes motion as its basis and regards motion as its activity (*karman*).
Here, taking non-awakening (*a-prabodha*) is ignorance (*avidyā*); motion is false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which is identical to the "activity" mentioned in the *Awakening of Faith*.

That which "manifests" corresponds to the transformation of the "characteristic of the seer" (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*) in the *Awakening of Faith*. That which is "empty in form" corresponds to the "manifestation" (*pratibhāsa*) in the *Awakening of Faith*.

These two together constitute the "objective realm" (*viṣaya*) of the present text. However, the subsequent section of the *Awakening of Faith* also combines both the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) as the objective realm;

thus it states: "All causes of defilement are termed ignorance (*avidyā*); the deluded mind is termed the karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*); and the deluded objective realm refers to the six sense-objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*)."
Second, the "illusory manifestations" section, which discusses the secondary branches at the end in three parts. First, it introduces the subsequent section by following from the preceding one:

due to the arising of objects as conditions, within the subsequent realm, these illusory manifestations serve as objects. If one discriminates them sequentially, they are the causes for the external realms;

they are the objects arising from fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodhi*). Based on these objects, the secondary branches arise; thus, non-awakening itself possesses the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the internal realm.
Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*): these two types of objective realms differ. To speak in terms of ultimate reality, there is only one objective realm;
it is divided into branch and root based on the distinction between the unreal and the real. If this realm is regarded as unreal, it belongs to the "outside the boundaries" (*sīmā-bahis*).

The moment one grasps this realm as real, it is immediately "inside the boundaries" (*sīmā-antaḥ*). Since this is the case for the objective realm, ignorance and deluded conceptualization (*avidyā-vikalpa*) are likewise so. Only...

First is ignorance (*avidyā*). Because it does not comprehend true reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is called the "root. Because it does not comprehend the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is called the "branch.
It is merely a single deluded thought (*vikalpa*): because one gives rise to deluded thoughts regarding true reality and clings to the existence of false appearances, it is called the "root";
because one gives rise to deluded thoughts based upon the dependent nature and clings to the existence of real characteristics, [it is called the branch].

It is said: "The branches and the extremities. However, these branches and the root are one entity yet distinct. Furthermore, there are two meanings. First, distinguishing them according to their respective phenomena:

one may only say that when reaching the root there are no branches; one cannot say that while at the extremities there is no root. For example, when coarse delusions fall away and one reaches the stage of subtle delusions, the coarse delusions then cease to exist.
Yet, while the coarse delusions are present, one cannot be separated from the subtle ones, because it is due to the coarse delusions that [the subtle] are obscured.
Because the mind has no separate essence. Second, by integrating phenomena through principle (*li*), one realizes that these branches and the root share the same pure mind as their essence.

Therefore, the coarse and the subtle, cause and effect, are fully exhausted only upon reaching the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), because the five abodes and two deaths are inseparable.
Question: It may be so that principle integrates [phenomena], but regarding the preceding discussion of phenomena themselves, how can the branches not be separate from the root? Is it only...
Question: Do the final delusions also extend to the final fruits? Answer: They also extend to the fruits. As previously stated, a single objective realm is distinguished as either empty or real.

If one regards the objective realm as empty, it then belongs to that which is outside the realms (*dhātu*). Is this not precisely because the final does not depart from the fundamental, and thus extends to the fruits? Question:
One should understand that the point where the retributions of the six paths are empty is precisely what lies outside the realms. If that is so, then conversely...

Question: Is there the matter of the six realms existing outside the realm [of reality] as something falsely reported? Answer: Their substance is one while their functions differ. Outside the realm, the phenomena of the six realms do not exist;

here, we take the substance of the six realms as being empty, which is identical in meaning to the empty fruits outside the realm. Second, "The semblance-consciousness" and below demonstrate the meaning in two parts.

First, the demonstration of the three characteristics: first, ignorance; second, deluded thought; third, deluded objects. Question: If it is by means of the semblance-consciousness, the semblance-form, and the semblance-...

Regarding the three "dusts" (*rajas*) and these three [factors], how are they correspondingly divided? Answer: That which resembles consciousness (*vijñapti*) encompasses both ignorance (*avidyā*) and delusive thought (*vikalpa*).
Taking the failure of that which resembles consciousness to understand [reality] as ignorance, and taking the delusive grasping of that which resembles consciousness as delusive thought;

the resemblance to form (*rūpa*) and the resemblance to dust combine to constitute the objective sphere (*viṣaya*). Question: What is the distinction between form and dust? Answer: In the present text, the primary retribution (*pratyupabhoga*) is taken as [the basis for form].

Form (*rūpa*) takes the retributive environment as its object. If one correlates this with the six gross delusions (*ṣaḍ-audārika*) from the *Awakening of Faith*, the semblance-consciousness constitutes ignorance (*avidyā*), which corresponds to the four gross delusions from the "mark of intellectualization" (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) to the "mark of calculating names" (*nāma-vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*). Because these four gross delusions are afflictive obscurations (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), they are neither karma nor retribution.

Ignorance thus becomes false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which is the fifth gross delusion, the "mark of the arising of karma. False conceptualization then becomes the false objective realm. This is...

The sixth is the characteristic of suffering bound by the six coarse karmas (*ṣaḍ-audārika-karma-bandhana-duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*). Those [six] were previously divided into six, but here they are combined into three.

Furthermore, within the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith), there is likewise its own system of inclusion, exclusion, expansion, and contraction. First, it presents nine characteristics, namely the three subtleties (*tri-sūkṣma*) and the six coarsenesses (*ṣaḍ-audārika*).

Next, it analyzes the five consciousnesses (*pañca-manas*), which excludes four of the six coarsenesses and retains only the three subtleties—the wisdom-characteristic (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the continuity-characteristic (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*). Finally, it analyzes the six defilements (*ṣaḍ-āśrava*). Regarding this...
Within the six coarse [delusions], the fifth and sixth are subsumed, merging with the third and fourth. Initially, ignorance arises from what resembles consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The text states that "what resembles consciousness" refers to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. Question: Regarding the terms "resembling consciousness" and "resembling objects," do they refer to the internal or external realms?

If one says they belong to the internal realm, then they would be substantially existent; how could they be called "resembling"? If one says they belong to the external realm, they should point to the eight consciousnesses; why then is it said...?

Regarding the six consciousnesses: the answer is that if one considers them from the perspective of their conventional status (*yathābhāga*), one falsely clings to the realms as being substantially real.

However, if one discusses them according to their actual reality (*tattvataḥ*), all objects are merely false appearances. Now, speaking from the perspective of actual reality, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are designated as "semblances.
As for the phrase "not clearly understanding" and so forth in the text, this passage specifically takes the aspect of non-understanding itself to be ignorance (*avidyā*). Second, with respect to...
"Below, 'not understanding' [means]: through ignorance, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is formed; this refers to taking the grasping subject itself as a false conceptualization.
Third, 'below, because of false conceptualization, a false object is formed': that which is taken to be a real entity is precisely the false object of grasping."
Second, regarding the false attachments, the following indicates that while the mind which is perfumed is impartial, the perfuming agents themselves are distinct.
This perfumed mind is no different from the previously mentioned fundamental pure mind.

Next, the following section explains the meaning by means of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). The preceding section merely indicated the general meaning, stating only that one fails to understand and thus falsely clings to things as being real.

Now, it is pointed out that this failure to understand is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*); this false clinging is called "deluded conceptualization" (*vikalpa*); and these real things are called "objects" (*viṣaya*).
The explanation is presented according to these names and characteristics in two parts. First, the three characteristics are explained. First, regarding ignorance, it is said: "delusion."
"Object" (*viṣaya*) refers to delusion regarding phenomena; it receives this name in contrast to delusion regarding principle (*tattva*). Regarding "delusion with respect to objects":

this name is given in contrast to "delusion with respect to causes. To explain: when fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) takes ignorance as its cause and gives rise to the three subtle states, this is "delusion with respect to causes.
When one is deluded regarding objects as conditions and gives rise to the six coarse states, this is "delusion with respect to conditions. This is because...
To falsely grasp at an empty object as being real is precisely a lack of understanding; this constitutes ignorance (*moha*) regarding the conditions of formation.

That conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the falsely constructed object are present in the text can be seen therein. Second, the fruit plants seeds and perfumes the mind. As for the meaning of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"Just as worldly clothing has no fragrance in itself, yet if a person perfumes it with incense, it then possesses a fragrant scent. However...

The arguments of that treatise shall be examined here in connection with the specific matters at hand. If, fundamentally, [the seeds] were truly non-existent, how could perfuming occur? That treatise elucidates four types of perfuming;
its details and omissions differ from those in the present text, so they need not be reconciled here—the seeker may understand this for themselves.

Now, I shall proceed directly with the current text and explain it by dividing it into two parts. First, regarding individual perfuming: there are generally four dharmas: first, ignorance; second, delusive conceptualization.

Third, the false objects; fourth, that which resembles consciousness (*vijñāna*). Question: Previously there were only three; why are there now four? Answer: Previously they were explained in combination.
Thus, that which resembles consciousness was combined within ignorance (*avidyā*) and delusive thought (*vikalpa*), and was therefore called "that which resembles consciousness.

The meaning of not understanding is precisely ignorance at the stage of the fruit; the meaning of the delusive grasping of that which resembles consciousness is precisely delusive thought. Now, they are explained separately.

Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, there are two differences regarding the fruit of the empty semblance: first, the *pratyaya-vedanīya* (direct retribution); second, the *niśraya-vedanīya* (dependent retribution).

Taken together, both belong to the realm of delusion (*mṛṣā-viṣaya*). When distinguished, the dependent is the objective field (*viṣaya*), and the direct is the semblance-consciousness (*pratibimba-vijñāna*).

The text consists of three parts; the first concerns ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding the terms "time of the fruit" and "time of the seed," these refer to the ignorance of the fruit and the seed, respectively, in terms of their fundamental and derivative aspects.

Treatise: There are both individual and relative [explanations]. If explained individually, the root and the branches each manifest separately: the root is the "seed" (hetu) and the branches are the "fruit" (phala).
Furthermore, ignorance and deluded conceptualization serve as the cause—the seed—while objective conditions serve as the fruit.

If explained relatively, the root serves as the seed because it is the beginning; since one is deluded regarding the present object, the root is the starting point. The branches are the fruit, arising from those objects.
Because of the arising of false attachments within the realms (*dhātu*), we now take the *pratipakṣa* (counter-argument) to subdivide the fruit. Regarding "the fruits and so forth":

if one were to establish the perfuming of seeds according to the tenets of the Hīnayāna, it would merely perfume the six consciousnesses and thus become a derivative branch. Now, following the perfect principle, it perfumes the True Mind and thus constitutes the root.
This is produced from the branches and fruits; the original seed is also called the "ignorance that dwells in the ground" (*mūlasthāny avidyā*).

The term "dwelling ground" (*bhūmi*) refers exclusively to the root [afflictions]. This is established based on a metaphor. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "These four dwellings are not fundamental delusions;

they are like branches and leaves that depend upon a tree rather than the earth. Therefore, the various different types of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the realm [of desire] are not called 'one place,' nor are they 'dwellings on the ground.
Furthermore, it cites the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*: 'The dwelling ground of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*... [text fragment].
Its power is the greatest; it can only be severed by the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom.

Since the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are likened to the branches and leaves, they merely abide upon the trunk of ignorance (*avidyā*), yet do not abide in the ground. Thus, ignorance itself is designated as the "ground-abiding" (*sthāna-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there are two meanings: first, regarding the four abidings outside the realms (*dhātu*), the views are taken as the "abider," like the tree, while ignorance is taken as the [ground].
"Abiding" (zhù). Taken collectively, these are termed "abiding grounds" (zhùdì). As Jingxi said: "Seeing is that which abides; ignorance is the ground.

Second, because ignorance is like a tree and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is like the earth, it is called "abiding ground. However, the actual attainment of the name "ground" derives from the nature of phenomena.
For example, although "non-abiding" (wǔzhù) applies generally to both the true and the deluded, when investigated in reality, non-abiding is entirely [the nature of phenomena].
True. However, because it is explained through the perfect [teaching], the true dharma is itself the source of delusion. Since the source is not distinct, delusion likewise has no abiding place.
Thus, Jingxi said: "Dharmatā is precisely non-abiding; non-abiding is precisely ignorance; ignorance, too, is non-abiding.
Is this not a definitive indication that non-abiding is indeed dharmatā? Because it is identical to ignorance, he says "also. Question: Regarding the stage of abiding...
The name already takes up the fundamental cause; the sixfold inquiry exhausts the source. Why, then, are the preceding four abidings also so named? Answer: There are two meanings here.

First, regarding the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-naya*): within the realm [of desire], they are not so named; outside the realm, they may be designated as such. Second, regarding the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-naya*): the sixfold inquiry exhausts the source.

Although one investigates from the preceding stages, which proceed sequentially according to their arising, when answering comprehensively from the perspective of the subsequent stage, they share the same source at that very place.
For this reason, the four abodes are all termed "grounds" (*bhūmi*). Question: If fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) is taken as the ground of abiding, why is it called "non-abiding"?

Answer: When considering identity while discussing separation, it differs from the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature); thus, it is named a "ground of abiding. When considering separation while discussing identity, it is one with the *dharmatā*;
thus, it is named "non-abiding. This takes the *dharmatā* as the ground. If, however, one were to take ignorance itself as the ground, [it would not be so called].
The ground of ignorance has no abode; because it is that upon which others abide, it is called a "ground of abiding" (*sthiti-bhūmi*). Question:

Within the realms [of existence], the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) do not accord with the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-zhi*); may they also be termed "grounds of abiding"? Answer: This meaning also applies. The *Mohe zhiguan* states:
"Attachment is precisely the four grounds of abiding. It can also obstruct wisdom, yet it is a response to a different mind. As for the response to liberation..."

Both. This passage likely refers to their respective domains. Generally, they abide within the stages of delusion and are termed the two types of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). In the Hīnayāna, they perfume the *kṣaṇika-vijñāna* (event-consciousness);

here, they become the *karmavijñāna* (action-consciousness). The three types of false objects resemble consciousness; in the Hīnayāna, they perfume the mind and, by depending on it, attain abiding; here, they become seeds that depend on the eight consciousnesses for their abiding.
As for the absence of the term "resembling consciousness" (*sadr̥śa-vijñāna*) in the text, it should be understood as being subsumed under the term "resembling objects" (*sadr̥śa-viṣaya*).

Second, "Now, below this, [the four dharmas] mutually perfuming one another" has two parts. First, the general indication: regarding the fact that the preceding four dharmas each perfume individually, this refers to the function of their respective divisions;

as for the fact that these four dharmas now perfume together, this discusses the meaning of their mutual reliance. Second, "What is it? and so forth, which provides the specific indication, has two parts. First, the mutual perfuming of the branches and the root within the self-nature:

the "resemblance-consciousness" (pratibhāsa-vijñāna) is the retributive aggregate (vipāka-skandha); "ignorance" (avidyā) is the lack of comprehension; and "delusive thought" (vikalpa) is the capacity for grasping.
The delusive object is that which is grasped. These four [factors] combine and perfuse the pure mind, manifesting as the fruit of illusory forms.
Second, furthermore, the root treatise [and its commentary] together consist of two parts. First, the presentation of the meaning has two sections. First, the commonality of cause and fruit:

because the preceding root text states that "the mind, depending on perfuming, undergoes transformation; through non-awakening, it moves spontaneously, manifesting illusory forms. In this passage, only ignorance and...

Karma is the cause of these two dharmas; together with their respective permeations (*vāsanā*), they manifest as the fruit of illusory appearances. Now, adding seeds to these two dharmas, these three dharmas act as causes that collectively permeate the pure mind (*viśuddha-citta*), manifesting as the fruit of illusory appearances.
The text is divided into three parts. First, it demonstrates that seeds coexist with ignorance (*avidyā*), which involves two points:

first, because seeds abide in dependence upon ignorance; second, because [seeds... *(Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Yogācāra philosophy, likely discussing the relationship between seeds, ignorance, and the manifestation of deluded phenomena. The translation reflects the available portion of the text.)*
If the consciousness (vijñāna) were absent, ignorance (*avidyā*) could not manifest its fruit alone.
Second, "if it were absent" refers to ignorance coexisting with karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). Third, "if it were absent" refers to seeds coexisting with karma-consciousness;
here too there are two meanings: first, that seeds cannot manifest their fruit alone; second, that seeds abide in dependence upon karma-consciousness. Therefore, it is said: "it is also thus."
The self-substance is not established. Question: Previously, when the branches and the extremities co-influence, why is there a semblance of consciousness and delusive objects while no seeds exist?
Now, when the root and the source co-influence, why do seeds exist while there is no semblance of consciousness or delusive objects? Answer:
This is distinguished according to the different meanings of "branch" and "root. When the seeds of ignorance first begin to delude, they rely upon the pure mind.

[The consciousness] arises. It does not rely on a semblance-consciousness (*pratibimba-vijñāna*). Although the fundamental karmic consciousness (*mūla-karma-vijñāna*) can manifest objects, it does not delusively grasp these empty objects as real.

Therefore, regarding this fundamental [consciousness], these two [types of seeds] are not considered to be perfumers (*vāsaka*). As for the perfuming agents of the derivative [consciousnesses], they do not denote seeds;
therefore, they are not discussed. Question: Since the four dharmas that collectively perfume are all derivative, why is it said that when the fruit is produced, it is called "empty" (*śūnya*)?

Question: What is the nature of this? Answer: While the perfuming [agent] is minor, the accomplishment of the meaning of the fruit is substantial; speaking in terms of reality, these two are thus. Below [the text] states that within the fruit, the cause is present.
The passage says, "resembling consciousness and resembling objects. That which is "false" refers to the seeds within the fruit that contain the cause.

"Ignorance" (avidyā) refers to the ignorance that contains the cause within the fruit. "Deluded attachment" refers to the karmic consciousness (karma-vijñāna) that contains the cause within the fruit.
The two characters "still containing" (huan ju) apply throughout the subsequent text.

Because the three causes—the seeds of ignorance and karmic consciousness—jointly produced the fruit in the preceding section, the fruit now still contains these three causes. This, then, proceeds entirely from the root.

This is the fundamental exposition. Furthermore, this passage is similar to the preceding one; it takes up what was previously stated to initiate what follows, explaining how objects arise through conditions within the realms, appearing as consciousness and leading to false attachments.
Second, this section concludes the preceding discussion. Regarding the phrase "briefly explained":

first, it briefly explains that the movement of non-awakening (*abodha*) serves as the cause for the two phenomena, without detailing the seed (*bīja*) as the cause; second, it briefly explains the manifestation of false appearances.

Yet it was not explained in detail that [the result] manifests through combination. Third, it was briefly stated that the result is produced by means of causes, but it was not explained in detail that the result itself still possesses the causes.
Question: Why were seeds previously omitted and left unmentioned? Answer: For the time being, this was based on the initial stage of delusion; seeds had not yet been discussed.
However, the doctrine of seeds is merely a provisional teaching; in ultimate reality, all things manifest from the nature (prakṛti). Thus, a sutra says:
"The karmic formations of all suffering are inconceivable."
Second, the conclusion below: "In this way, the seed and fruit arise in succession. First, regarding the discussion of seed and fruit in relation to the branches and the root:
the initial passage follows from the preceding description of the empty forms outside the realm, giving rise to ignorance within the realm; this is precisely the seed producing the fruit.
Next, in the explanation of the "perfuming of the mind at the level of the secondary branches," it says:

"Because the fruit, namely *avidyā* (ignorance), perfumes the mind, it causes the mind to be non-awakened," which refers to the fruit giving rise to the seed. In the explanation of the "fundamental [ignorance]," it says:

"Therefore, within the empty semblance, there is still the presence of that which resembles consciousness," which refers to the seed again giving rise to the fruit. Thus, in both cases regarding the secondary branches, the relationship between seed and fruit is discussed individually.
Regarding the fruit: within the fundamental [nature], the fruit is the fruit of empty forms, and the seed is the cause consisting of the three dharmas—the seeds of ignorance and karmic consciousness.
From the cause, the fruit is produced; the fruit, in turn, possesses the cause. This means that the seed can produce the fruit, and the fruit can produce the seed.
Since the branches and twigs already take the combination of the four factors as their cause to manifest the fruit of a hollow appearance, this is the case of "the seed producing the fruit.

If one applies this analogy to the root, then within this very fruit there again exists the cause consisting of the four factors of the branches and twigs; this is the case of "the fruit producing the seed."
Therefore, the general conclusion states: "The fruits and seeds arise from one another.

Second, regarding the subsequent section on "encountering [the truth] below" to extinguish delusion and return to the True: first, extinguishing the delusive afflictions within the realm; second, extinguishing the delusive afflictions outside the realm.

This explains the accomplishment of the two types of awakening. Question: Why is it that the two types of awakening are explained specifically during the section on extinguishing the delusions outside the realm? Answer: Because [they arise] from...

Regarding the meaning of "the true gives rise to the delusory," there are generally three points. First, although the two designations "true" and "delusory" exist, when one speaks of the true giving rise to the delusory, in that very place there is neither a subject that gives rise nor an object that is given rise to;
this is because while the names of the true and the delusory differ, their essence is one. Second, from the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), ignorance arises as the delusory;

regarding this arisen delusion, one need not distinguish between branches and roots, or whether it is external or internal to the realms. Third, from the true nature of phenomena, the delusory arises; within this arising delusion, there is no distinction between the primary and the secondary, nor between the internal and the external.
Because the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought (*saṃjñā-kleśa*), as well as ignorance (*avidyā*), are of the same essence.
Thirdly, from the true nature of the Middle Way, the delusion of ignorance beyond the realms (*dharmadhātu-bāhya-avidyā*) arises, forming the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, from the deluded grasping of that ignorance which takes the unreal for the real, the delusion of the afflictions of view and thought within the realms (*dharmadhātu-antaḥ-dṛṣṭi-kleśa-saṃjñā-kleśa*) arises, forming the discriminating nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Therefore, the principle of extinguishing delusion and returning to truth also has three aspects. If...

According to the first meaning, there is no delusion to be extinguished and no truth to which one may return. According to the second meaning, the extinction of afflictions within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is itself the extinction [of those] outside the realm of phenomena.

According to the third meaning, regarding the simultaneous and gradual entry: first, one extinguishes that which is within the realm of phenomena; at this stage, prior to abiding [in the stages], one has not yet seen the true nature (*tathatā*).

It is only upon reaching the extinction of that which is outside the realm of phenomena that one distinguishes the two types of awakening. First, regarding the extinction of the two delusions within the realm of phenomena...
Discussing the extinction of delusions solely within the context of the *dhātu*, there are four points. First, regarding "meeting a friend who provides clarification, all are of one kind":

this refers to the fruit of perfect extinction (*pariniṣpanna-nivṛtti*), which differs in meaning from the previous teachings. Because one knows the source of delusion, its flow ceases of itself; therefore, it can be said that "all are produced by the One Mind.

Second, "hearing this and below" refers to practicing contemplation based on what has been heard. In the subsequent section on practicing contemplation of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of the imagined), it says: "But if one can..."

One knows that objects are empty. Third, from "if this" onwards, the explanation establishes the removal of obstacles. These are the ignorance-obscuration (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*), the affliction-obscuration (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*), and the object-obscuration (*viṣaya-āvaraṇa*).
Once such an understanding is formed, these three obstacles are removed. Below, regarding the section on the cessation gate within the nature of differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it says:

"Because the attachment to reality ceases, this is the means of removal. At the stage of fruition, the ignorance that deludes regarding phenomena, along with discursive thought (*vikalpa*) and so forth, are eliminated.
4. At that time, the following section concerns the benefits gained through wisdom. Within the section on the benefits gained through the nature of discernment (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it says:
"Because the activity of the wisdom that perceives no objects (*anartha-jñāna*) follows the movements of the mind, this is precisely the attainment of benefit."

Second, although the following section distinguishes between the two delusions as being extinguished together in relation to the realms beyond, there are two reasons for this: first, by means of principle, one integrates the delusions; the two delusions are of one essence.

If the branches and tips are extinguished, the root is also eliminated. Second, when the branches are completely eliminated, it must first be understood that the root arises from the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*);
the aspect of the root is empty in essence, while the delusory branches are taken as real. Now, when the attachment to their reality perishes, it is said that the branches and tips are eliminated.
For those who eliminate the grasping at reality, this is done by knowing that the root is empty; thus, this very knowledge is what extinguishes the root.

Therefore, when the branches are extinguished, the root is also eliminated. The text consists of two parts. First, a direct explanation of their simultaneous extinction. This has three sections. First, ignorance.
Second, delusive conceptualization; third, the objective realm. Regarding these three meanings, first the commonalities are discussed, followed by a detailed analysis.

Within the section on ignorance (*avidyā*), the initial discussion of commonalities is intended to demonstrate that when the derivative, secondary delusions are extinguished, the fundamental [ignorance] is also eliminated. Why is this so?
Because one is deluded by false appearances, they arise from the single nature; yet that which exists is non-existent, and this is termed the persistence of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Now, by eliminating the secondary (the "branch"), one is first able to realize that false appearances are identical to the nature. Is this not also the elimination of the fundamental ignorance? As the text says:

"Although it is known that because the object is false, it is said that ignorance is extinguished at the time of the fruit"—this refers to the removal of the secondary branches. It is still [a matter of] seeing false appearances.
"Existence" means that the root is present. "Existence is non-existence, culminating in the fact that there is only the single mind":

if one relies on this knowledge to comprehend ignorance, it is precisely the dharmatā through which ignorance is eliminated. Because one does not know this principle, it is also called the "ignorance of the stage of the son" (*putrakāla-avidyā*) and so forth;
now, by means of this lack of knowledge, knowledge is revealed. If one does not know, it is non-existence.

This is clear. Furthermore, now that the initial mind extinguishes the branches and their extremities, since this principle is known, is it not the case that the extinction of the fruit also removes the seed?

Next, [the text] merely states that it is subtle and inferior, and thus redundant and sparse. If one says they are extinguished together, why was it previously stated that "the fruit is the extinction of ignorance"?

Therefore, it is redundant and sparse to say that it is merely more subtle than the preceding ignorance of deluded phenomena; hence, when speaking of the fruit, it is simply called the extinction of ignorance. This is how it should be understood.

It is understood that, in terms of horizontal reduction, the two delusions are extinguished simultaneously; yet, in terms of vertical stages, it is argued that the branches and their extremities are extinguished first.

Although one understands through insight that ignorance exists only as non-existence, as long as this non-existence has not been realized, one still perceives it as existing. Question: Is there a difference between insight and the [spiritual] stage? Answer:

Insight is the perfect interfusion of phenomena according to the Dharma, whereas the stage follows the thickness or thinness of one's emotional afflictions. If insight conforms to these afflictions, [it remains at the level of the stage].
If they are distinguished, then their liberations are also diverse. If the stages are clarified in terms of the Dharma, then the stages are also sudden and so forth.

For now, however, I shall distinguish the stages according to the marvelous capacities and discuss liberation in terms of the Dharma; therefore, I clarify them in contrast. As for "ignorance regarding phenomena," this is contrasted with "ignorance regarding principle."

However, regarding the dharmas of delusion (*kleśa*), they receive the names "principle" (*li*) and "phenomenon" (*shi*); their meanings are not uniform. If we discuss the branches and the root separately:

among the derivative branches, *dṛṣṭi* (view) is the delusion of principle, while *vitarka* (thought) is the delusion of phenomenon. This is because *dṛṣṭi* constitutes false conceptualizations regarding the principles of illusory dharmas, thereby obstructing true principle;

whereas *vitarka* consists of the phenomena of greed, delusion, and distraction, thereby obstructing the state of meditative concentration. Since the roots themselves are designated as distinct views...

Consider it differently. Otherwise, the phenomena, principles, meanings, and categories would all be considered merely "branches. If one discusses them in terms of branches versus the root, then one knows that in the present text, *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *saṃjñā* (thoughts) are treated as "phenomena" (*shi*), while ignorance (*avidyā*) is treated as "principle" (*li*).
Furthermore, views and thoughts are called "phenomena" because they arise from being deluded by the illusory manifestations of ignorance;

since these illusory manifestations are phenomena, they are termed "delusion regarding phenomena. This is because the afflictions are termed "delusion regarding objects," as the Hīnayāna states: "This..."

The delusions of view and thought are confused regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The Mahāyāna exegesis states that the essence of both the ultimate and conventional extremes is ignorance;

therefore, they are called "delusion regarding phenomena" (*dharma-moha*). This reveals that the fundamental [ignorance] arises from being confused regarding the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and is thus called "delusion regarding principle" (*tattva-moha*).

The above analysis is based on distinguishing between these two types of affliction. If one takes the three types of afflictions as a whole for comparative discussion, then the *paryavasthāna* (afflictions like greed and anger) constitute the phenomenal aspect.

The two delusions constitute the principle (*li*). The *Record of the Vimalakīrti* states: "Because the dust-like delusions do not obstruct the principle; the four abidings obstruct the truth, while ignorance obstructs the middle.

Furthermore, within this, ignorance constitutes the principle and the two delusions constitute the phenomena (*shi*). The *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti* states: "Delusion regarding the principle is to be deluded about the Middle Way;
delusion regarding the phenomena is to be deluded about the Two Truths. This is the delusion regarding the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Moreover, if the three delusions are each...

The Treatise states that both [ignorance] pertain to both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*). For instance, because the afflictions of seeing and cultivation do not realize that their own essence is the conventional nature of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), they are called "delusion regarding phenomena.

Because they do not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are called "delusion regarding principle" (i.e., ignorance). If one is deluded regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional (*prajñapti*), such that their own essence is not wisdom but an obstruction, it is termed "delusion regarding phenomena.
If one is deluded regarding the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), it is termed "delusion regarding principle. As the Great Master said: "Both are..."
Delusion. Taking principle as an obstruction to wisdom; furthermore, it is said that both are delusions regarding phenomena and constitute the "dust-sand" obstructions to wisdom.
