If one is deluded regarding the path of supernatural powers and transformations, this is called delusion regarding phenomena. If one is deluded regarding the samādhis of conventional truth, this is called delusion regarding principle.

Furthermore, if explained according to the teachings, the afflictions of the *Tripiṭaka* and *Pratyekabuddha* vehicles are phenomena, while the afflictions of the *Vaipulya* and *Pūrṇa* (Perfect) vehicles are principle. This is because they pertain to the realms within and beyond the triple world.
They are distinct in their separation.

Furthermore, one does not descend into false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). The first discussion concerns this sameness. Moreover, because one does not cling to empty forms as real, it is said that "false conceptualization is extinguished.

This refers to the extinction of the false conceptualization of the branch-like, derivative consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). It is like seeing an empty appearance and yet claiming there is a separate mind.
"Those who [hold such views]": the karmic consciousness is able to grasp, meaning that it regards these illusory marks as distinct from the pure mind. "This grasping is also a false conception":

because it is contrasted with the secondary manifestations (the branches), it is said to be "also" [a false conception]. It is also called "illusory marks" because the secondary manifestations grasp at reality as their mark.
Now, these are empty marks (*śūnyalakṣaṇa*). They are not merely called deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*); therefore, it is said that they are "also called" [deluded thoughts].

If, according to this meaning, there still remains a separate mind that falsely clings to these empty marks, then the deluded thoughts of the fundamental karmic consciousness (*mūlakarmavijñāna*) will not be eliminated.

However, when one now extinguishes these derivative deluded thoughts, one is able to realize that the deluded thoughts and empty marks of the fundamental consciousness are all of one single nature (*ekasvabhāva*), no different from the pure mind (*viśuddhacitta*).
Therefore, the two delusions are removed together. Next, regarding those who are further estranged: this is also discussed in terms of stages vertically, as intended in the preceding passage.
Thirdly, concerning the objects below this: the initial discussion is the same. Because they do not know that the object is the pure mind, the characteristics of their faculties are not uniform;
thus, the fundamental delusory objects have not been removed. Now, at the time of removing the secondary delusory objects, the principle of understanding is likewise the same.
One realizes that all fundamental delusory objects are identical to the pure mind. Since every manifestation is identical to the nature, all myriad objects are one.
Is it not the case, then, that the fundamental delusory objects are simultaneously eliminated? Yet now it is said that they appear different from the mind;

this differs from what was previously stated regarding a "separate mind," for the former referred to the subject that grasps, while the present follows the object that is grasped. The subsequent elaborations follow the text.

Second, the conclusion of this section has two parts. First, regarding the summary of the commonality: the phrase "by these" indicates that in the preceding text, both the subsidiary and the primary afflictions must necessarily be eliminated together.
If there were no such statement in the preceding text, why would it say here, "by this, they are also partially eliminated"?

If [the afflictions] were not eliminated gradually but rather simultaneously, this would be an oblique explanation based on understanding, using the subsidiary to manifest the primary. Second, [it continues]: "But..."

Regarding the passage "The secondary [defilements] are bound together yet sparse; however, when their characteristics are subtle and equal," this is discussed in terms of the vertical progression through stages, wherein the coarse impurities fall away first.

Second, regarding the passage "Now, for the time being... and so forth: this explains that by means of the cessation of the defilements of the fruit, the defilements of the seed are subsequently extinguished, thereby demonstrating that both types of defilement are extinguished simultaneously at the initial moment of the Path.

Why is this? Because although the previous section demonstrated the severing of the branches and tips, it was done in terms of the mind of liberation, wherein both types of defilement are extinguished together.
Because the characteristics [of this] are difficult to perceive, I shall now again explain it by way of the meaning of the stages (*avasthā*).

Since the extinction of the secondary afflictions (*śākhā-kleśa*) leads to the extinction of the fundamental afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*), this demonstrates that both the secondary and fundamental afflictions are extinguished simultaneously through their respective resolutions. The text consists of two parts: first, the presentation; second, the explanation, beginning with "This meaning... and so forth.

First, the explanation of how the extinction of the afflictions of the fruit leads to the extinction of the afflictions of the seed. This has three parts: first, the formal proposition; second, the actual explanation, beginning with "The two meanings... and so forth.

The second section is explained in two parts. First, regarding the wisdom that can eliminate [delusion]: it is identical to the wisdom of ultimate emptiness as the means of elimination, for it differs from a partial emptiness.

Therefore, the wisdom that eliminates the derivative (the branches) can also eliminate the root. Second, "The second" refers to the following: because coarse delusions have perished, subtle delusions become thin and faint.
After the coarse delusions have perished, although the ignorance of the causal stage (*bīja-avidyā*) continues to permeate the pure mind moment by moment, it nevertheless arises again...
Regarding the "abiding stage" (*bhūmi*): since the coarse [delusions] have already been extinguished through illumination, the afflictions that arise are likewise slight and subtle.

It is said that because there are no coarse delusions acting as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*), one should know that this meaning refers to the spontaneous severance of delusions upon entering the first *bhūmi*; therefore, they are described as "slight and subtle.
If coarse delusions had not already perished beforehand, how could there be such spontaneous severance and extinction? This concludes the third point. The second is as in the passage on "delusion."

The following section reveals that the two delusions are extinguished simultaneously in two parts. First, the initial presentation: by citing the vertical progression of the final stage, it reveals the horizontal simultaneity of the initial understanding.

Second, the subsequent explanation clarifies the meaning of simultaneous extinction: because the "subordinate" (sub-) ignorance is extinguished part by part, the wisdom that is free from objects likewise increases progressively, ultimately causing the ignorance of the "resultant" (phala) stage to be extinguished;
thus, through the extinction of the subordinate understanding, the extinction of the resultant realization is achieved.

Second, regarding the delusions below the stage of self-delusion that exist outside the realm of cessation, the two types of awakening are explained as three. First, the Dharma [is discussed] in two parts:

first, concerning partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*), it clarifies awakening within the pure mind; second, concerning ultimate realization (*niṣṭhā*), it clarifies the pure mind’s own self-awakening.

Now, awakening within the pure mind takes cultivation as its merit, whereas the pure mind’s own self-awakening takes the nature (*prakṛti*) as its merit; therefore, they are equal in terms of the stage of partial realization.
Up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). In the text, it simply speaks of "dustless wisdom" (*nir-rajas-jñāna*), which is precisely that which can know those illusory forms;

its essential nature is solely the one mind. Because this meaning belongs to the awakening to the pure mind, and in order to distinguish the ultimate [fruit], it first demonstrates the wisdom of partial realization at the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
Therefore, it says, "This wisdom is itself the Vajra," and so on, up to, "Once this wisdom is perfected," and so forth.
Thereafter, this wisdom further perfumes the mind to bring about the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Therefore, it is said that "habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are likewise destroyed accordingly, until even their empty forms are forever extinguished. Having thus attained the ultimate realization of the pure mind, this stage marks the cessation of cultivation and entry;
thus, the pure mind itself constitutes self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana*). Jingxi says: "Apart from True Suchness (*tathatā*),..."
All practices and entries belong to the provisional (upāya). This is intended to mean that the ultimate fulfillment of the *tathatā* at the stage of fruition is the "Pool of Coolness.

This section has two parts: first, regarding those abiding above [the stages]; second, regarding the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*). The first part also has two sections. First, it demonstrates the basis for what is to be eliminated:
because karma and afflictions are thin, internal consciousness is sharp, and external forms are subtle, the grasping at reality does not arise.

What is called "together" (俱) refers to what is commonly taught both internally and externally. Regarding that which "resembles form and resembles consciousness," this now pertains to its own respective category;

it is called "resembling" (*sadr̥śa*) rather than being identical (*sama*). The preceding text pointed to the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses]. In the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* (*Catur-smr̥tyupasthāna*) and the *Subcommentary* (*Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is cited as saying:

"There is only a single consciousness, which is further divided into two kinds: first, the conceptualizing [consciousness]; second, the non-conceptualizing [consciousness]. The conceptualizing consciousness is termed 'discernment' (*vijñāna*)."
Consciousness. That which is non-discriminative is called "consciousness resembling objects" (*viṣayābhāsa-vijñāna*). All worlds are constituted by this consciousness resembling objects;

one should know that this includes the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and so forth. As for what is meant by "consciousness cognizing consciousness," this refers to delusion upon delusion, which is identical to the "nature of discrimination" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) discussed below.
Non-discriminative consciousness is the eighth consciousness, termed "consciousness resembling objects."

This is indeed the same as the current text. The previous identification of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses as "semblance-consciousness" follows their actual nature (*vastu*), rather than their respective divisions.
Without this meaning, the two passages would be difficult to reconcile. In the section beginning with "The second, 'no objects,' etc.," it demonstrates the wisdom capable of extinction;

this is precisely the wisdom that awakens the pure mind. "Returning to permeate the mind" means permeating the mind with wisdom. The subsequent section beginning with "The second, 'in this way,' etc."...

"Awakening to the ground where ignorance dwells and exhausting its obscurity" means that the obscurity is exhausted. "That which is able to equalize" refers to the function of stainless wisdom, which can awaken to the pure mind and realize that phenomena external to the mind are empty objects;
thus, returning to one's original nature, there is only the single mind.

Second, regarding this wisdom, the following section clarifies the pure mind of self-awakening from the perspective of ultimate realization, which is further divided into two parts. First, the fruit of realization is demonstrated.

As for the phrase "this wisdom" and so forth, it refers to the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is free from dust and is termed "Vajra-wisdom. There are two meanings to the term "free from dust."

First, there are no real objects, which reveals that objects are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Second, there are no images of objects, which reveals that objects are merely the Truth (*tattva*).

Here, we follow the latter meaning. "Absence of objects" refers to the Dharma; it is established by way of being free from faults. "Vajra" refers to a metaphor; it is named after the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, the wisdom of the absence of objects is pervasive, as it encompasses both the True and the Semblance [stages]. The Vajra-wisdom is restricted, as it pertains specifically to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Alternatively, both may be pervasive; this wisdom...

"Having been accomplished" refers to the accomplishment of the wisdom of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-jñāna*). "Thereby further perfuming the mind" means that this wisdom is used to further perfume the ultimately pure mind.

Regarding "the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of a single moment of ignorance": first, the term "single moment" refers to the active affliction (*paryavasthāna*) itself, which is designated as "habit-energy," because the final, subtlest moment of ignorance is termed "habit-energy. Second, it refers to a single moment of ignorance...

Furthermore, one practices within the household; because ignorance is finally exhausted therein, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are accordingly destroyed, and the fruit of wondrous enlightenment is attained.
If one seeks proof through this passage, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Habitual tendencies are precisely the final grade of ignorance."
Furthermore, the "homogeneous habit-energies" (*nāma-vāsanā*) cultivated within the household constitute the underlying propensities (*anuśaya*). Why is this?

If it is said that the final grade of ignorance—the actual propensities (*mūla-anuśaya*)—has been exhausted, leaving only the homogeneous habit-energies of ignorance, then since the most subtle ignorance has already been eliminated, its habit-energies ought likewise to perish accordingly.
How could they persist once the actual propensities have been fully exhausted? This refers to the seed-habit-energies.
"Destroying" means the thorough exhaustion of the causes of transformation. "The empty forms are forever extinguished" means the ultimate disappearance of the effects of transformation.
Regarding the third point, "the two empty forms: the pure mind awakens by itself," first, it is shown that the essence of the mind is quiescent illumination; "mind" here refers to the pure mind.
Illumination is itself awakening. Because the tranquil essence of the pure mind awakens by itself, it is called "tranquil illumination.
Regarding "realizing true suchness through its essence": because one awakens to the pure mind, it is termed "realizing true suchness through its function";

since the function realizes the essence, now, when the pure mind awakens by itself, it is termed "realizing true suchness through its essence," because the essence itself is self-realized. The phrase "How are these two... and so forth explains the two. First, regarding...
This is the explanation of the non-duality of subject and object. The section beginning with "How can there be two? explains that outside of wisdom (*jñāna*), there is no reality (*tattva*).
If there were a reality external to wisdom, one could say that wisdom awakens to a pure mind; however, since there is no reality distinct from wisdom, reality itself is wisdom.
Therefore, the pure mind is self-awakened. Third, this is the conclusion below. It concludes the preceding meaning by means of the non-duality of essence and function.

The essence is the pure mind; the function is awakening-wisdom. If essence and function were two, one could say that "by means of the function, one awakens to the essence," which would mean awakening to the pure mind.
Now, since the function is identical to the essence, the self-nature is self-awakened and the self-substance is self-realized; this is precisely the pure mind.
Regarding self-awakening, the wise also say: "The internal nature illuminates itself; it does not depend on knowledge from another. The two following metaphors are as follows:
water being still is its moisture; internal illumination is its light. Moisture is the essence and illumination is the function;

since the meanings of essence and function differ, it is said that the meanings of illumination and moisture differ. Yet, they are always profoundly still and one because both illumination and moisture are water; therefore, illumination and moisture [are identical].
This awakening is the pure mind. Moistening and illuminating is the self-awakening of this pure mind.

The three minds also merge with the lower [state]. Moistening is the essence and illumination is the function; this is the differentiation of the meanings of stillness and illumination. Yet, being eternally profound and one, the essence is fused and non-dual.

Because illumination and moistening are moistening and illumination, they are the identity of illumination and stillness, and stillness and illumination. Since illumination is itself moistening, it is the identity of illumination and stillness.
Compliance with the essence means that moisture is itself illumination; thus, it is the compliant function of quiescent illumination.

Illumination within moisture is illumination of its own essence, which is called "awakening to the pure mind. Moisture illuminating itself is the essence illuminating itself, which is called "the pure mind’s self-awakening."
Third, the concluding statement: "Therefore, it is said that the two meanings are one essence. This is because the initial response stated:
"Although two meanings are spoken of, their essence is not distinct. "Taking non-discriminative wisdom as the awakener" concludes that awakening resides in the pure mind.
"The pure mind possesses the nature of wisdom" concludes that the pure mind is self-awakened.
Fourth, this concludes the major section on the Buddha-nature of Prajñā from the perspective of the lower [stages].
Second, "Furthermore, from this point on" refers to the Buddha-nature of liberation as the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

Furthermore, the passage from "this pure mind" to "the nature of skillful application" points to the nature capable of possessing merit and skillfulness. From "for the sake of pure karma" to "the two Buddhas of retribution and response" is entirely... [omitted].
The nature fully endowed with merit constitutes the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (recompense Buddha), which is the recompense of the marks and signs as numerous as motes of dust.
The nature fully endowed with skillful means constitutes the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (response Buddha), which is the response manifested according to sentient beings.
These two constitute the matter of liberation from the nature of complete liberation. Therefore, taking this mind as the Buddha-nature is to take it as equal and pure.
The mind that constitutes the nature of the two Buddhas—retribution and response—is as follows.

Second, there is again a further detailed explanation below. First, the explanation of the essence has two parts. First, regarding the cultivation of merit, it is explained that the essence is revealed as awakening by means of counteracting non-awakening.
This has four sections. First, regarding the cultivation of counteractive measures: furthermore, because non-awakening is extinguished, the mind is said to be awakening. [This refers to] extinction.
It is ignorance (*avidyā*). Because the movement of its meaning has ceased, it is said that "the mind is unmoving"; this means the cessation of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).

Because false appearances have dissolved, it is said that "the mind is without characteristics" (*animitta*); this means the cessation of objective realms (*viṣaya*). It is because of ignorance, deluded thoughts, and objective realms that this essence of the mind functions as awakening, as cessation, and as being without characteristics.
Second, from "However, this... onwards, the text discusses the essential nature itself. Now, regarding this essence of the mind...
It is not awakening, nor even non-characteristic (*animitta*). If this were so, then the essence of mind could not be taken as awakening; how then could it be called Buddha-nature?
Therefore, the third section, beginning with "Although," explains the reason for this. It correctly employs the names in opposition to designate equality.
"Although" is a phrase that acknowledges the preceding while introducing the subsequent, a term used for both concession and refutation. Although its essence is thus... [it is not].
Regarding non-awakening and awakening: if one speaks of this essence of mind as "awakening" in contrast to the cessation of non-awakening, there is no impediment whatsoever.
Fourth, this concludes the explanation of how it receives its name; here, "awakening" is discussed in terms of the essence of the mind emerging from obstacles through the application of antidotes.

It is precisely that which is neither awakening nor non-awakening that is named "awakening. It is an awakening that does not awaken through the functioning of cognition; rather, it is the awakening of awakening that constitutes awakening. Second, furthermore, below:

the nature-virtue (xingde) is fundamentally without non-awakening, and thus the manifestation of the mind is called awakening. Part two has two sections. First, the direct explanation has four parts. First, regarding the fundamental absence of non-awakening:
this does not concern the cultivation of virtues as a remedy for non-awakening; it truly concerns the nature-virtue being fundamentally without [non-awakening].
Awakening is said to be the awakening of the mind; "primordial stillness" (*benji*) is another name for "immovability. "Equanimity" (*pingdeng*) is a synonym for "signlessness" (*animitta*).

Although karma moves, it manifests as stillness and equanimity, which is likewise identical to non-awakening. Its nature is fundamentally non-existent; how could it be extinguished through cultivation?
