In its own right, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) also possesses phenomena, transcendence, the provisional, the real, and differentiation as well as non-differentiation.

If one were to discuss the Perfect Teaching solely in contrast to the partial and the complete regarding a single meaning—such as the coarse and the subtle—one would fail to provide a self-examination from the standpoint of the Perfect itself.

Therefore, it is not permissible to claim that the phenomena of the Provisional and the essence of the Provisional within the Perfect Teaching are coarse; for by losing the true nature of the Dharma (dharmatā), one becomes obstructed in the gateway of meaning. It is not merely that the meaning is hindered.

Furthermore, I fear you have not yet mastered the Patriarchal Teachings. Why is this? It is because Jingxi clearly permitted that one may discuss the "coarse" and the "sublime" from the perspective of the Perfect [Teaching] itself.
Thus he said: "If one examines it within the inconceivable, one may also discuss what is sublime and what is not.

For example, among the Three Virtues (tridharmadhātu), if explained according to the first three *siddhāntas*, their meaning corresponds to the coarse—namely, the Three Virtues as the Worldly, the Liberative, and the Productive. Regarding the *prajñā*...
If one destroys evil, it is therefore called coarse; only upon seeing the Dharma-body does it first become termed "wondrous.
As it is with these three virtues, so it is with the remaining nine. Now, following this analogy, it is said: since the ten kinds of triple dharmas are thus, all dharma-gates are likewise.

Therefore, the provisional within the perfect—when taken as its own substance—is coarse; yet when it is identical to the real, it is wondrous. The provisional receives the name "wondrous" by analogy with the preceding analysis of merit and function. Thus it concludes.

The two meanings of the Dharma can be understood through reflection. However, there was once a senior scholar who heard me establish that the provisional [teachings] are identical in essence to the real;

he claimed that this essence is coarse because it is identical to the real, and therefore subtle. At first, he adamantly refused to accept that the essence of the provisional within the Perfect Teaching is coarse, and thus offered his own interpretation.
While his argument seemed to yield, he then countered by saying: "This is from the perspective of the Perfect [Teaching]."
[The opponent] himself distinguishes between the "coarse" within the sublime and the "coarse" of the partial teachings; it must not be equated with the latter. I say:

Because I have encountered this present challenge, I have unconsciously conceded that the provisional (quán) within the perfect (yuán) is coarse. However, as for the single [teaching of] the three [vehicles], how could the teaching be partial? The "coarse" and the "perfect-coarse"—the two types of coarseness—have distinct essences (*tǐ*).
Alternatively, someone says: "It is coarse because of emotional attachment. To this I now reply: If it were coarse solely due to emotional attachment, why would it be only...?

The provisional is coarse; the real should likewise be coarse (and so forth). Question: This passage cites the threefold [thousandfold world] as being without distinction to provide general proof for both phenomena and principle.

Does this mean that the three thousand phenomena and principles are entirely without distinction? Answer: Although this is the case here, one must not cling to a single point to the exclusion of other meanings.
Since the three thousand dharmas encompass everything, they may be characterized as distinct, non-distinct, neither distinct nor non-distinct, or beyond both.

Only non-differentiation and differentiation: within a single speck of dust and a single thought, nothing is not fully present. Therefore, the three thousand dharmas universally encompass all meanings.
If one pursues the ultimate in principle and distinguishes meanings from that principle, the three thousand dharmas are called "non-differentiated.
If one pursues the ultimate in phenomena and distinguishes meanings from those phenomena, the three thousand dharmas are called "differentiated. Since both these phenomena and this principle...
The essence of the treasury is without differentiation, yet it harmonizes with the distinctions of conventional function.

Whether in principle or in phenomena, both may be termed "differentiation within non-differentiation" and "non-differentiation within differentiation. From this perspective of defining the meaning, the three thousand [realms] of both phenomena and principle each pervade differentiation.

They are distinguished as being without difference, or they are distinguished according to the non-difference of their respective intrinsic natures (dharmatā) regarding phenomena and principle; thus, the three thousandfold world of phenomena and principle are all termed "without difference.

Alternatively, they are distinguished according to the differences in their respective conventional functions; thus, the three thousandfold world of phenomena and principle are all termed "with difference."

Furthermore, this principle of phenomena (shili) is called "delusion" when it resides within the minds of sentient beings, and it is called "awakening" when it resides within the minds of the Buddhas.

Therefore, the three thousand phenomena of the phenomenal realm (sanzhen) exist simultaneously with delusion and awakening; because they differ in their phenomenal manifestations (shi), they are all termed "differentiated.

If one points to delusion, it is precisely awakening; if one points to awakening, it is precisely delusion. Therefore, the three thousand phenomena of the phenomenal realm exist simultaneously with the principle of reality (li); because they are identical in their underlying principle, they are all termed "undifferentiated. It is simply...
Because of the perfect integration of a single thought-moment, there is no meaning that is not possible.

Regarding the four similes, there are two parts to the presentation of examples. First, the direct application of the similes, which is itself divided into three sections. First, the direct analogy to the Dharma. Since the text is already divided into three parts: [the following continues].

The present analogy is likewise so. The first analogy demonstrates that the essence of the *dharmadhātu* (the Treasury) possesses both differentiation and non-differentiation. While the preceding teaching concerned only its nature (*svabhāva*), the present analogy applies to both.

Regarding the two aspects of the image’s nature: first, the primary analogy. As for the substance of the mirror, it is the *śūnyatā-garbha* (the Empty Treasury). Its possession of the nature of all images is the *aśūnyatā-garbha* (the Non-empty Treasury).
The substance of the mirror is itself the nature of the images; the Empty Treasury is itself the Non-empty. There is no distinction between differentiation and non-differentiation.
[The text] distinguishes two parts. From "If this... below, it explains the two metaphors. First, regarding "the absence of nature does not manifest":

this is because only when the principle is fully present can there be phenomenal function. Next, regarding "knowing the nature through the image": although in reality there is no distinction, the manifestation of arising reveals the presence of both [nature and function].

From "As that... below, it applies the metaphor of the absence of nature not manifesting. "Though it is bright and pure" refers to the interior of space being like a mirror, bright and pure; [this applies] specifically to...

Space is clear and pure like fire; they share the same designation of "clear and pure," and both are likewise called "space. Yet, while they illuminate objects and manifest images, there is a distinction between the mirror and the fire.

This is because, within [the analogy], they are not equal in their partiality. Since the third [element] manifests below, it serves as an analogy for knowing the nature [of reality] by means of its images.
Second, regarding these two aspects of the inferior marks: first, they manifest fully based on their respective conditions;

second, they descend again. Purity and impurity are unimpeded; the marks of the ten realms differ from one another, yet they coexist within a single mind without mutual obstruction. This lack of mutual obstruction is precisely non-differentiation.

Nevertheless, although there is no differentiation, the functions of sentient beings and Buddhas are distinct, which constitutes differentiation. This differentiation and non-differentiation— *Note: The original text contains technical terminology related to Huayan Buddhist philosophy concerning the interpenetration of phenomena (dharmas) within the "One Mind" (ekacitta), specifically addressing the relationship between the purity and impurity of the ten realms (daśadhātu).*
It does not depart from the essence of the treasury (*garbha*). Just as a mirror and its manifold images may serve as a metaphor for this dharma, [the text says] "although" and so forth.
In the explanation through metaphor, the essence of the treasury is entirely one; the metaphor of the lump of clay is not analogous to the essence of the treasury.

The essence of the treasury is entirely one and can only be compared to a mirror. The text is divided into three parts. First, the general demonstration: although there is the nature of the image and the appearance of the image...
[The interlocutor replies: "They are distinct. [The author says: "As for the statement 'it is but a single mirror,' if one seeks the meaning through this analogy, it seems to present an obstacle.

Why? Because the nature of a reflection has no form; thus, one may say that it is but a single mirror, perfectly interfused and non-different. However, while the characteristics of the reflection depend upon the mirror, they are not identical to the mirror.
This is because the mirror is solely luminous while the reflection possesses various colors; the mirror is perhaps circular while the reflection has length or shortness. How can this be?"

One may say that they are perfectly interfused and non-different. It should be understood that when discussed in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are distinct; when discussed in terms of essence (*svabhāva*), they are identical.
Since there are no separate characteristics apart from the essence, one uses the image to illustrate the point: thus, the roundness of the mirror and the nature of the image’s color are non-distinct.

Being identical means being identical with the characteristics; therefore, it is pointed out that the mirror is the image. Consequently, the roundness of the image and the mirror become the same. Now, we are specifically discussing identity in terms of the essence.

It is then said that the forms of the images are likewise perfectly interfused and not distinct; there is only a single mirror. Second, from "How can this be? below, the text provides the formal analogy, which consists of three parts:

first, the analogy for the nature of the pores of all sentient beings; second, from "Just as the hairs... below, the analogy illustrating the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*); third, from "The one being pure...
below, the analogy illustrating the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings. Regarding the two natures of purity and impurity, these are categorized according to the world.

The supramundane distinguishes between the pure and the defiled; thus we know that the aforementioned natures reside within the four and the six. Do not say that because the pure and the defiled differ, the stained and the pure are distinct.
Therefore, below, the analogy explains how the neutral nature subsumes both phenomena and characteristics. First, the analogy for the nature; first, the analogy for a single hair.

The nature of the "Hole" (*kōng*) is capable of encompassing the natures of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Second, as in the previous example of lifting up what was lowered, this serves as an analogy for how each individual nature of all phenomena encompasses the natures of all phenomena.
In the preceding section on phenomena, each was individually divided into two categories—mundane and supramundane;

however, in the present text, it is stated collectively that these "encompass the remaining natures of all images," and further states, "lifting up each and every remaining image-nature. As for these "remaining" [natures]:
This comprehensively encompasses both the pure and impure aspects, as well as the mundane and supramundane natures. Second, regarding the two parts of the subsequent analogy:
first, the analogy that demonstrates the characteristics; second, the actual analogy itself. First, the analogy: it shows how a single pore can encompass all things. Second, "Just as... and so forth:
this uses the example of a single pore to illustrate other things, demonstrating its capacity for inclusion. Now, this analogy is also not identical to the dharma [it illustrates].
This opens the way for both the mundane and the supramundane. The following section uses a metaphor to explain the meaning. The text states:

"Because all image-phenomena take that very nature of the image as their substance," and so forth. This intends to clarify that the efficacy of the mutual inclusion of image-phenomena is due to their nature;

if one does not trace back to the nature, there is no principle of inclusion. If someone were to simply say that phenomena themselves mutually include one another, how could such a principle exist? Or as it is said:

The colors of crimson and purple do not immediately possess the fragrance of orchids and spikenard. However, if one merely asserts the principle that "form" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "nature" (*svabhāva*) mutually encompass one another, then one contradicts the scriptural passage stating that "form" and "form" mutually encompass one another. If it is claimed that these forms are the nature and therefore mutually encompass one another, we now raise this objection:
Since form is already the nature, why does form not encompass [itself]? If form does not encompass [itself], is form then not the nature? Thus, one should know that this view is merely...
"Existence" refers to the complete loss of the name, which is the meaning.
From "Secondly, because of this... onwards, it is established that, in terms of the Dharma, the one who is born and the Buddha share the same pure mind, which is perfectly interfused and unimpeded;

this can be believed through the observation of metaphors. However, one must further know that the single great jewel-mirror, whether in the state of birth or Buddhahood, has never for a moment been separate. If...

It is said that when clouds exist, they are obscured by dust; when present with a Buddha, they are polished until they can reflect light. This is not the intended meaning of the current metaphor. The intended meaning here is this:
this mirror is singular, unobstructed, and eternally luminous. Images of both purity and defilement appear within it simultaneously without hindrance.
Although the images of purity and defilement differ—just as there is a distinction between the delusion of ordinary beings and the awakening of Buddhas—the mirror of luminous purity remains but one.
If the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha is non-dual, then this clarity of the mirror is the clarity of innate, natural virtue; it is not the clarity produced by polishing away the turbidity of dust.
Although the clarity of the polished mirror and the clarity of the original [mirror] are identical in their luminosity, that which constitutes their luminosity is distinct.

The clarity of the polished [mirror] is initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*); the clarity of the original [mirror] is primordial enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). As soon as one says that this mirror is the original, [it is understood].
"Those who possess clarity" have already lost the essence of that clarity; therefore, even fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is subsumed within its functioning.

Regarding the phrase "For this reason," there are two parts: citing the scriptures as proof and providing analogies. First, the direct citation of the scriptures and the analogies. First, the citation of the scripture, which is the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Master Zhangan explains that a single virtue of the *Prajñāpāramitā* possesses these three aspects, using a clear and pure mirror as an analogy.

It is then said: This mirror illuminates all at once. Because it illuminates within [the conventional], it is a mirror; because it illuminates the ultimate, it is pure; because it illuminates the conventional, it is luminous.
Because it is luminous, images appear clearly and provisionally; because it is pure, flaws are exhausted and the real is revealed;
because it is a mirror, its substance is perfect, and the three wisdoms are manifested within the center. Thus, it is said that the luminous and pure mirror encompasses all phenomena. Second, this...
The following section explains the meaning of the terms. The analogy possesses six aspects: first, the mirror; second, purity; third, clarity;

fourth, correspondence; fifth, the face; and sixth, the image. If one speaks in terms of their essential substance, there are actually only three: first, the mirror; second, the face; and third, the image.
That which is called purity, clarity, and correspondence lacks independent existence. Purity and clarity are simply the mirror itself. Correspondence...

"Correspondence" refers to taking the aforementioned three dharmas as this "corresponding correspondence. The mirror is that which can correspond; the facial reflection is that which is corresponded to.
The face is that which corresponds; the mirror is that which is corresponded to. Because of this corresponding correspondence, the image immediately appears.

Using this analogy to illustrate the Dharma, its meaning is most clear. The mirror is a metaphor for the essence of the pure mind. Corresponding correspondence is a metaphor for the pure mind-essence being endowed with [the capacity for reflection].
This is the nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*). "The face" is a metaphor for the two types of karma—defiled and pure; "the image" is a metaphor for the two types of retribution—defiled and pure.
If one were to establish the actual reality through these metaphors, there would be only three things: first, the pure mind; second, karma; and third, retribution.
What is called the "nature of all phenomena" (dharmatā) refers to the fact that all phenomena are like the karmic retribution corresponding to the object;
"nature" refers to the pure mind that corresponds to that object. Because of these three—the pure mind, the karma, and the retribution—it is called the "nature of all phenomena.
The single character "nature" (性) has its essence in the pure mind, while the two characters "all phenomena" (諸法) have their essence in karmic retribution.
Therefore, we know that the ten [realms] of the nature (*dharmatā*) have no separate substance. The ten substances are phenomena (*dharma*), while the substance of the nature is principle (*tattva*).

Because this principle is not limited, it possesses all ten; thus, it is called the "ten realms of the rational nature. Now, because the substance of the pure mind can possess all dharmas, it is called "identical" (*jì*).
This is a metaphor for the substance of the pure mind possessing the natures of all dharmas. Question: Is this now being addressed by way of a metaphor?
It is endowed with the nature of all phenomena. If one follows Zhanran’s commentary, it should be said that its clarity is used as a metaphor for being endowed with the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

What is the difference in meaning? The answer is: that which can respond to whatever is confronted is precisely the mirror’s clarity; although the names differ, the meaning is in fact no different. As the text says:
The phrase "each is unaware of the other" serves as an analogy for the pure mind and so forth. The expression "unaware of one another" refers to the inconceivable (*acintya*).
Therefore, the sutra concludes by stating: "All things are devoid of intrinsic nature; the Dharma-eye is inconceivable.

Now it is said that because karma and its retribution are both the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), their nature is fundamentally unborn. When karma perfumes the pure mind, the karma itself cannot know [the mind]; how then could it...?
It perfumes the pure mind; yet, even as it follows the perfuming of the pure mind, it does not know itself. How does it follow?
Because the retribution induced by this [perfuming] is also unknowable to itself. How is it induced? Therefore, it is said that "each is mutually unknowing.

If one were to provide an interpretation based on discursive thought (*cintā*), then because phenomena and principle differ and cause and effect are distinct, it is said that "each is mutually unknowing. As for karma:
"Below. This explains the combined text of the sutra. As for why only the face and the mirror are joined but the image is not:
since there is karma and there is nature, the retribution exists between them; therefore, it is not mentioned separately. Moreover, the sutra text is precisely intended to discuss karma and nature.
However, the analogy of the bright mirror, the face, and the image is a provisional construction by the Tathāgata, as found in the *Ten Gates of Non-duality*. Therein...

The metaphor of the ten realms as actual creation is as found in the present text. Furthermore, the *Wujing wenju* (Exegesis on the Wondrous Sutra), in its explanation of the non-arising of object and wisdom, also employs the mirror metaphor to illustrate actual creation, which is identical to the present text.
The *Ji* (Commentary) states: "The mirror represents the causes of the ten realms, which is the same as the present mirror metaphor in which the dharma-nature directly gives rise to all phenomena;
the forms represent the conditions of the ten realms, which is the same as the present face metaphor for the two aspects of defilement and purity."
This refers to karma. The "images" represent the fruits of the ten realms; they are like the present metaphor for the two types of retribution, defiled and pure.

Furthermore, the record states: "The mirror’s luminous nature possesses the ten realms; the images produced therein cultivate the ten realms. Therefore, both form-images and cultivated-nature (xing) are fully endowed with the ten realms, and neither transcends the principle of *dharmatā*.
Just as the mirror’s interior and exterior are one and the same, so too are the luminosity, forms, and images—the basis of cultivated-nature—identical to the mirror itself. Now...

Although the preceding passage distinguishes between this "nature of the image" (*xiangxing*) and the "characteristics of the image" (*xiangxiang*), they are nevertheless perfectly interfused and not different;

they are but a single mirror. Furthermore, the record states: "Because all things are simultaneously extinguished, everything is said to be 'non-existent. One no longer makes distinctions between what is innate (*xing*) and what is cultivated (*xiu*).
This is identical to the following passage: "If one discards the capacities of these two natures to discuss the essence of the mind (*xintti*), then that is not [the true mind]."
Defilement is not purity; they are perfectly interfused and equal, beyond the reach of names and designations.
Second, "Furthermore, below," again cites various texts to prove the essence of the *dharmakāya*. These passages consist of two parts.

Although what is cited therein intends to clarify that the essence of the *dharmakāya* is singular, the application of its meaning and the intent of the texts differ slightly. The first part clarifies the mundane...

All supramundane dharmas are established by depending upon a single essence. Next, the intent is to clarify that although mundane and supramundane dharmas differ, the essence upon which they depend is one and the same.
This first section has two parts. First, citing a sūtra, it specifically clarifies that mundane dharmas arise from the essence of the mind.
This is stated as "one" based on the teaching that the essence of the *dharmatā* is interfused; this is not [intended] to exclude other [distinctions].
This intent should be understood as a single, unified focus. Yet, since the questioner is Mañjuśrī, how could he not understand?
He asks this only because he stoops down to accommodate deluded beings; thus, his inquiry gives rise to the subsequent answer that reveals the definitive meaning.
As the Sūtra says: "You now ask about this principle in order to awaken the masses of the ignorant. Therefore, he asks: "How can [the mind] be produced?"
Regarding the various karmic retributions, they are now demonstrated according to the definitive intent; thus it is said that the essence of the *dharmatā* is fused and explained as "one.
If one realizes this unity of the fused essence, one should not harbor doubts concerning the various karmic retributions. Someone might say:
"This 'one' of the fused essence can only be explained as a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) to clarify the meaning of 'one. Why? Because of this nature..."
The ten hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses are fully present without exception. Because they are perfectly interfused, they are collectively termed "one"; thus it is called "the one nature.

Therefore, know that this "one" is the perfect interfusion of the three truths; consequently, it is designated as "one. Is this principle not so? If you say it is not so, what then of the meaning of "suchness"?
If you say it is so, why did [the previous teaching] discard "contemplation" and take the three as the phenomena while taking the one as the principle?
If this is taken as the principle, does it not reveal that there is a single nature rather than three? Answer: This point is extremely difficult. For now, let us simply ask:
when discussing the ultimate truth, which among the three and the one possesses substantial reality? If you say that both lack substantial reality, [how can they be distinguished]?
What did the Patriarch mean when he said it is not that the substance of the mind is empty and non-existent?

If you say that each of the three and one possesses a substantial reality, then there ought to be four substances. If, at the time of perfect interfusion, they were like dust particles forming a single mass, then what would happen?

If you say that in reality there are three, but because these three are perfectly interfused and unimpeded, they are called "one," then in that case, "one" is merely a provisional name, while the "three" are...

Regarding the substance (*dravya*): why did the Patriarch say that although there are three names, they are one body? If it were as previously stated, one must universally say that although there is one name, there are three bodies.
Furthermore, when they are perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*), is it like gathering three particles of dust into a single lump of clay?
If you say that the inconceivable substance is not fixed as either three or one—that the three bodies are precisely the one—then [the principle is established].
Regarding the statement that "the one essence is itself the three essences": why did the Patriarch say, "Although there are three names, there are no three essences;
although it is a single essence, three names are established"? Is it that the three are called 'names' and the one is called 'essence'?

Please keep this meaning in mind; from now on, let what I have said be considered correct. It is precisely because of this nature (*dhātu*) that it cannot be taken as one, and there is nothing by which it can be named.
The "Strong" is designated as "One," yet this One is inconceivable and endowed with all virtues. Therefore, this One possesses Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle Way.
Because it is able to possess these virtues, we know that this One is a perfectly integrated nature (*yuanrong xing*).

To speak of it as "One" does not mean it is a fixed, determinate one. Question: Do you still allow that this single nature is called "One" by virtue of being a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)? Answer: Precisely so.
The general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is termed "one. Therefore, in establishing the general and the particular now, we take this single nature (*eka-svabhāva*) as the general.
Furthermore, in establishing this single nature now—wherein "one" is three and three is one, neither three nor one yet both three and one—this "one" is what is called the single nature.
Is this not the general? Question: How does this differ from that [previous case]? Answer:
Both parties claim that because of their perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), they are collectively designated as "one. Although their words are the same, their underlying meanings differ. Why is this?

That school designates them collectively as "one" because the three truths (*sandì*) are perfectly interfused; our school designates them collectively as "one" by virtue of the perfect interfusion of the essential nature (*xìngtǐ*).
That school holds that because the three truths are perfectly interfused, the three are identical to the one, and the one is identical to the three. Our school, however, [holds that...]
Because the essence of nature is perfectly interfused, the three are one and the one is the three. Question: You now speak of the "perfectly interfused essence of nature.
Furthermore, this "essence of nature" refers to the Three Truths. Is this not identical to the perfect interfusion of those Three Truths? Answer:

When discussing essence and function at their most profound level, the "three" refer to function, while the "essence of nature" refers to essence. Because the essence is perfectly interfused, [the function is so as well].
Excellent. If these are distinguished separately, the essence of nature (*xingti*) is perfectly interfused, while the three [truths] belong to the realm of differentiation.
As for what is called "the three are its function," it is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*: "To speak of 'one' is to lose the function; to speak of 'three' is to wound the essence.

Regarding what is called "the essence of nature is perfectly interfused, while the three belong to differentiation," this is also as stated in the *Śāstra*: "The three truths are identical to the one truth; the one truth is identical to the three."
The Truths. Differentiation and non-differentiation; non-differentiation and differentiation; neither differentiation nor non-differentiation;
yet differentiating while not differentiating. The realm of all Buddhas is fully endowed with such inconceivability. Question:

Since the text already contains both "neither-nor" and "both-and," why now do you take only the first two phrases to prove difference and non-difference? Answer: First, [the first two phrases establish the basis for the subsequent analysis].

Regarding the clarification of the three truths (*triratna-satya*): they are not exhausted by being pointed out either from the perspective of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) or from their manifestations in various places.

First, as for pointing them out from the essence of phenomena: this refers to the totality. Within the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*), all three are fully present; therefore, while the single nature is without differentiation, the three are differentiated within that oneness—thus, it is one yet three.

Because it is like the character *i* (the letter *i*) or the character *mu* (the eye), the three truths are called inconceivable (*acintya*). Furthermore, as for pointing them out in various places: [it is as follows:]...
Regarding this: in all places, within each phenomenon (dharma), there are the three truths. To take the case of "three within one": first, the point regarding the three truths is as follows:

"one" is emptiness; "three" is the conventional; that which is neither one nor three is the Middle, which is the dual negation. That which is both one and three is the Middle, which is the dual affirmation.
Although the meaning of these points—made from the perspective of the essential nature of phenomena and according to their specific locations—is not... [incomplete source].

The same applies here. It is not that one must point to "one" as being non-differentiation and "three" as being differentiation. Therefore, we now cite scriptural evidence based on the essence of the Dharma. Now, the question is asked:
If the nature of "one" is extinguished (*wang*), how can it be fully possessed? The answer is: Because this single nature is capable of both extinguishing and illuminating.
Because it is capable of extinguishing, all three truths are extinguished; because it is capable of illuminating, all three truths are fully possessed. However, this single nature is fundamentally...
It is not that extinction and illumination are absent; it is inconceivable to discuss extinction or illumination separately.
Second, "Now, immediately below" [the text] generally clarifies how both mundane and supramundane dharmas arise based on the substance of the mind. First, the meaning is shown.
Second, from "Therefore," the treatise is cited as proof.

Second, "Furthermore, below," [the text] proves that both mundane and supramundane dharmas equally rely on the substance of the one mind. This has two parts: first, citing the text; second, explaining the meaning of this passage.
Regarding the second part, there are two sections: first, explaining the meaning according to the text to reveal that all Buddhas share the same substance; second, from "By means of...

onwards, expanding upon the meaning to clarify that sentient beings and Buddhas share the same substance. The first section consists of: first, indicating the meaning; second, providing proof, which simply states the five [points].

The Way and the Buddha do not speak of the Three Vehicles because, when viewed from the perspective of the Three Vehicles, they are also called "returning against the current" in relation to the Five Paths;

however, they do not exhaust the source in the same way. When viewed from the perspective of the Perfectly Ultimate, even the Buddhas still abide within the cycle of transmigration; yet, they differ from the Five Paths. Since both of these directions are encompassed herein, [the term "Three Vehicles"] is not mentioned.
Second, clarifying the meaning of the distinct names for the causal and resultant *dharmakāya*. This has three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation;

third, the conclusion of the explanation, which further has two parts. First, the question: "The 'etcetera' mentioned above" refers to what was previously stated in the section on the Perfectly Interpenetrating Dharma-gate, namely, that because it possesses the nature of defilement (*saṃkleśa-dhātu*), it is able to manifest all defiled phenomena of sentient beings. Therefore, this *tathāgatagarbha* is designated as being "obstructed. Regarding its primordial abiding:

The Dharma-body further possesses a pure nature; therefore, it is able to manifest all the pure virtues equal to those of all Buddhas. Thus, this *tathāgatagarbha* is established as that which emerges from obstructions.

Although the preceding text mentions the Dharma-body in terms of being "within obstructions" and "emerging from obstructions," it is not specifically pointed out here because it will be clarified in the third section.
Therefore, at present, we shall simply distinguish between the two kinds of Dharma-bodies: that of sentient beings and that of Buddhas.
However, it is not that sentient beings do not exist within obstructions, nor is it that the Buddhas do not emerge from obstructions.

Now, this passage specifically addresses the capacity to discern the object, while the third [section] addresses the object to discern the capacity; therefore, the meaning of "obstruction" is not explicitly clarified in the present text.

The second [section] provides two answers. First is the heading. Regarding "there are two meanings": the first meaning refers to the cultivation of defilement and purity, which invokes a single *dharmakāya*;

consequently, there is a distinction between the two *dharmakāyas* of the ordinary being (*sattva*) and the Buddha. Thus it is said: "Based on phenomena (*vastu*), these two names are spoken in reference to the essence (*tattva*).

The second meaning refers to the nature (*prakṛti*) of defilement and purity, which invokes a single *dharmakāya*; consequently, there is a distinction between the two *dharmakāyas* of the ordinary being and the Buddha. Thus it is said: "Based on the nature..."
The text speaks of these two as "essence" (*tǐ*) and "phenomenon" (*shì*), yet further states that they are distinguished by "phenomena" to clarify their nature.

This is because while the phenomena already manifested—whether defiled or pure—are vividly apparent, the nature capable of possessing them is dark and without marks. Therefore, the inherent nature is revealed through what is manifested;

thus, it is again said that they are distinguished by "phenomena. However, the primary meaning follows the actual substance of the dharmas, for the very substance of defilement and purity is itself...
Because it is cultivated. Since the essence of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is a single unity, this very unity manifests as cultivation;
thus, through such cultivation, one invokes this unity, resulting in the two types of dharmakāya: the defiled and the pure. Next, the meaning of "unity" will be explained in detail.
Since the nature-essence is capable of encompassing both defilement and purity, these very states of defilement and purity are termed "nature. This is based on...
The two natures are used to distinguish the one essence, resulting in the two kinds of *dharmakāya*:

that of the sentient being and that of the Buddha. Second, regarding the explanation of the two [aspects] below, there are three parts: first, distinguishing the substance by means of phenomena; second, the initial heading; third, the demonstration starting from "Now, as for the *dharma*... and so forth. First is the heading. Second is the demonstration starting from "Now, as for the *dharma*... and so forth. Fourth is the conclusion. (Note: The original text appears to have a structural numbering error; the commentary provides four sections for the second part.)

The first section on phenomena has two parts. First, the causes differ because their essential natures (*tattva*) are distinct. Second, from "If again... onwards, it is because their essential nature and substance are one.
This refers precisely to how the distinctions in principle (*li*) are differentiated according to the phenomena, while the lack of difference in phenomena arises from the unity of principle.

The textual structure is clear and requires no further commentary. The second section on analogies has two parts. First, the analogy for when the causes differ because their essential natures are distinct. Second, from "If again... onwards, the analogy for...

The substance and the phenomenon are one. Since this metaphorical passage already illustrates the meaning of conforming to the nature of the Dharma, there is no further need to discuss the substantial nature of the human image in the mirror or the substantial nature of the horse image in the mirror.
Therefore, it simply states "the human image in the mirror" and "the horse image in the mirror.

[Section Three: "Purifying the Mind" below [the preceding section] provides the application. [Section Four: "Because of this" below [Section Three] distinguishes the two intentions. First, the direct explanation; second, "Because it is constant" below [the first].
Citing the scriptural evidence: the phrase "the distinction of permanence" specifically refers to the difference in the practice of cultivation.

As for the "distinction of nature" mentioned in the subsequent text, although the essence of the Dharma is the same, it differs according to its meaning. Regarding the statement "not delivering sentient beings":

since the Buddha has no sentient beings to deliver, and that Buddha himself likewise has no Buddhahood to achieve, within the act of delivering sentient beings there are no sentient beings to be delivered; this does not mean [that he does not deliver them].
[The passage] "crossing over" [refers to] attaining Buddhahood, which is likewise so. Third, this clarifies the conclusion below.

Second, regarding the phrase "that which is spoken," it distinguishes the nature (*dhātu*) based on phenomena. By means of the nature, it explains the two bodies of reality (*dharmakāya*) in terms of their essence.

Fourth: first, the heading; second, "that which is called" and below, the demonstration. First, the demonstration of distinguishing the nature based on phenomena: "there is defilement and there is purity, manifesting as that which is endowed."
If the nature were not complete, it could not manifest. Therefore, the completeness of the nature is revealed by way of its manifestation.

However, regarding the meaning of this completeness and manifestation, the discourse on nature and phenomena (*dharmatā* and *dharma*) does not follow a single path. If one considers the ultimate as non-existent and the conventional as existent, the nature is not called "complete," whereas phenomena are said to be "complete.

Within the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*), not a single dharma can be apprehended; yet within the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), all dharmas are fully present. This is what is meant by "completeness."

This is precisely the meaning of "provisional" (*prajñapti*). If one considers the sudden transformation of phenomena from their nature (*dharmatā*), then "nature" is termed "endowment" (*yōu*) and "phenomena" are termed "manifestation" (*xiàn*).
Therefore, in the present text, when discussing the two natures, both receive the name "endowment"; when speaking of the two phenomena, both are designated by the term "manifestation.

If one considers that endowment has no separate existence apart from manifestation—since the entirety of endowment is fully present within manifestation—then phenomena and manifestations are also called "endowment. Manifestation...

There is no distinction between manifestation and inherent presence; therefore, that which is inherently present is also called manifest. Although this is the case regarding the meaning of "departing" and "approaching," what is the ultimate intent?
One should understand that the term "inherent presence" (ju) refers to the essence (ti) fundamentally arising from nature (xing).

If the essence were not nature, how could the myriad dharmas be suddenly and simultaneously complete? As for the term "manifestation" (xian), the essence fundamentally arises from phenomena (shi). If the essence were not [phenomena]...
It is not the phenomenon itself. How is it that the myriad dharmas manifest sequentially and gradually? It is precisely because this reality is possessed by its nature;

since the nature can summon the phenomenon, the phenomenon is also said to be "possessed. It is precisely because this nature can manifest the phenomenon; since the phenomenon summons the nature, the nature is also said to be "manifested.
Just as in the present text, this true mind is able to manifest pure phenomena, it is therefore through the true nature—

It is designated as "manifestation. However, the essence of this true nature (*tathatā*) is not itself a manifestation. Because the manifesting object is used to designate the manifesting nature, the nature is also called "manifestation.
Question: What is meant by saying that the essence of true nature is not itself a manifestation? Answer: To explain this through an analogy:
when an image appears in a mirror, is it the image that manifests, or is it the mirror that manifests? If one were to say it is the mirror that manifests, then at the time the image exists—
This is also a manifestation of clarity. When there is no image, it is likewise a manifestation of clarity. What, then, is meant by "the mirror manifests"?
Thus we know that the very substance of the manifestation is itself the image; it is simply because the clarity of the mirror is able to manifest this image that we say "the mirror manifests.

However, while the name is established based on the phenomenon, the meaning is truly difficult to comprehend. Please clarify this by reversing the meaning of "manifestation. If one grasps this meaning, then [the nature]—

Regarding "the manifestation of names through phenomena": each arises from its own specific function. Regarding "the manifestation of phenomena through the common name": this is designated in terms of their mutual correspondence. Question:
Previously it was said that the myriad dharmas manifest sequentially and gradually; is there not also simultaneous manifestation? Answer:

As soon as one speaks of "simultaneous manifestation," this manifestation is identical to "possession" (or "endowment"), precisely because it is simultaneous. It is, for example, like the case of "possession": as soon as one speaks of "gradual possession," this...

The possession [of the three thousand worlds] and their manifestation are identical; this is truly because they are gradual. Question: Regarding the "three thousand," is this spoken from the perspective of possession (*ju*), or is it spoken from the perspective of manifestation (*xian*)?

Answer: If one takes the function of each individual part, then in principle it is possession, and in fact it is manifestation. Possession has no separate possession; it is precisely the possession of manifestation.

Manifestation has no separate manifestation; it is precisely the manifestation of possession. Therefore, only when possession and manifestation are neither deficient nor redundant is the perfection achieved.
Therefore, whenever one speaks of the "three thousand," it necessarily implies that they are both inherent and manifest; this encompasses all things without exception.

If we proceed according to the principle of following the phenomenal from the inherent, then because the manifest follows the inherent, both are termed "inherent"; thus, there is the "three thousand inherent in principle."
Because the "possessions" (具) arise from the "manifestations" (現), both are termed "manifestations"; thus, the manifestations of phenomena constitute the three thousand [realms].

Therefore, each possession and each manifestation is itself the three thousand. This is the ultimate limit of all that can be reached. Question: If the nature (性) is the agent of manifestation and phenomena (事) are the objects manifested...

Since both are currently produced together, it should follow that the nature (*svabhāva*) is the creator and the phenomenon (*vastu*) is the created. Why? Because it was previously stated that the phenomenon is the creator and the principle (*li*) is the created.
Answer: The meaning of "creating" is not uniform across all contexts. Discussing the phenomenon itself, the mind (*citta*) is the creator and the phenomena (*dharma*) are the created.
However, when discussing the relationship between phenomenon and principle, there are two directions. When establishing the phenomenon based on the principle, then the principle... [is the creator].
When phenomena are produced through the interaction of the agent and the object, then phenomena constitute the agent and principle constitutes the object; this is like the case of "discussing" (tan).

When principle suddenly encompasses all phenomena, then principle constitutes the agent and phenomena constitute the object; when the essence and its attributes conceal one another, then phenomena constitute the agent and principle constitutes the object. Question:

Zhiyi (Sì-míng) states that that which differentiates agent and object is "creation" (zào), while that which merges agent and object is "inclusion" (jù). What is his meaning? Answer: His explanation is excellent; it is correct.

Because the essence of the Dharma is such. That which constitutes the essence is the nature (*dharmatā*); since nature is harmoniously one, it is undifferentiated. That which constitutes the manifestation is phenomena (*dharma*);
since phenomena are distinct, they are differentiated. Question: If the meaning is indeed excellent, why do you now repeatedly speak of the "possessor" (*yogin*) and the "possessed" (*yoga*)? Answer:

Because the purport of "possession" is difficult to clarify, we must first use the categories of "possessor" and "possessed" to illuminate that teaching so that its purport may be seen. If its purport is seen, then as for the possessor and the possessed—
The meaning is spontaneously undifferentiated.

Second, it is shown by means of the fundamental and the derivative. Regarding the nature (*prakṛti*) in terms of its essence, there are two dharmakāyas; one should know that the nature is fundamentally one.
Because this single nature is endowed with both cultivation and defilement, it is called the "defiled nature. This defiled nature, when considered in relation to the single nature, is as follows:
Therefore, it is called the *dharmakāya* of sentient beings. Because this single nature is fully cultivated for purification, it is called the "pure nature.

Because this pure nature is identical to the single nature, it constitutes the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas. Question: Regarding the two natures of defilement and purity, what is the difference between the character "nature" (*svabhāva*) and the *dharmakāya*?
Answer: Their substance is the same, but their meanings differ. Because their substance is the same, they are both one.
Regarding "nature": because their meanings differ, the *dharmakāya* is the essence (*tǐ*), while the two natures are its functions (*yòng*). Question:

If it is said that nature is fundamentally one, and that the two natures are spoken of only because of the cultivation of both the defiled and the pure within it, then why is it necessary to speak of "endowment" (*jù*) rather than merely speaking of the "present"?

Answer: If one were to speak only of the present, one would see only that defilement and purity originally did not exist but now do; one would fail to perceive the single nature as perfect and immediate (*yuán-dùn*).

...the merit thereof. Question: Previously, you stated that because the matter is concise and the substance is limited, it speaks only of the manifest; is this not the Perfect and Sudden teaching? Answer: The meaning of the text is indeed perfect.

This is because the text states that those phenomena are also "identical, equal, and of one flavor," and further states they are the "Dharma-realm Dharma-gate of constant identity and constant difference.
The intent of these two sections is analogous to the union and separation of cultivation and nature in the Perfect Teaching. If the nature is unified, then all three are present.

This is called the "True Cause" (*zhengyin*). Taking this True Cause in its entirety, it arises as the two types of cultivation (*xiu*). For example, when discussing the substance (*ti*) in terms of phenomena (*shi*), one speaks only of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) being able to manifest both the ordinary and the holy.
If one sets aside the nature (*xing*) and the conditions for enlightenment (*yuanliao*), taking these conditions for enlightenment in their entirety, they arise as the two types of cultivation.

For example, when distinguishing the nature in terms of phenomena, one speaks of the two natures being able to manifest both defilement and purity. Question: It was stated previously that the first section is derived directly from the essence of the Dharma-body (*dharmatā*). How is this so?

If we speak in terms of the three causes, by analogy it should be said that there is only one nature and two cultivations (*śikṣā*). How does this meaning differ from the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*)?
Answer: First, in the distinct teaching, the true cause (*bhūtadhātu*) is not identical [to the other two], because it serves as the basis for the two cultivations.

Second, in the distinct teaching, the single nature cannot fully encompass the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the understanding (*bodhi*). Now, although this dharma is designated as "one nature" based on its essential substance (*dharmatā*), yet this dharma...

The essence is the dharma-body endowed with merit; it is the primary cause (*pradhāna-hetu*) of both the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) and the contributory cause (*upaniṣad-hetu*). Therefore, it differs from the [separate] nature. Question:

Regarding the three meanings of "nature" (*prakṛti*) discussed separately, how are they further explained? Answer: First is cultivated merit (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). Because the seeds have existed since beginningless time, they are provisionally termed "nature" in contrast to their present existence.
Second are the conditional and contributory causes. Because they abide in reliance upon the nature, they are also provisionally termed "nature"; however, this is not because they are identical to it.

Because [the nature] is possessed, it differs from the Perfect [Teaching]. Question: If one follows the essence and nature of the dharmas, the substance of the conditions (pratyaya) and understanding (jñāna) is that which is cultivated through practice.

When discussing their convergence, does the nature’s conditions and understanding return to the conditions and understanding of practice? Answer: The meaning of separation and convergence is not of a single path.

If one discusses separation and convergence in terms of the essence of the dharmas, it is indeed as you have asked. However, if one discusses separation and convergence in terms of the possession of qualities...

This refers to the nature-virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*) where the conditional (*pratyaya*) and investigative (*pariniṣpanna*) aspects return to the fundamental true cause (*tathatā-hetu*). It is only through this that these virtues inherent in the nature (*prakṛti-samvidyamāna-guṇa*) are manifested.

Third, "if one discards the following" indicates that, directly from the essence of the mind, there is only the single Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). If one discards the capacity of the two natures, [the Dharma-body is not realized].

The single character "ability" (*neng*) refers to the two natures (*xing*). Because these two natures can manifest two phenomena, if one now discards the ability to manifest, it is equivalent to discarding the single nature of defilement and purity.
If one were to say that only the two phenomena are discarded, the text would necessarily have to discard the locus of the two natures.
Alternatively, setting aside for the moment the principle of the two natures' ability to manifest, it is therefore said that [one discards] the single nature.
It is possible. In reality, the two natures are not discarded. Now, if you say that the two natures are not discarded, why do you say that the essence of the mind is neither defiled nor pure?
Furthermore, the two natures of defilement and purity are precisely the functioning of the nature (*dharmatā*); if they are not discarded, why do you speak of the essence of the mind?
Moreover, if [the two natures] were not discarded in the preceding passage, why does the subsequent passage speak of "relying on this equal *dharmakāya*"?

There exists the nature of both defilement and purity. Question: Can this nature be discarded? Answer: Following the fundamental substance of the Dharma, the nature cannot be discarded; it is the defilement and purity that can be discarded.
That the nature could be discarded would be due to the presence of defilement and purity; therefore, it is said that the capacity for defiling and purifying the two natures can be discarded.

That which cannot be discarded is because its efficacy arises from the nature itself; therefore, it is said that the Buddha possesses the nature of evil and sentient beings possess the nature of goodness. If one attains this...

The purport of all these texts is clear. As for the statement that "perfect interfusion and equality cannot be named," although such a description is given, the names themselves have already been manifested.
This is the ultimate point of the Tathāgata and the very foundation of the cultivation and realization of Nanyue and Zhiyi.
Yet, regarding this nature, how could it be that the various phenomena of defilement and purity can never be absent? Nor could it be that...
One might ask: can the various phenomena of defilement and purity ever truly perish? That which can perish is emotion (*qing*);
the phenomena of defilement and purity are themselves emotion. That which cannot perish is nature (*xing*); the phenomena of defilement and purity are, moreover, identical to nature.
Regarding the statement that "the various phenomena of defilement and purity are themselves the sentient being": they can be conceived of by virtue of being a sentient being.
If one were unable to conceive of them, how could they be called defiled or pure? Yet, in various texts, the "ten realms and thousand suchnesses" are pointed out as being inconceivable;
this is because the ten realms and thousand suchnesses are precisely this [sentient being]. Therefore, they are given the name "inconceivable. Alternatively, [it may be understood as follows:]...
It is said that "inconceivable" is spoken of in a partial sense; it merely means that it is not conceivable by the three teachings, but how could it therefore not be perfect?
If spoken of in terms of causes, it merely means that it is not conceivable by those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment, but how could it therefore not be the Buddha? Now, I say this is not so.
The reason it is called "perfect" and called "Buddha" is precisely because this nature cannot be conceived. Therefore...
Even the Buddha cannot conceive of such inconceivable words. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are themselves inconceivable;
yet the causes and conditions of the lower stages and all sentient beings—the three paths—are also inconceivable.

This is the "inconceivable that transcends all relativity" (*juedai busiyi*). Question: Why was it previously stated that the inconceivable can only be known by the Buddha? Answer: [As explained above].
The Buddha is able to know because he knows that this Dharma is inconceivable. Question: Is it able to know the coarse? Answer:
The knower is itself the known; knowing is non-knowing. How could there be anything coarse? This should be understood through its essential meaning. Question:
Previously you said that because of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, it is precisely for this reason that it is named "inconceivable. Is this not intended to reveal—?
The inconceivable essence is a single nature. Because this essential nature is perfectly interfused and unobstructed, it causes all phenomena to be identical with this very nature.
Since they are identical with this nature, all phenomena are perfectly interfused; this is termed "inconceivable.
What is the basis for establishing this intention? Answer: In the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, it says: [Question: What is it?
This is the inconceivable. The answer says: The inconceivable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like empty space;
it is without thought or deliberation, profoundly and eternally quiescent. To enter all phenomena and fully penetrate and manifest them—this is precisely the inconceivable.
The single character "enter" (*ru*) is the principle established here; let the wise examine this in detail. Furthermore, realize that this "entry" is, in its entirety, entry itself; it is not...

This refers to entering other lands as being definitive. Since this single nature (*ekadhātu*) is already inconceivable, for what reason is it further called "one," "nature," "equality," or "Dharmakāya"?
These names are established for the sake of sentient beings; these names are not ultimate.
Therefore, it is said that all verbal expressions belong to the provisional (*upāya*). They are merely attached to the world for the sake of sentient beings.
It is established that because there are no distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in the world, it is designated as "one. Now it is likewise so;

because there are no distinct characteristics of identity or difference regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is designated as "one. Since, in the world, form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are taken as the reality (*tattva*) of all phenomena, they are called "mind" (*citta*).
Now it is likewise so; since it is the reality of all dependently arisen minds and phenomena, [it is designated as such]. Thus, by way of the world...
Because it can serve as the locus of reliance for all things, it is called "equality" and is called the "Dharmakāya.

Now, likewise, because it can serve as the locus of reliance for the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, these names and designations arise solely through provisional establishment in accordance with the world.

When one investigates the fundamental nature of the essence and the source of the mind, in reality, they cannot be grasped by conceptual deliberation. If one understands that these names are themselves the nature, then the nature...
Since the essence is both substantial and true, it appears that what is designated by worldly names is actually real; yet this reality, in turn, becomes empty.

The names that designate these natures are provisional, yet they possess reality. Therefore, it is said that in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), names have their corresponding realities, whereas in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), names have no corresponding realities.
However, this distinction between existence and non-existence is merely spoken for the sake of sentient beings. As the text says: "Based upon this equal Dharma-body..."
Regarding "the nature of defilement and purity," etc.: that is, the single nature of the dharmakāya constitutes the two natures of defilement and purity.
Because of these two natures, there is the distinction between the dharmakāya of ordinary beings and that of sages.
Third, the following section clarifies the underlying intent.

The fourfold analysis consists of three layers: first, the question; second, the answer. Habitual cultivation constitutes the nature of delusion (*mṛṣā-dharmatā*); its non-alteration constitutes the true nature (*bhūta-dharmatā*).

Now, regarding the meaning of "nature" (*dharmatā*), it may refer to immovability, or non-alteration, or the actual nature (*svabhāva*), or the constituent nature (*prakṛti*), or habitual cultivation.
[The four names] are established. If one distinguishes them by way of principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), "real nature" (*shixing*) is the middle truth;

it is unchanging and immovable. "Empty nature" (*kongxing*) is the truth of emptiness. "Nature-as-division" (*xingfen*) is the conventional truth. Furthermore, because they are neither distinct nor opposed, these four names all pervade the three truths.

Although there are both pervasive and specific applications, none of these four names fail to belong to the nature-reality (*lixing*). Only "perfected through practice" (*xicheng*) belongs to phenomena (*shi*).
It is established through habituation and arises from conditions. When categorized by its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it refers to the basis of that which arises from conditions;

yet, since the nature of this categorized essence also follows from its own substance, it is identical to what is established through habituation in being equally categorized as a phenomenon (*vastu*). Furthermore, that which is already established through habituation is also said to be unchanging.

It is also called "true nature" (*dharmatā*). Thus, all these names generally pertain to the phenomena (*vastu*). In the present text, for the time being, it is designated as "nature-reality" (*li-xing*) because it is natural and unchanging.
Now, let us evaluate the former claim that "the nature is complete" while "the characteristics are not complete" based on this principle. One may ask them:
"If that which possesses the nature of defilement is identical to the nature-reality, then is the reality itself defiled? For that which is called 'defiled'..."

The name "defilement" (kaṣāya)—how could its principle itself be defiled? If you say it is of a defiled nature, I now ask: regarding the single character "nature" (svabhāva), is this "nature" itself defiled?
Fearing that you may still not understand the intent of this question, I shall now inquire further by means of the natures of the four great elements.
As for the nature of things, it is like fire being hot, water being moist, wind being mobile, and earth being solid; each possesses its own respective nature.

Because their shared characteristics are identical, and because the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is non-differentiated. Now, regarding the question of the inherent presence of water and fire within the nature:

they would necessarily claim that it merely possesses the *nature* of water and fire. To this, we now ask further: does it possess the nature of the distinct parts of water and fire, or the nature of the totality?

Is it the nature of rationality? If you say it is the nature that possesses the constituent parts of rationality, then you are speaking of a rationality that both possesses and does not possess [its own nature].
If you say it is the nature that possesses rationality, consider this: fire must be hot and water must be moist.
Since rationality is neither hot nor moist, how can it be called the nature of fire or the nature of water? I do not yet understand the nature of fire and water.
This is named according to its rational nature (li-xing) and manifested through its phenomenal substance (shi-ti). If one speaks from the perspective of substance, it possesses the phenomenon;

one should not speak of the "nature that possesses the phenomenon. If one speaks from the perspective of principle (li), since principle itself is neither heat nor moisture, how could these two names [fire and water] be obtained?
A name must depend on a reality. Since principle is neither heat nor moisture, how could it be called "fire" or "water"? This is the essential point.
This is obscure and, from of old, has been difficult to fathom; there is nothing like it in other schools. Furthermore, they take this nature (*prakṛti*) as that which is possessed.
Some say that the Way of the rational nature (*li-xing*) is inconceivable; how could one possibly use such emotional conjecture?

Today, whenever I see scholars attempting to exhaustively investigate the single substance of the three names—the meaning of the perfect endowment of nature and characteristics—it simply does not pass through. Thereupon—

It is said that this is "inconceivable" (*acintya*). However, such an evasion has existed since antiquity. For example, in the *Profound Preface* (*Xuanyu*) to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, another commentator explains the metaphor of "inserting Mount Sumeru into a mustard seed" by saying:
"Since one does not know whether it enters or does not enter, and since this is inconceivable, how can one definitively judge whether it enters or does not enter?
Zhanran [Zhang’an] refutes this, saying: "This is also untenable. Regarding the fruits of the Buddha and the higher stages..."
This is inconceivable; it should all be considered inexplicable. As for everything else, it is said to be explicable. Is this single point alone then said to be unknown?
Now, following the same principle, suppose one encounters a person who asks: "How can it be that the nature is fully present while the characteristics are not? One would then distinguish by saying:
"The nature is fully present, sudden, and eternal, whereas the characteristics are transformative and contrived. Furthermore, that which is "sudden and eternal" in the nature is also—

How can that which is inconceivable be discerned? Yet, when encountering the present inquiry as to how the nature of reality (dharmatā) is—whether it is called "hot" or "moist"—this too is, for the time being, inconceivable.

Why, then, do you say at this point that it cannot be discerned? If one were to claim it cannot be discerned solely because it is inconceivable, how could you then say that the nature does not possess its characteristics? Furthermore, how can you raise such an objection?

He said that the appearance of clouds is a transformation; how could such an appearance exist within the nature [of water]? That person replied, "Since it is an inconceivable appearance, how can one fathom it with the intellect?
He then laughed and acquiesced. When his arguments were exhausted and his reasoning failed, he resorted to the defense of "inconceivability.
Now, when faced with the question of what constitutes the moisture and heat of the nature, he again resorts to "inconceivability."
If one examines this through deliberation and inference, is it not also a case where the meaning is exhausted and the principle is lost?

Therefore, I infer that scholars today suffer from a lack of clarity regarding the "instruments of discourse" (tánjù), and thus they follow their own minds in faith without perceiving the subtle threads of contemplation (guānlǚ).

Their talk concerning the "perfect fusion of the three-in-one" (sānyī yuánróng) is likewise the same. When confronted with the present inquiry: "Since these are three, how can they be one? Since they are one, how [can they be three]?"...

When asked what these three are, he immediately replied, "Inconceivable. However, if one simply interprets this "inconceivable" in such a way, the relationship between mind and object remains obscure, and one merely relies on blind faith.

Now, when we speak of the "inconceivable," one must understand it with absolute clarity, without the slightest delusion, and thoroughly investigate its very source; only then can it be tentatively called "inconceivable."

Second, the phrase "therefore it is said" below introduces the scriptural evidence. Third, from the words "Buddha-nature" below, the analogy is explained: the sutra states that Buddha-nature is not something created through effort;

by this analogy, one should understand that defiled nature is likewise not something produced through practice. This distinction between delusion and awakening is made for the time being; in reality, defiled nature is itself the Buddha.

If one were to simply claim that the three thousand [realms] are produced by phenomena and thus called "permanent" and "indestructible," how could the name "transformation and production" be considered "permanent"?
Did Zhili not say that what is permanent must be unchanging, and that what is impermanent cannot be the nature?
Some say that one must not cling to names. However, if names were not correctly established, why would Jingxi not take principle as the constructed and phenomena as the permanent?

Thus we know that the permanence of phenomena must necessarily arise from their identity with nature. If one were to simply regard phenomena as impermanent, since phenomena are already identical to the permanent, how could phenomena not be permanent?
How then would one resolve the fact that worldly appearances are permanent? If these appearances were not permanent, it would necessarily...
It should be corrected to read: "The nature of the world is eternal.
This second section has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. However, this text states: "Within Buddha-nature there are sentient beings."
This clarifies that the nature of phenomena is inherently capable of encompassing all phenomena.

Regarding the statement that "the Buddha-nature exists within the bodies of sentient beings," this clarifies that the substance of the Buddha-nature is concealed by the phenomenal characteristics (*saṃvṛti*) of sentient beings. The Buddha-nature is the principle (*li*); sentient beings are the phenomena (*shi*).

This is a case where the principle is inherent within the phenomena, and the phenomena are inherent within the principle. If one were to discuss this in general terms, there should be six propositions. The first is the principle...

1. Phenomena possessing phenomena; 2. Phenomena possessing principle. These two correspond to the relevant passages in the text. 3. Principle possessing principle: the text states that the true essence is fully endowed with both the nature of defilement and the nature of purity.

4. Phenomena possessing phenomena: the text states that within the worlds of the ten directions, even a minute speck of dust is not constricted, and the kalpas of the three periods of time can be integrated into a single brief thought.
5. Principle possessing both principle and phenomena: as in the case of *Amoghasiddhi* (Non-empty).
The *Zang* (Treasury) establishes both the two natures—defilement and purity—and the two matters—defilement and purity. The six matters are complete with both principle and phenomena;

they are manifested by means of the completeness of principle within phenomena. Why is this? For instance, regarding the completeness of phenomena within phenomena, the merit arises from the completeness of principle within phenomena.

Now, since principle is already able to be complete with both phenomena and principle, phenomena must likewise be complete with both phenomena and principle. As the subsequent text states: "If the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) subsumes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)," and so forth.

All phenomenal characteristics are fully exhausted. Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), each individual phenomenal characteristic exhaustively encompasses all other phenomenal characteristics within the conventional truth.

Nevertheless, these six meanings fundamentally derive from the essence of phenomena (*dharma*). It is only through the principle (*li*) that they are inherently complete, while it is through phenomena (*shi*) that they are actualized;

when analyzing the meaning according to the dharma, there are six distinct differences. What are they? First, as for "the principle further encompassing the principle," this is because the principle is differentiated by virtue of phenomena.
Regarding the two natures of defilement and purity: the principle (*li*) further possesses principle, and phenomena (*shi*) further possess phenomena.

This is because phenomena are identical to principle; thus, these phenomena are further able to possess phenomena. One must rely on the two meanings of "merging into function" (*gonggui*) and "conforming to the dharma" (*jiufa*).

When phenomena act as the possessor (*nengju*), the merging into function resides in the principle. Because phenomena conform to being identical with principle, phenomena are able to possess [phenomena]. If one follows the merging into function toward the principle...
Regarding "being able to possess": if one proceeds from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*), then phenomena are the "possessor" and principle (*li*) is the "possessed.

This is explained by analogy with this case. If one proceeds from the perspective of merit returning to phenomena, then phenomena are the "possessed"; if one proceeds from the perspective of conforming to phenomena, then principle is the "possessed.

The answer consists of three parts. The first is the direct answer, which comprises the two phrases: "principle possesses phenomena" and "phenomena possess principle. The text states: "The dharma-nature is able to give rise to all phenomena," and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "the substance of clouds acts as the concealing characteristic," this must be carefully distinguished. This is because the term "endowment" (*ju*) may refer to the existence of something as an endowment, or it may refer to the inclusion of something as an endowment.

Now, "existence as an endowment" corresponds to the meaning of "separation" (*li*) within the Perfect Teaching, while "inclusion as an endowment" corresponds to the meaning of "identity" (*ji*) within the Perfect Teaching.
The present text encompasses both meanings. For instance, when it says that Buddha-nature is endowed with sentient beings...
It merely states that this clarifies the meaning that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is capable of producing all phenomena.

This is equivalent to saying they "possess" [it], because since all phenomena arise from the nature of phenomena, all phenomena belong to the nature of phenomena. Sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature;

it is merely said that its essence is obscured by its manifestations. Because all phenomena are able to obscure the nature of phenomena, once the nature of phenomena is obscured, it exists within all phenomena.

The Buddha-nature arises entirely from the meaning of "separation" (*li*). If it were to arise from the meaning of "identity" (*ji*), then because the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is identical to all phenomena (*dharmas*), the dharma-nature would be immediately and fully established within each phenomenon;
and because all phenomena are identical to the dharma-nature, sentient beings would be immediately and fully endowed with the Buddha-nature within their own state.
Question: Regarding what is called "immediate and full establishment" or "endowment," if these refer to identity, then by the principle of identity, they ought necessarily to be co-present.

Is it the principle (*artha*)? Answer: It may be that through identity there is inclusion, or through inclusion there is identity; it may be that identity is itself inclusion, or inclusion is itself identity.
These various differences do not transcend substance (*tattva*) and principle. From the perspective of substance, identity is itself inclusion and inclusion is itself identity;
the equal and wondrous nature (*prakṛti*) can both be identical and inclusive. This identity and inclusion do not go beyond one [another].
As for their nature (*dhātu*), how could there be any difference in essence? It is simply because this nature is, in its very locus, all phenomena that it is called "identical" (*jia*).
Because all phenomena are fully present in their very locus, it is called "complete" (*ju*). Because they are identical, they are fully present; because they are fully present, they are identical.

Therefore, one may say that if "completeness" is not discussed, the meaning of "identity" is not established; and one may also say that if "identity" is not discussed, "completeness" is not established.
The meaning is not established. The distinction between these two names arises from a difference in meaning. As stated below, two examples are cited as metaphors;

however, the text of these metaphors can corroborate the present meaning. The thesis established here is that principle (li) inherently contains phenomena (shi), and because principle contains phenomena, phenomena contain principle.
It is simply that form arises from emptiness and thus form possesses emptiness; one can never say that emptiness [arises from form].
