When form arises, emptiness is what possesses form, just as water forms into waves. One can never say that water is formed by the waves. Question: Emptiness has no separate emptiness;

it is precisely form that is emptiness. Water has no separate water; it is precisely the waves that are water. Why then can one not say that emptiness arises from form, and that water is formed by the waves?
Answer: This point is also difficult to grasp; we shall now investigate it thoroughly. If we rely on the [Tian]... [text truncated]
However, that wondrous nature which cannot be conceived through thought does not even admit of the two designations "dharmas" and "dharma-nature.

It is like not speaking of emptiness as being distinct from form, or water as being distinct from waves. Because sentient beings do not understand this and are deluded regarding this wondrous nature, they perceive various dharmas;
thus it is said that dharma-nature gives rise to the various dharmas. This is like emptiness being the cause of form, or water being the cause of waves. This...
Since all phenomena arise from the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), the *dharmatā* exists within all phenomena.
It is like space existing within form, or water within waves; this is explained by contrasting phenomena with their *dharmatā*, which is why it is said that they "arise" and "exist.
However, if one speaks by regarding the *dharmatā* in relation to phenomena, then the *dharmatā* is itself the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena—just as water is itself space. Thus, it becomes...
The waves of form: all phenomena are the suchness of the dharma-nature; thus, the waves of form become the water of emptiness.
Although these two exist, it is not the case that they do not first arise from the dharma-nature as the water of emptiness for all phenomena and as the waves of form.

Therefore, one may say that all phenomena are the dharma-nature and the waves of form are the water of emptiness; one can never say that all phenomena first arise from the dharma-nature as the waves of form.
This is emptiness-water. Subsequently, the dharma-nature is the water of the emptiness of all phenomena, while form is its wave.
This is explained by establishing the teaching through the relative opposition of delusion and awakening.

If one gathers the dharma-nature and all phenomena within the essence of the naturally wondrous nature—which is fundamentally non-dual—then the dharma-nature and all phenomena have no priority or posteriority; they are neither identical nor separate.
Just as space, form, water, and waves cannot be distinguished as preceding or following, nor are they different or identical; one should simply understand this through the aforementioned principle.
Thus, one will see for oneself that all various explanations converge upon this point. The third section concludes with these words.
The third section has two parts. First, the question. This question arises from what was said previously regarding the presence of Buddha-nature within the bodies of sentient beings.
Although the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is one, the names applied to it must differ according to delusion or awakening.

Furthermore, the preceding text referred to this True Suchness by means of the awakening of the Buddhas, calling it "naturally pure *nirvāṇa*. Why, then, does it not now refer to it by means of the delusion of sentient beings?
If True Suchness (tathatā) is defined as the nature that defiles birth-and-death (saṃsāra), how can it be further designated as the Buddha-nature? The answer is twofold. First, the direct response:
because it inherently possesses the nature of defilement, it is able to give rise to birth-and-death; yet this very nature of defilement is itself the nature of purity.
Therefore, it is also able to possess the nirvana of the pure nature. Since it thus possesses the pure nature, it must necessarily possess the capacity to transcend obstructions.
Now, taking sentient beings as the subject, because they possess a defiled nature (*prakṛti*), the defiled phenomena of birth and death have already been established.

Therefore, it is not further stated that there is a "defilement of the nature" within birth and death; rather, it simply points to the existence of the "purity of the nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) which is nirvāṇa.

The intention is to cause sentient beings to cultivate the pure qualities that transcend obstacles; thus, it is said that "there is Buddha-nature. As for the phrase in the text, "the reality within the缠 (entanglements)," "reality" (*vastu*)...
It is precisely suchness (*tathatā*). It may also be explained as the "reality" of reality. Second, regarding the two [aspects] distinguished below: first, establishing the two natures universally;

the two natures exist without deficiency both in the state of being born [as a sentient being] and in the state of Buddhahood. Second, naming them specifically; below, they are designated exclusively as "Buddha-nature."

The first section presents two points. First, there is the fear of conflating [the nature] with defiled phenomena. Second, from "Furthermore" onwards, it is for the purpose of giving rise to pure conduct (*śuddha-caryā*).
Regarding the fact that the sūtras and śāstras speak of the nature as being exclusively "pure" or "Buddha-nature," the intent is to bring about pure conduct.

The text is divided into two parts. First, it addresses the faults of the feverish affliction (*saṃtāpa*) and its cessation; second, it addresses the virtue of coolness (*śītalatva*). Now, in this treatise, the specific mention of these two matters regarding the two natures is intended to reveal...

Matters are accomplished through their inherent nature (*dharmatā*). To abandon faults and pursue virtue must necessarily reside in purity. Second, if one is solitary and base, or feels attraction and aversion, the text says:

"The nature of the deluded and ignorant is originally nameless, yet it is fully endowed with all names. Although it is endowed with all names, these names have no substantial reality; the substance is entirely the nature itself.
Since this nature is perfectly wondrous, how could it be fixed as either defiled or pure, or neither defiled nor pure? It is suddenly and utterly without distinction. This is capable of...

One who understands this vaguely recognizes the nature of consciousness. One who cannot understand this hears of the defilement of the auditory nature and, taking it to be truly defiled, consequently feels no longing for it.
Hearing of the purity of its inherent nature, one takes it to be truly pure and thus feels delight in it.

This fear and this delight—neither delusion nor folly—is what could they possibly be called? Question: Since hearing of defilement constitutes delusion, it cannot be termed "defilement" [itself]. If one hears...
Question: If purity is merely for the sake of the ignorant, why then refer to it as "purity"? Answer: Names are skillful means; thus they possess the merit of leading one into reality.
Ignorance is the initial stage, yet it serves as the veil through which one perceives the nature. Therefore, by specifically speaking of the "pure nature," one is enticed and encouraged forward.

Because of this veil, one seeks [the truth], and in seeking, one must follow a teacher. The teacher will necessarily transmit that the nature is not merely pure; the nature is moreover endowed with defilement. Thus...
Defilement is purity; it is only when one sees that which is neither defiled nor pure that one reaches the ultimate.
Therefore, the conclusion below states: "In various sutras and treatises, when discussing the fundamental nature of the Buddha and sentient beings, they all speak of 'Buddha-nature' and 'pure nature.

However, within the teaching gate of our Master and Patriarchs, we employ different names in accordance with the *siddhānta* (the established tenet), yet this is not [to be understood as a contradiction]."

The first [point]. First, by contrasting nature (*xing*) with cultivation (*xiu*), the absence [of cultivation] is shown to indicate the presence [of nature]: the Buddhas have no cultivated evil, yet they possess the nature of evil; sentient beings have no cultivated good, yet they possess the nature of good.

This is as stated in the *Miaofa lianhua jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra). Second, by contrasting nature with cultivation, the presence [of both] is shown to indicate the presence [of both]:
the Buddhas possess purity, while sentient beings possess defilement. This is as in the current passage establishing the objection. Third, by...

Cultivation pertains to the nature of arising and ceasing; cultivation involves existence and disappearance, whereas nature is eternally abiding. Cultivation is partial, while nature exists as both. Regarding cultivation being partial:
it refers to a single person’s beginning and end, wherein the two matters of defilement and purity are only fully present. Regarding nature existing as both:

as this text states, "Whether one is obstructed or free from obstruction, that which is attained is termed 'nirvana of inherent purity. Both [aspects] together are designated as 'inherent defilement.'"

Regarding birth and death: fourth, by correlating cultivation with nature. Based on the entire reality of the *dharmadhātu*, cultivation is both defiled and pure, and nature is likewise both defiled and pure.

As the subsequent text states: "If one considers the meaning of being obstructed or emerging from obstructions by taking all ordinary beings and sages collectively, then within a single moment, the *tathatā*-dharma-body simultaneously possesses both functions:
that of being in obstruction and that of emerging from obstruction. Since cultivation is fully present [in this way]..."
This can be understood through its nature. Fifth, by correlating cultivation with the desire for nature, it causes the ignorant to joyfully practice;

thus, while cultivation encompasses both defilement and purity, its nature is purely pure, as in the concluding text of the present section. Sixth, by correlating cultivation with the desire for nature, it causes the practitioner to realize that cultivation is itself nature;
only when one sees that nature is fully replete does one reach the ultimate perfect practice. Therefore, nature speaks of both defilement and purity, as Jingxi said: "Suddenly..."

One has not yet heard the name of "inherently evil nature" (which, when delusion is pointed out, refers to the circulation through the three paths). How then can one believe in the existence of "inherently virtuous practice" (which, when pointing to phenomena, refers to the three causes of cultivated virtue)?
Seventh, by contrasting cultivation with nature, one conforms to the essence of the Dharma: cultivation possesses both defilement and purity, whereas nature is neither defiled nor pure.
As it is said: "Abandoning the capacities of the two natures, one discusses only the substance of the mind; this very substance is neither defiled nor pure."

The Threefold Principle of the True Essence of the Three Knowledges (*trividyā*) regarding its presence within obstructions and its emergence from them, in three parts: first, the presentation of the headings; second, the explanation, which has two sections. First, the question:

the intent of the previous section’s inquiry concerned the capacity that distinguishes the object; since the *dharmakāya* is one, why are there the *dharmakāya* as the cause when defiled and the *dharmakāya* as the fruit when pure?
Now, the intent of this section’s inquiry concerns the object that is distinguished by the capacity; since the *dharmakāya* is one, how can it be said to exist [within obstructions]?

Obstruction and emergence from obstruction: because the *dharmakāya* is that which is obstructed and that from which one emerges, while defilement and purity are that which obstructs and that by which one emerges.

There are two answers to these two points. First, the direct answer to the previous objection has three parts. First, defining the names: obstruction and emergence from obstruction exist both as phenomena (*vastu*) and as intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).

Now, following only the aspect of phenomena, it is said that the essence of the mind is equal, being neither obstructed nor unobstructed; and even if one were to approach it from the perspective of the two natures, the essence remains the same.

Regarding the passage by Rong: "As for the phrase 'merely concerning the nature of defilement' (*raṅ bźin gyi ñon moṅs pa*), the character *raṅ* (defilement) is likely an error. It should read 'two natures' (*gñis kyi raṅ bźin*) in order to properly explain the meaning.

As for the mention of the names 'obstruction' (*sgrib pa*) and 'stain' (*dri ma*), the intended sense is that there exist the names 'obstruction' and 'that which emerges from obstruction,' as well as 'stain' and 'that which is not stained.

The text is abbreviated and simply says 'obstruction-stain' (*sgrib dri*). This is likely because [the author] feared that if people saw the subsequent term 'obstruction-stain,' they would [misunderstand it as a single compound]."

Change "two" to "defilement. Question: Why does the current text discuss the obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) by distinguishing them solely in terms of phenomena (*dharma*) and not in terms of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*)?

Answer: The defilement and purity of intrinsic nature and the defilement and purity of phenomena share the same essence but differ in meaning. Here, we follow the difference in meaning and do not distinguish them according to intrinsic nature. Why is this?
Because the defilement and purity of intrinsic nature, being intrinsic nature itself, are essentially fused into a single flavor; although there are two [aspects], [they are one].
Name and reality are of one substance; they do not constitute two distinct substances within a single phenomenon. Question:
Previously it was said that phenomena have no substance and possess only names; why now do you say that a phenomenon has two substances? Answer:

Did I not previously state that regarding what is called "substance," there is the "substance as defined according to the name" (*sui-ming bian-ti*) and the "substance as established by its actual reality" (*ke-shi lun-ti*)? If one defines substance according to the name, then the phenomenon of defilement arises.

The essence of death is [samsāra]; the essence of the purification of phenomena is nirvāṇa. Therefore, the two essences are different. However, if one discusses the essence according to its ultimate reality, both samsāra and nirvāṇa are merely names and appearances.
When discussed according to ultimate reality, their essence is of a single nature. Thus, the phenomena of things have no [independent] essence. Question:
Since the essence has been distinguished according to the names, how can it be that the two names "nature of defilement" and "nature of purity" do not also correspond to their respective names?

Question: Why is it said that there is a substance within phenomena? Answer: Regarding the names "defiled" and "pure" applied to nature (*dhātu*), when one distinguishes the substance according to the name, these two names—defiled and pure—are obtained based on phenomena.
Since the substance is distinguished according to the name, the substance remains a phenomenon; it is merely different in terms of its meaning.
Because the meanings of the defilement and purity of nature differ from those of phenomena, the substance underlying the names "defiled" and "pure" [is distinct].

This refers to the nature (*dhātu*). Since it is the nature, and the nature is ultimately real, it does not possess a dual essence. Therefore, one may say that its essence is fused into a single flavor.

In this way, it further establishes the "treatise on the essential reality" (*keshi lun ti*). Question: Having distinguished the essence according to names, what is the "treatise on the essential reality"?

"Is there a source for this? He replied: "Since the principle and meaning are already correct, why must one seek for the literal expression? Fearing that others might not believe it, I shall now provide proof. Jingxi said:
'The method of establishing names each corresponds to what they signify; therefore, we speak of them in relation to their substance' (this is the same as following the name).

Now that the revelation is complete, the names have no separate referents and the substance has no separate principles" (this is the same as grasping the reality). Furthermore, the text here [regarding] the cause and effect..."
The application of these meanings differs. Previously, there were two sections: first, the Dharma-body was distinguished by means of two matters, as the Dharma-body gives rise to these two matters.
If one follows this meaning, the present text should have stated that "the Dharma-body gives rise to hindrances and emerges from hindrances.

However, the present text instead states that "the true mind, in opposition to its nature, gives rise to defiled phenomena; the true mind, in accordance with its nature, gives rise to pure phenomena. This [approach] differs from what was previously discussed regarding that which is produced, even though—
The capacity to give rise [to phenomena] is the same, yet there is a difference. These two points distinguish the *dharmakāya* in terms of the two natures (*dvividha-svabhāva*).

Although the two matters arising from the two natures are the same as the "capable of giving rise" (*nengqi*) and "given rise to" (*suqi*) in the present text, they differ in how they apprehend the defiled and the pure.

This is because the former does not take what is given rise to, but takes what is capable of giving rise to distinguish the two *dharmakāyas*. The present text, however, does not take what is capable of giving rise to, but takes what is given rise to to distinguish the emergence from obstacles.
Obstruction. Question: What is the distinction between these similarities and differences? Answer: Previously, the two *dharmakāyas* were distinguished based on defilement and purity;

therefore, both the nature (*svabhāva*) and phenomena (*vastu*)—whether defiled or pure—were taken collectively to define the *dharmakāya*. Now, however, obstructions and the transcendence of obstructions are clarified in relation to the *dharmakāya*;

therefore, only the defilement and purity of phenomena are taken specifically to discuss being obstructed or transcending obstruction. This is because the nature of defilement and the nature of purity are essentially fused into a single flavor.

Because it is capable of being severed. How could one discuss that which is obstructed versus that which has emerged from obstruction? One may cultivate the unwholesome and thereby cultivate the purification that severs it.

Therefore, in terms of the phenomenon (*vastu*), one distinguishes between the obstruction and the emergence from obstruction by way of its essence (*bhāva*). Within this essence, that which has already arisen is not taken up.

This is because the distinction between the phenomenon and the essence has already been explained. There is a difference in what can give rise [to these states], for when the phenomenon is distinguished by its essence, it is due to the two natures of defilement and purity.
Because they share the same dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Second, this meaning is explained below through the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), which is divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation, which consists of two sections: being in obstruction and emerging from obstruction. First, being in obstruction:

according to this text, there are five kinds of dharmas, arranged in three layers of subject and object. The five dharmas are: first, defiled karma; second, defiled activity; third, *tathatā* (suchness).
The four are the nature of defilement; the five are the nature of purity. The former two refer to phenomena (*dharma*), while the latter three refer to principle (*tattva*).

Although the substance of phenomena is one, their functional activities are differentiated based on cause and effect, or based on the past and present. Although the substance of principle is one, its aspects of suchness are differentiated based on its essence and its qualities. Regarding the subject and object:
first, the activity of defilement acts as the perfuming agent (*pariṇāmanaka*), while True Suchness in its state of defiled nature acts as the perfumed basis (*pariṇāmya*). Second...
The defiled nature of *tathatā* acts as the producer (*utpādaka*), while the functioning of defilement acts as that which is produced (*utpanna*).
The three functions of defilement act as the opposers and the obstructors, while the pure nature of *tathatā* acts as that which is opposed and that which is obstructed.

Because this pure nature and *tathatā* are of one essence, the state of being obstructed is termed the *dharmakāya*. If explained solely through this principle, the meaning of the text will become clear and self-evident. Question:

The pure nature (*śuddha-svabhāva*) is that which is obstructed; the functioning of defilement (*saṃkleśa-vṛtti*) is that which obstructs. Now, as for this defiled nature, is it that which is obstructed, or is it that which obstructs? Answer:
If one follows the nature toward the defilement, then because the essence of defilement shares the same activity, it belongs to the category of that which obstructs.

If one follows the defilement toward the nature, then because the essence of the nature shares the same principle, it is that which is obstructed. Now, [the text] merely states that the defiled nature is that which gives rise [to obstruction], but does not say...

Regarding that which is obstructed and that which acts as the obstructor: because the names and meanings of "grasping" (upādāna) differ, and because its nature is defiled while the nature [of the object] is pure, it is said that only the functioning of grasping—which accords with the nature—is the obstruction to the illumination of that nature. This is because the two names, "defiled nature" and "pure nature," are distinct.
Because the nature of defilement differs from the object of defilement, it is only the function of defilement that is said to act as an obstruction.

This is because the two meanings of "grasping" (*upādāna*)—namely, the nature of defilement and the object of defilement—are distinct. If one were not to distinguish them by means of their identical substance yet differing meanings, it would likely prove difficult to provide a precise and appropriate interpretation when explaining the preceding and following contexts.
Second, regarding the five factors that emerge from the obstructions, there are likewise five: the agent and the object.

Fourth, the five dharmas: first, pure activity; second, defiled function; third, pure function; fourth, suchness; and fifth, pure nature. Regarding the fourfold relationship between the agent and the object:
first, pure activity is the perfuming agent (*kṣobhaka*), and suchness and pure nature are the objects perfumed (*kṣobhya*).

Second, suchness and pure nature are the agents of origination, and pure function is that which is originated. Third, pure function is the agent of removal, and defiled function is that which is removed.

The four purities function as the manifesting agents (*abhivyañjaka*), while the pure nature of *tathatā* is that which is manifested (*abhivyakta*). If one were to distinguish this in contrast to the state of being obstructed:

within the state of obstruction, there is no purifying function; however, the presently existing undefiled nature exists even within the state of obstruction, yet it lacks both the capacity to remove and the object to be removed.
Thus, the agent and the object are merely three [in number]. This difference arises because, at the time of being obstructed, the purifying function has not yet come into operation. Because...
Because the defiled nature within the state of emerging from obstructions is not manifest; and because the function of the purification of phenomena is not something to be negated.
One should know that these all differ in their functions as they are explained according to the occasion. Now, why is the defiled nature not manifest?
If it were not manifest, how could one claim that the Buddha possesses an inherently evil nature? Furthermore, why is the pure function not negated? If it were not...

How could one claim that "breaking" refers to the icchantika’s severance of the roots of goodness? Now, the defiled nature is not taken as that which is manifested, simply for the sake of conforming to the name "pure illumination" and for the convenience of aspiration.

Now, the pure function is not taken as that which is broken, simply for the sake of conforming to the correct treatise, wherein breaking and manifesting must proceed by returning from the false to the true. As the text says: "The great wisdom of perfect enlightenment, together with the pāramitās..."

Regarding "honey": it refers to the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*), which are designated simply as the function of purity. The distinction between the character *wen* (text) and the character *zhào* (illumination), as well as the difference between their nature and their phenomena, can be understood by one who investigates them.

Second, from "Because of this" onwards, there is the exposition of the simultaneous possession and the gradual possession. First, the simultaneous; second, the gradual; third, from "However, this" onwards, is the concluding indication.

Second, the selection of other meanings. There are two layers of question and answer. Regarding the first question: previously, when discussing the names "defilement" (*mala*) and "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*), the focus was primarily on phenomena (*vastu*).

Now, one asks whether that which contradicts the nature (*dharmatā*) may also be called an obstruction or defilement. [The response is: If it can be so named, then it is indeed an obstruction; it is precisely what is being refuted. Why?
As stated previously, the defiled nature and the pure essence are fused into a single flavor (*ekarasa*) and do not obstruct one another. The text says: "It should..."

Regarding the statement "it is called an obstructive defilement" (*āvaraṇa-kleśa*): "defilement" (*kleśa*) is synonymous with "impurity" (*mala*). This is merely a variation in the phrasing of the text.

If one were to refer to it by its essential nature as "defilement," that has already been mentioned several times previously. The present intention of the question concerns obstructive defilements; thus, the term "defiled impurity" (*kliṣṭa-mala*) is used merely for the sake of continuity in expression. Second, the answer.

Regarding the phrase "both are such": because of the intent of the preceding question—that the nature (*svabhāva*) should be called an obstruction—it is now answered that when nature is designated as an obstruction, it is indeed an obstructive nature, and this obstructive nature is also termed a "nature-obstruction" (*svabhāva-āvaraṇa*).
To say "both are such" reveals that it is not merely a matter of phenomena (*vastu*), nor does it reveal that it is not merely a matter of names being contradictory;
rather, both are designated as "obstructions" and "defilement-obstructions. As for the two terms "nature" and "nature-obstruction" being inverted, it is simply...
The designations differ in this way. Furthermore, by contrast with the obstruction of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), the present obstruction of nature (*prakṛti-āvaraṇa*) is revealed.
Obstruction is itself nature, and nature is itself obstruction; therefore, there are two names. Regarding what is called "the differentiation within equality":

as for the term "differentiation," first, when faults are contrasted with virtues, it is termed either "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*) or "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*). Second, when speaking of the faults themselves, it is termed either "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*) or...
It is called "defilement. Thirdly, it is derived from its designation; it may be termed "obstructive nature" (*āvaraṇa-svabhāva*) or "nature-obstruction" (*svabhāva-āvaraṇa*).

Although these differ in name, their essence is in fact equal. Regarding the "interfusion of subject and object": the obstruction is the subject that obstructs, and the nature is the object that is obstructed.
Now, "nature" (xing) itself is designated as the "obstruction" (zhàng). Since nature is fundamentally interfused, how could the subject (the obstructor) and the object (the obstructed) be distinct?

Furthermore, in this context we are discussing nature; thus, the obstruction is the very agent that obstructs. Since nature is taken as the agent of obstruction, it is the agent of obstruction within the state of perfect interfusion.

The word "object" (suǒ) follows by association from the preceding text; the concluding response merely states, "Do not say they obstruct one another and are not interfused. Therefore, we know that it is precisely through the obstruction [of nature] that [interfusion is established].

Obstruction constitutes the difficulty. The second [section] consists of two parts: question and answer. The first question is: "There must also be a self-nature that exists both within and outside the obstruction. To exist within the obstruction is the nature of defilement;
to exist outside the obstruction is the nature of purity. Although the preceding text mentions both the obstructor and the obstructed, it does so generally with reference to *tathatā* (suchness).

The nature [of phenomena] being obstructed by defilement is termed "defiled nature. Although the subject and object are perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*), it has not yet been explicitly stated that defiled nature is itself pure nature.

The intent of the present question is as follows: since you speak of the equality and differentiation of the perfectly interfused subject and object, and given that defiled nature exists within obstruction while pure nature is beyond obstruction, it should also follow that the very essence of defiled nature is both within and beyond obstruction.

Yes. Based on the intent of this question, which aims to clarify the nature of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), the subsequent answer explains that since the nature of defilement is perfectly interfused and identical to purity, it further demonstrates that the nature of purity is perfectly interfused and identical to defilement. This response is twofold. First, the direct answer.

Initially, it shows the perfect interfusion of the nature of defilement. The text states: "Based on the nature of opposition, it is said that there is not a single pure nature that is not defiled. Regarding the nature of defilement—

There is no separate pure nature apart from the external; rather, it is the very self-nature that acts as the obstructing agent, which is the defiled nature, and the very self-nature that is the object of obstruction, which is the pure nature.
Since there is no pure nature distinct from the defiled nature, it is said that "the self-nature is the object of obstruction.
"Self-nature" refers precisely to the actual substance of the defiled nature. Among the two types of pure nature, it is said that there is not a single instance of defilement.
Regarding "the nature which is not pure": apart from purity, there is no defilement. That which takes its own essence as the agent of removal is the pure nature;

that which takes its own essence as the object of removal is the defiled nature. Since there is no separate defiled nature outside of the pure nature, it is said that "its own essence is the object of removal.
This "own essence" refers to the very substance of the pure nature itself. Within this defiled nature, one perceives perfect interfusion.
As for "therefore": because the self-substance is that which is obstructed, that which is obstructed is precisely the pure nature that emerges from obstruction.
Since defilement is identical to purity, they are thus perfectly interfused. Seeing perfect interfusion within the pure nature occurs because the self-substance is that which is to be removed;
that which is to be removed is precisely the defiled nature existing within obstruction. Since purity is identical to defilement, they are thus perfectly interfused. Furthermore:
Furthermore, the expressions "abiding in hindrance" and "emerging from hindrance" both apply to both the defiled and the pure; they differ only in terms of subject and object.

For instance, taking the True [Nature] as the subject, it abides within hindrance; taking delusion as the object, it is the hindrance in which it resides. Now, because we take that which is resided in [the delusion], it is considered defiled.
If one takes that which is capable of emerging as belonging to the pure, then truth is indeed what emerges from the obstacles, while falsehood is the obstacle from which one emerges;

since we now take that which is capable of emerging, it is therefore pure. If one takes that which emerges as belonging to the defiled, yet considers the nature of defilement itself to be that which is to be eliminated, one might fear that people will doubt this, wondering how a nature that is inherently evil could be severed—how then can it be called "that which is eliminated"? Now, let us inquire further.
Regarding this passage, which states that "the self-substance is that which is to be eliminated": is it a cultivation or is it an inherent nature?

If one says it is a cultivation, the current text itself states that there is not a single defiled nature that is not pure. Since it is an inherent nature, we know that the defiled nature is what is to be eliminated. Furthermore, let us inquire:
when the text says that "the self-substance is the obstacle," is this the defilement of the nature? And as for the defilement of the nature...

Since it has already been established as that which can obstruct, how could it not be that which is to be eliminated? Thus, one knows that the defilement and purity of the nature have no separate substance;
their substance consists in cultivation. Therefore, only upon attainment do the names "that which can obstruct" and "that which is to be eliminated" arise.

Now, having realized that the single nature is fully endowed with both defilement and purity, this very nature is called the "nature that can obstruct" and the "nature that is to be eliminated. Although there are these two names, [they refer to the same reality].

In reality, there are no two distinct entities; therefore, that which can obstruct is not an obstruction, and that which is to be eliminated is not eliminated. These are merely names; they do not exist as anything other than a single nature.
One who understands this in such a way will see that nature is omnipresent, and that its omnipresence is nothing other than nature itself—an inconceivable, naturally wondrous essence.
Second, regarding the meaning: because of the two designations "defiled" and "pure," there are no two distinct entities. Since there are no two distinct entities...

Therefore, defilement and purity are mutually identical. Since they are mutually identical, they are of one flavor and equal. Although they are of one flavor and equal, this does not obstruct the two designations.
Thus, there is the dharma-gate of consciousness being both constant and different, and the principle of equality and differentiation.

Investigating this according to the intended meaning of this exposition, we know that the second question and answer concerns the differentiation between the defilement and purity of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*).

Regarding the three aspects of the mutual inclusion of the functions of these four matters: first, the heading; second, the explanation, which begins with the question. First, the question: "As for the essential nature... up to [the end].

"Can be understood in part" means that because the previously explained self-nature of defilement and purity exists in a state of being obstructed or unobstructed—and because there is no purity outside of defilement and no defilement outside of purity—they are said to be "perfectly interfused.
Because the underlying principle has already been clarified, it is said to be "understandable. Because those at the initial stage hear this for the first time, it is called "in part.
Furthermore, it is called "in part" because they understand only the principle (*li*) but have not yet understood the phenomena (*shi*). This concludes the preceding statement.

Regarding the question of what the characteristics of phenomenal dharmas (*vastu-dharma*) are: it was previously stated within the Dharma-gate of the Perfectly Interfused and Unobstructed Dharmadhātu that "therefore, worldly and supramundane phenomena are likewise perfectly interfused, mutually inclusive, and unobstructed; the worldly is defiled, while the supramundane is pure.
Now, referring back to the aforementioned passage, it is said that defiled and pure phenomenal dharmas may also be mutually inclusive in an unobstructed manner. However...

Above, the mutual inclusion of phenomena (*dharma*) has been analyzed; since their efficacy arises from the principle (*tattva*), the essential meaning is already clear. Now, as for the question "What are their characteristics?":
first, although one hears that phenomena are integrated by virtue of the principle, one now doubts whether there might be some phenomena that are not so integrated;
second, although one hears that phenomena are integrated by virtue of the principle, the specific characteristics of this integration have never been extensively demonstrated. Therefore—
This question will be explained in detail following its presentation.
The response has three parts. First, the direct answer to the preceding objection has two parts. First, the general formulation:

"If one addresses it specifically regarding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and so forth," one must understand that, when analyzed, there are three principles of phenomena (*dharma*). First, the deluded subjectivity that grasps; second, the objects that are grasped.

Regarding the three aspects: first, the phenomena of deluded attachment; second, the deluded mind that clings to them; and third, the ultimate truth upon which they depend. If one follows the objects of attachment according to the subjective clinging, those objects remain entirely unharmonized.
However, if one follows the objects of attachment according to the principle upon which they depend, those objects can be seen to mutually encompass one another.

To speak of "the objects of deluded attachment through discrimination" means that the characteristics of the phenomena follow after the subjective mind. To speak of "the dependent origination of the nature of the mind" means that one relies upon the fundamental nature of the mind.
Regarding the function of support: it is precisely because phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa) follow from principle (li). Thus, these phenomena may be either fused or not fused. Question:

If one follows this teaching, where principle is fused while emotions are obstructed, and phenomena are neither fused nor obstructed yet are both fused and obstructed—why was it previously stated that phenomena are "fused and obstructed"?
Answer: If one understands that phenomena are themselves the equal essence-nature (tattva-svabhāva), which is neither phenomenon nor principle, then for this reason—
Phenomena are neither fused nor obstructed. If a phenomenon is considered from its own essence (*svabhāva*), it is obstructed; if it is considered from its basis (*āśraya*), it is fused.
Taken together, phenomena are both fused and obstructed. When it was previously said that the essence of a phenomenon is obstructed, this was precisely from the perspective of its own essence.
When the present text says that phenomena clung to through delusion are not fused, this is precisely because they are the very essence of the phenomenon itself.

This is precisely why they are not fused. Regarding the mutual inclusion of the functional aspects of the mind-nature and dependent origination: this refers to phenomena (*dharma*). They are mutually inclusive by virtue of their basis. Question:
Why has it not been explained directly from the standpoint of the essential nature of phenomena thus far, but rather stated that "phenomena arise from emotional afflictions as obstructions"?

Answer: There are two meanings regarding the cause by which the characteristics of phenomena are obtained. If one proceeds from the standpoint of their essential nature, then [they are included] based on...
They exist through deluded sentiment; because of non-awakening, objective realms arise. If one follows their basis, they exist by depending upon true nature (*dharmatā*).
Since that which is unchanging itself functions as the conforming condition (*pratyaya*), this phenomenal aspect has two roots:
its essence follows from sentiment, while its basis follows from nature. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "All sentient beings do not know these two kinds of roots."
The first is the root of beginningless birth and death; it is that which you and all sentient beings now take as your own nature—the mind of grasping and dependence.
The second is the pure essence of beginningless bodhi and nirvāṇa;

it is that which is now set aside by the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-dhātu*) and ignorance, which are capable of producing all conditions. For this reason, it is called "phenomenal characteristics" (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*).

From the perspective of emotion (*qing*), there is obstruction; from the perspective of nature (*xing*), there is integration. Question: One may simply say that the substance and characteristics (*ti-xiang*) are obstructed by emotion.

Why, then, do you say that the phenomenal characteristics (*shi-xiang*) are themselves obstruction in their very substance? Answer: Because the substance of phenomenal characteristics has both a "substance as support" (*you-yi-ti*) and a "substance as its own being" (*dang-ti-ti*).
Nature is the support, while emotion is the substance as its own being. This meaning is difficult to perceive; I shall now use the analogy of waves to illustrate it.
There are two fundamental causes from which waves arise: first, they arise from water; second, they arise from wind.
As for the essence of a wave, motion constitutes its primary nature, while water serves as its basis. Regarding the motion of a wave, such motion necessarily arises from the wind.
Therefore, one should know that wind itself constitutes the substance of the wave, while water itself is the basis upon which the wave depends.

By using this analogy to contemplate phenomena (*dharma*), the underlying principle becomes clear. Since the substance and its state are identical, one knows that the substance itself is characterized by obstruction.

Question: Can it be said that water itself constitutes the substance of the wave? Answer: This meaning also exists. Question: How does this differ from [the claim] that motion itself constitutes the substance? Answer: If one follows...

This is called "discerning the essence. Therefore, the wave takes movement as its actual essence. However, if one discusses the essence according to reality, the wave and its movement have no essence other than being a mere appearance;
when discussing it according to reality, water is taken as the essence. Question: One can only take water as the supporting essence (*āśraya*).
Why do you say that water is the actual essence of the wave? Answer: In fact, water is the support for the wave; [it is] the actual...
The name "substance" (*ti*) is derived from its initial state. Initially, movement was taken as the substance itself; now, by means of the realization of reality, that initial state is sublated.
This substance is entirely identical to water. The intent is to clarify that there is no separate substance, but rather that the substance itself is entirely the basis upon which it depends.
If one follows this meaning, it may also be said that the subsequent substance is both fused and wondrous. Or, as it is said: "As if..."
The reasoning of the previous argument is incorrect. In truth, when phenomena correspond to their essence, they are eternally identical and eternally fused;

they are not actually separate or distinct. It is only due to emotional attachments that they are perceived as being apart or as obstacles. These obstructions reside in the mind, not in the phenomena themselves. Let us therefore employ the analogy of waves and water to clarify this principle:
the waves are like phenomena, and the water is like the fundamental nature. The waves are eternally identical to the water, and the nature is eternally [identical to the phenomena].
It is the very nature [of the waves]. There has never been a day when waves were separate from water; there has never been a moment when a phenomenon was not identical to its nature.

It is only because deluded people claim that the waves are not water—just as they claim that phenomena are not their nature—that they speak thus. This delusion arises from emotional obstruction, not from a separation between the phenomenon and its nature;

therefore, one cannot say that the essence of the phenomenon is itself an obstruction. To say today that "the phenomenon is the actual substance" is false; to say that "the nature is the actual substance" is the truth.
Furthermore, to know through delusion is to be lost in confusion and emotion; to know through reality is to attain awakening and wisdom.
To be deluded regarding reality and follow delusion is to falsely claim that phenomena are not harmonized; thus, the non-harmonization of phenomena is itself delusion.
To follow delusion while clinging to reality is to mistake the nature for phenomena—all of this is delusion. To awaken to that delusion and follow reality is, indeed, reality.

It is because one knows that phenomena are capable of being integrated. Thus, that which is capable of integration means to realize the delusive and follow the real; it is to point to phenomena and see them as identical to their nature.
These are all the real. Delusion is said to be non-integration; the substance of phenomena is delusive, and therefore phenomena are not integrated. True knowledge is capable of integration.

The substantial entity is the nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, the capacity to integrate is found in the nature; the function of integration resides in the nature, while the function of obstruction resides in phenomena (*vastu*).
Thus, the substance of phenomena is obstruction. As for the statement that "the waves are always identical to the water," this is because the entirety of the water constitutes the waves;

therefore, the waves are always identical to the water. This is the function of the water. That the waves are not identical to the water is because the substance of water is stillness, whereas the substance of the waves is motion. Motion...
To be hidden in stillness yet to see only its movement and not its stillness—this is the function of the waves.
Speaking in truth, since the source is water, how has it ever not been such? This is spoken from the perspective of one who possesses knowledge.
To speak falsely, one sees only its movement and not its stillness, claiming that the waves are not water; this is spoken from the perspective of the deluded. As for the deluded person...
From this day forward, let us speak only of what is seen in the place of movement; therefore, the wave is "not identical" [to the water].

When one knows that it is precisely from the original source that the water is seen, then the wave is "identical. That which is "not identical" is delusion; that which is eternally "identical" is reality.

Delusion is obtained through phenomena; reality is obtained through nature. Thus, while phenomena are obstructive, nature is harmonious; its principle is self-evident. Now, for the sake of those who are obscured, I shall explain further.
To speak further: the essence of the Dharma-realm does not transcend phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*). Phenomena are the essence of deluded emotions and false imaginings;
principle is the essence of realized wisdom and ultimate truth. Wisdom and reality are inherently fused, whereas delusion and falsehood constitute obstruction.
Therefore, the function of fusion resides in principle and wisdom; the function of obstruction resides in phenomena and emotion. If one were to say that the function of obstruction resides in...
Sentiment does not reside in the phenomenon; it must be dissolved through effort, and this effort lies in wisdom, not in principle.

If one says that by means of wisdom one accords with principle and is thus able to dissolve [sentiment], then it must follow that by means of sentiment one conforms to phenomena and is thus able to obstruct [wisdom].

Some claim that the function of obstruction lies in sentiment, while the function of dissolution lies in the phenomenon; they claim that the function of differentiation lies in sentiment, while the function of non-differentiation lies in the phenomenon.
Regarding the phenomenon (*vastu*): if this were so, the essence of the phenomenon could not constitute a distinction.

If one claims that the phenomenon is a "distinction within non-distinction," unlike the fixed distinctions of conventional sentiment, this is merely to be deluded by the name while failing to seek its meaning.

Because of such delusion regarding sentiment, one loses the principle from the very substance of the phenomenon; thus it is called "fixed distinction. Because of understanding through wisdom, one [perceives] from the phenomenon...
Because one attains the principle by relying upon it, it is called "the non-differentiation of differentiation. In reality, the two types of differentiation share the same essence;
they are merely given two names due to the attainment or loss of the principle. How could it be that while there is emotional differentiation, there is no differentiation in phenomena?

Nevertheless, it is the emotional intellect that is capable of both delusion and awakening, whereas phenomena and principle are the objects of delusion and awakening. Although in delusion one is deluded regarding both phenomena and principle, it is only...

The substance of delusion resides in phenomena; therefore, it is said that "delusion refers to the internal and external. Although awakening involves awakening to both phenomena and principle, the substance of awakening resides in principle;
therefore, it is said that "awakening is solely the one mind. When it is said that sentient beings possess only principle, this is precisely discussing their merit from the perspective of phenomena.

When it is said that Buddhas have attained phenomena, this is precisely explaining the meaning from the perspective of principle. This purport is profound and subtle, yet people find it difficult to penetrate.
[The commentary] says: "If one does not penetrate this, what can be done?

Second, the explanation of the characteristics of the lower [stages]. This has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the mutual inclusion of the many and few among ordinary beings and sages.

Regarding the first, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra*, which says: "The Buddha sees that within the minds of all sentient beings, there is a Tathāgata sitting in the full lotus posture."
Now, regarding the mention of "pores," we know that whether it be form or mind, all are fully possessed by the Buddhas.

Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) points out that although sentient beings possess [the Buddha-nature], it is merely their "principle-nature" (*lixing*). This is because the eleven realms have not yet manifested; therefore, they are termed "nature" (*xing*) rather than "manifestation" (*shi*).

They are called the "ten cultivated" because they have already been manifested. Although there are two names—nature and cultivation—in rigorous analysis of their essence, there is nothing that is not of a single nature.

The entire body constitutes the ten; therefore, when discussing the mutual possession of each of the ten realms of nature and cultivation, the Buddha-realm of nature possesses the sentient-being realm of nature, the sentient-being realm of nature possesses the Buddha-realm of nature, and the sentient-being realm of cultivation possesses the Buddha-realm of cultivation.
Regarding the "dhātu" (realm): in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), it is stated that by cultivating the Buddha-realm, one fully cultivates sentient beings;

thus, from the perspective of nature (*prakṛti*), sentient beings possess the Buddha-realm of nature, and because this distinguishes the fullness based on nature, it is said to be merely the "nature-realm" (*li-xing*).

However, in the present text, since the mutual inclusion of phenomena (*dharma*) is clarified, it is stated that within the cultivation of sentient beings, one fully cultivates the fruit of Buddhahood. Furthermore, in the *Fuxing*, it is explicitly taught that each possesses [the other]; therefore, [it refers to] deluded sentient beings.
Sentient beings inherently possess the ten realms. Since the Buddha-realm they possess has not yet been perfumed and has never manifested, it exists merely as the principle-nature (*ri-sei*).
Now, in discussing mutual possession, sentient beings within delusion possess all Buddhas of the ten directions who are currently manifesting perfect enlightenment;
therefore, they also possess the phenomena of cultivation. Furthermore, in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), this is discussed by contrasting awakening with delusion.

Regarding giving and taking: because the Buddha has already awakened, his awakening is not distinct from that which is awakened to; the phenomenon of awakening is itself the principle. Since the principle is able to be interfused, phenomena are likewise complete.

Therefore, it is said that the Buddha is able to possess all phenomena, and thus it is called the "fulfillment of the Buddha-fruit. Speaking from the perspective of phenomena, sentient beings are deluded;
their delusion is not distinct from that which is deluded, yet the phenomenon of delusion is not the principle. Since the phenomenon is not the principle, the principle cannot be interfused with it.

Therefore, the phenomena are not fully accounted for; rather, the phenomena are set aside to emphasize their underlying principle. Thus it is said that they are "merely the rational nature. This is why the expression "separated by fruition" arises.
Furthermore, it is stated that even down to ordinary beings, there is merely the rational inclusion.

The present text does not discuss the setting aside of phenomena, but rather accords with them according to the dharma-principle. Therefore, it discusses inclusion in terms of phenomena. Second, regarding the length of the ten [stages] and below...

The large and the small encompass one another; the three periods of time, when condensed into a single thought, become long and short, while a minute speck of dust in the ten directions becomes large and small.

For this reason, the following passage cites scriptural evidence, the textual characteristics of which confirm only the inclusion of the large and small, as well as the long and short. Furthermore, within the discussion of the "long," it itself treats the mutual inclusion of these characteristics.

Third, the subsequent examples below clarify the intended meaning of the analysis. The first example clarifies that the phenomena under discussion (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*) and their mutual inclusion do not exceed the ten realms (*daśadhātu*), consisting of the primary retribution (*sambhoga*) and its basis (*āśraya*).
Within the primary retribution, if one summarizes them broadly, there is nothing that does not result in the manifestation of a Buddha.

Within the environmental retribution (*bhogya*), if one excludes them broadly, there is nothing that does not result in the ten directions. Now, regarding this basis and primary retribution, various dharmas are cited in detail, yet they are summarized briefly.
An example is provided to clarify the meaning that there is nothing that does not mutually include one another. Therefore, it is said: "The remaining pure and impure [realms], and so forth, up to:

'and those dharmas that are not specifically paired, are all mutually inclusive. As for what are called 'not specifically paired' (bùduìfǎ), they are termed 'not paired' because they are not fixedly paired."
It is not that there is no resistance; for instance, when one lifts a brush, it faces the inkstone. It need not face the inkstone alone—it may also face the ink or the paper.
Therefore, this brush is called a phenomenon that does not face [a specific object]. This is unlike cases such as purity necessarily facing impurity, or existence necessarily facing non-existence.
The second section clarifies the underlying intent. Regarding the phrase "characteristics have no self-substance" (*svabhāva*): "substance" (*shí*) refers to essence (*tǐ*).

Because characteristics lack their own essence, their essence is the true mind; therefore, it is said that their arising must depend on the mind. Since the essence of the mind is already interfused, the mind must possess an essence.

This essence is precisely the reality; because it is real, it is interfused. Alternatively, one may say that "arising must depend on the mind" refers to the deluded mind. As for the essence of the mind...
As for "fusion" (*rong*): the substance of this deluded mind is itself the true nature (*dharmatā*). Since the nature is itself fusion, it is thus fused.

If one explains it in this way, then although there is a sequence—arising from manifestation and from marks, arising from deluded thought, and deluded thought arising from the true nature—since the true nature is already fused, deluded thought is fused;
since deluded thought is fused, phenomenal characteristics are fused. Discussing fusion in terms of phenomena, it is precisely [the fusion of] delusion.
To "contemplate" refers to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). That their efficacy lies in the ultimate harmony arising from true nature (*tathatā*) is as it is.

Alternatively, if one asks why phenomena do not harmonize in their own essence despite being inherently harmonious—remaining unharmonized only due to emotional afflictions (*kleśa*)—please consider this in light of the present text.

If phenomena were inherently harmonious in their own essence, why would it be necessary to state that "since the essence of the mind is harmonious, its characteristics are also unimpeded"? Furthermore, although the explanation follows a sequential order...

First, regarding the manifestation: the underlying intent is actually identical in both cases. Nevertheless, even though they coincide at the same time, one must not confuse or obscure the principles of the Dharma. Question:
What is the difference between this and the claim made by people of old that "only when form is subsumed into mind is it complete"?

Answer: First, the words are the same while the meanings differ; second, both the words and the meanings differ. Regarding the first case, where the words are the same but the meanings differ: if one takes the perspective of delusory [phenomena], then both form and mind are [delusory].
That which is called "form" (rūpa) is, in truth, such that both form and mind are collectively termed "mind. One may also say that by subsuming form into mind, form is only then fully realized.

If one were to claim that what accompanies the mental faculty (manas) is distinct [from this], one must know that the natural single nature (prakṛti-ekalakṣaṇa) is neither called form nor called mind;
it is only through worldly convention that it is provisionally designated as "form" or "mind. If one were to designate the natural single nature as "mind," then...
When false form and false mind are subsumed within the mind, only then are form and mind fully present.

Therefore, it is not merely that form is subsumed into the mind, but that the mind is likewise subsumed into the mind. If one names the natural single nature "form," then false form and false mind are subsumed within form;
only then are form and mind fully present. Therefore, it is not merely that form is subsumed into form, but that the mind is likewise subsumed into form.

Regarding "form" (rūpa): this is because when phenomena are subsumed within principle, their full significance is realized. The merit lies in the principle, while the application pertains to phenomena.
If one were to analyze directly from the perspective of phenomena alone, then both the deluded mind and deluded form would each be complete;

it would not necessarily be a matter of subsuming form and mind into mind, or subsuming form and mind into form. These two meanings differ according to the specific discourse, yet their essential intent is that they are simultaneous.

Regarding the differences in explanations: for instance, when the Great Master analyzed that a single moment of mind (*ekakṣaṇa-citta*) is endowed with the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), he stated that they are "not the same" out of fear that people would fail to grasp the reason for this endowment. Worldly people cling to fixed characteristics of identity or difference;
however, a single moment of mind is neither identical nor different, yet it is spoken of as "one. This is explained from the perspective of the ultimate function and its source. Great!
The Master further stated: "Even a mustard seed possessing a mind is endowed with the three thousand [dharmas]," and he also said: "Only fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth.

This is a direct explanation based on the phenomena themselves. Furthermore, if one were to directly base an easy point upon a phenomenon to facilitate understanding of a difficult one, one would necessarily ask:
"How does form possess [the three thousand]? The answer would be: "Because form is itself mind."
Sixth, the two-fold selection of other meanings. First, the double demonstration. First, the question. This question arises from a failure to understand the term "inclusion" (*she*).

Now, first, I shall clarify its meaning by means of the answering text. There are three [aspects]: first, mutual inclusion (*xiang she*); second, mutual equality (*xiang deng*); third, mutual identity (*xiang ji*).
If one understands them well, inclusion and the others are these three; though their names differ, their essence is in fact no different. This is for the sake of those who do not understand.

Therefore, according to the names, the meanings are understood differently, resulting in distinctions. Regarding "mutual inclusion" (xiāngshè): the large enters the small, and the small enters the large.
Regarding "mutual identity" (xiāngděng): although the large does not enter the small, the large is identical to the small;
although the small does not enter the large, the small is identical to the large. Regarding "mutual identity" (xiāngjí): it is not only that the large is identical to the small, but also...
Thus, the great is itself the small; it is not only that the small is identical to the great, but also that the small is itself the great.

Because of this principle, there are levels of depth; because they are identical, they are equal; and because they are equal, they mutually encompass one another. Therefore, the intent of the present question is:
since they can mutually encompass one another, must they necessarily be equal? The answer below states: "It is not merely that they..."
These [terms] are likewise mutually identical. The answer consists of two parts: first, the direct response; second, the explanation of the underlying intent beginning with "How so...

The phrase "constant identity and constant difference" appears here to clarify the mutual inclusion of phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, this "constant identity and constant difference" is spoken in reference to the functional activity of phenomena.
The second round of question and answer involves a commoner challenging a sage. The response states that because the sage acts in accordance with principle (*li*), all his deeds are successful;

thus, one knows that the integration of phenomena depends upon principle. Because the sage has realized principle, he is able to integrate them. The commoner, however, is deluded regarding principle and perceives only phenomena.

Since the substance of phenomena is identical to [the nature of] mental states (*qing*), it is said that their emotional attachments deviate from the ultimate intent. Therefore, [they do not succeed].
It is so. Some say that when the Sage speaks of "bestowing and acting according to principle" (*li*), it is because he is responding to biased attachments;
thus, both phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*) are equally termed "principle. Nevertheless, its perfectly interfused essence is not devoid of phenomena.

Now, when it is said that phenomena and principle are both termed "principle" in response to biased attachments, does this mean that one takes the fact that phenomena are themselves principle as the reason for the designation "principle"? Or does one take the phenomena...
The term "principle" (li) is established by its very essence. I request those of wisdom to investigate this meaning closely; you will surely admit that what I have now stated is correct. Question:
One might say that the single character "principle" refers to the *dao-li* (the principle of the Way) rather than *xing-li* (the nature of the Way).
Since the principle of inconceivable phenomena is fundamentally fused, the Sage speaks of this principle such that phenomena are fused. Answer: The following passage poses a question.

It is said that if a sage attains the principle (*li*), they should not perceive distinct characteristics (*biphas*). Is this question not prompted by the present passage stating that "sages accord with the principle"?

This is made clear because the "principle" here is not the conventional sense of "reasoning" (*daoli*). Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "True nature (*zhenxing*) is shared by all sentient beings;
because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to attain this principle, they possess great function (*dayong*). How could it be otherwise?
Is it not that the Great Master received this teaching from Nanyue? Furthermore, even if one were to employ the logic of *yukti* (reasoning), it would not undermine the meaning established here.
Why is this? For instance, phenomena (*vastu*) are characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); what other principle could there be by which they might be mutually subsumed?

The intent of the third set of questions and answers is as follows: From the perspective of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the principle-nature (*li-ti*) is without differentiation and without characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

However, in terms of phenomenal function (*shi-yong*), there are distinctions and characteristics. Contemporary scholars often say that the principle is "without characteristics," meaning it lacks fixed or singular characteristics;
they do not mean that it is entirely devoid of characteristics. Please examine the present text: when the Sage attains the principle, he does not perceive distinct characteristics.

Is it to establish a determinate characteristic, or an indeterminate characteristic? If you say that no determinate characteristic is perceived, why do you speak of encompassing the Great Dharma by means of those minor matters?
Therefore, one knows that from the perspective of the essential nature (*dharmatā*), even indeterminate characteristics may be extinguished.
This is because the essence of characteristics (lakṣaṇa) is in fact a single differentiated dharma-gate. Because one has not attained the principle, it becomes a fixed characteristic;
because one has attained the principle, it becomes an unfixed characteristic. Regarding the discussion of "perishing," it does not go beyond two meanings:

first, concerning the fixed and unfixed characteristics of the dharma-essence itself—when they perish, both perish together; when they exist, both exist together. This is because the essence of these two characteristics is in fact one.

Second, by means of the identity and difference [of phenomena], fixed characteristics are eliminated and indeterminate characteristics are preserved. This is answered by way of both "being identical" and "not being identical.

The intended meaning is that the Tathāgata not only realizes [the truth] but also attains its functional application; therefore, all those for whom characteristics do not exist are fully realized and attained.
The fourth section has two parts. First, the question: It asks by distinguishing between essence (*tattva*) and function (*vṛtti*).
Since the essence of equality is fundamentally devoid of characteristics, with respect to what could one discuss inclusion or non-inclusion?

Since the essence of phenomenal function is inherently differentiated, even if it is said that the Tathāgata does not destroy this function, how can the Great and Small Vehicles mutually encompass one another? Second, the answer: It explains the mutual identity of essence and function.
And he replied.

Regarding the fifth section on the two [aspects], first is the question: Since the previous answer stated only that "essence is function" (*ti ti shi yong*), and that essence is principle while function is phenomena—thereby establishing only the non-obstruction between phenomenon and principle (*shi-li wu-ai*)—how can one perceive the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai*)? For this reason, this question is posed. Alternatively, it may be said:
Since the Three Truths are already perfectly subtle and wondrous, why did the Great Master need to further speak of the three thousand [dharmas]?

Now it is said that the explicit teaching of the Three Truths consists solely in the mutual identity of phenomenon and principle. This is because he did not say that "one is false and all are false," nor that "there is no falsity that is not [the truth of] falsity."
Therefore, the three thousand phenomena are such that their phenomena mutually interpenetrate. Although this is so from the perspective of words, in meaning there is no difference.

This second answer does not go beyond the fact that the merit resides in principle (li) and the application resides in phenomena (fa) and phenomena (shi). As for what is called "application resides in phenomena and phenomena":

first, phenomena can be identical with principle; second, phenomena can be identical with phenomena. It is simply because one realizes that principle is harmoniously fused that there is no phenomenon that is not identical [with others]. This is due to the One.
All phenomena are, in their entirety, the principle (*li*). For this reason, all phenomena are mutually identical;

since even an ordinary body is identical to the golden body, how much more so is it that the *zhànglù* (sixteen-foot) form is not identical to the *zàngchén* (dust-mote) [form]? Question: Regarding what is called "the ordinary body is identical to the golden body,"...

Why does the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) state that "each and every realm-fruit possesses ten [realms] individually, without mutual confusion"? Answer: It is precisely because they possess them individually that this statement is made.
Furthermore, the text below says: "The mutual pervasion of each and every three-thousandfold world system is likewise.

Is it not the case that the ordinary body is itself the golden body? Moreover, within the context of individual possession, take for instance the Buddha’s possession of the ten realms; how could it be otherwise?
Is it that when one attains the realization that the realm of hell is itself the realm of the Buddha, this is the "Buddha-realm of the Buddha-realm"? Question: This principle is difficult to believe.

For instance, as we currently perceive the appearance of form, how could it be identical to the fragrance of the *lan-xiang* flower? Answer: It is difficult to believe for one who studies as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), but it is easy to understand for one who studies the Buddha.
Question: Previously, you stated that there is a distinction between the phenomenal activity (*vastu*) and its essential nature (*svabhāva*). If that is so, what is the nature of this phenomenon?
[Objection: This would be the same as [the view that] all phenomena are like dust. Why does the current text reject this from the perspective of "phenomena" (*shi*)?

[Answer: Here we are taking the actual reality to discuss the essence. What is called "phenomenon" is merely a name and appearance. [Question: If the function of a phenomenon depends upon principle (*li*), then it results in the mutual identity of phenomenon and principle;

one has not yet seen the mutual fusion of phenomena themselves. [Answer: Although the function resides in principle, the manifestations of the phenomena are distinct. This is due to the relationship between phenomenon and principle...

The mutual identity of phenomena (*xiāng jí*) refers to the dialectical relationship between essence and function; the mutual identity of all phenomena (*shìshì xiāngjí*) refers to the internal differentiation of function itself.

If one points to this function as existing in the fruit and claims it is entirely identical to the principle of the causal stage of sentient beings, one has not yet reached the ultimate intent of the Buddha.
The sixth section has two parts. First, the question: Externalists calculate that the self is all-pervasive yet not of a single mode;

some calculate that the self is large while the object is small and the object is within the self, others calculate that the self is small while the object is large and the self is within the object, and still others calculate that the self and the object are distinct.

Alternatively, one may reckon that the self and material objects are identical. Now, to provide a general account of these reckonings: Question: How does this differ from the pervasiveness of the True Mind?

Answer: There are two [points]. First, the presentation of external attachments and views. Second, first, the view that the self and material objects are distinct. "Subtle, wondrous, and vast" refers precisely to the reckoning that the self is great while material objects are small.
Second, "Even if," etc., refers to the reckoning that the self and material objects are identical. "This and that do not merge" refers to the self...

The essence is without marks. When the self is confronted with objects, it is immediately identical with them. Since the substance of objects is real, when objects are confronted with one another, they do not merge;
this is precisely to adhere to what is perceived by the world. Why? Because among the myriad things of the world, every object is formed through its identity with empty space.
Therefore, one clings to the divine self as being identical with space and with objects; yet, when it comes to the myriad objects themselves, each and every object...
Each is distinct; this entity cannot be that entity. Therefore, by clinging to the reality of things, the "this" and "that" do not merge.

Second, showing the internal [nature] reveals it is not dual. First, the heading. Second, "Knowing one... and below, the explanation of the two. First, showing the internal. Second, "It is not called... and below, revealing that it does not fail to emerge.
Second, the intent differs from that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): the characteristics of phenomena are fundamentally empty, yet the deluded take them to be real. The Buddha...
The Dharma knows emptiness; these two points are not the same. Therefore, it is said that this does not mean there is a real entity existing outside the mind.

This is precisely what is meant by "immediacy" (*ji*). The entirety of phenomenal phenomena is itself the true mind. As for the second point, although one might say they are "immediate," this would imply a union between a divine self (*śuddhātman*) and external objects;
thus, the meaning of "immediacy" would not be established. These two points are not the same. Therefore, it is said that it is not called "pervasiveness" because the mind exists within [the objects].

[This] is the arrival [of the conclusion]. Third, regarding this matter, the skillful means are shown again in three parts: first, the internal teacher poses the question; second, the outsider joyfully accepts;
