The Knowledge of Others' Minds. Third, the śramaṇa says: "In that case, [the following]... This section consists of two parts: first, the general summary; second, the detailed exposition. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections. First, showing that the essence of mind is one.

Because it is spoken of from the perspective of the essence of mind, there is neither large nor small; yet when explained from the perspective of the function of mind, large and small appear distinctly. Now, from...
This is the essence of the mind; thus it is said that since the mind is one, there is neither large nor small.

Second, below the section on "pores," it demonstrates the mind as the substance of things, pointing to this single mind as the substance of all things; therefore, the two objects—large and small—are fused into identity.

The second section, "By means of this," consists of two parts concerning the meaning and intent. First, the mutual inclusion of the characteristics of dependent origination, which has two sub-sections.
First, the demonstration of how these characteristics include one another, which begins with the mutual inclusion of the Great and the Small. The text states, "For this reason":

because it was previously explained that the essence of mind is singular and can serve as the essence of all things, by virtue of this principle of essential unity, the characteristics of small objects are cited to include the characteristics of great objects; there is no great object [that is not so included].

This is not the characteristic of a small object; it is the same when the great encompasses the small. Since their function arises from both the large and the small while their essence remains one, the two characteristics—the large and the small—are mutually integrated.
Within this integration, there is no "small" that is inferior. Yet, the characteristics of the large and the small remain distinct and vivid.

First, it is shown that the absence of the small characteristic does not mean it lacks the large characteristic. When the large characteristic enters the small characteristic, the large characteristic is not diminished; thus, there is no "large."
The characteristics are not small characteristics; thus, small characteristics accommodate great characteristics without the small characteristics increasing.

This efficacy arises because the two bodies are one and lack [distinctions of] large and small. Therefore, when the two characteristics of phenomena are mutually encompassed, the large and small remain perfectly distinct.

The second section below cites scriptural evidence. The passage concerning the mutual inclusion of large and small characteristics remaining perfectly distinct appears in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*. However, this scriptural text...
Regarding the discussion of the inconceivable (*acintya*): the masters of our school each hold different views.
Some say that "inconceivable function" refers to the fact that the functional activity of phenomena is itself inherently inconceivable; therefore, they are able to interpenetrate one another.

Others say that "inconceivable function" refers to the magnitude of the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) of the nature; therefore, their mutual interpenetration is not merely a matter of phenomenal function. Now, I shall follow the fundamental reality of the Dharma.

The "inconceivable" (*acintya*) refers to the essence of nature (*svabhāva*). "Function" (*yòng*) refers to phenomenal appearances (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Taking nature as phenomena, and realizing that phenomena are nature, is therefore termed "inconceivable.

[In the first school, they fail to realize this: function and phenomena cannot be harmonized; their success depends on attaining nature to achieve harmony. [In the second school, they fail to realize this: nature has no magnitude;
their success depends on the magnitude of the phenomena through which it is accessed. Furthermore, regarding "attaining nature to achieve harmony," Nanyue said: "A single hair..."
The pore and the city are both entirely taken as the substance of the single mind. One should know that the substance of the pore and the city is fused and equal.
For this reason, the small is cited to encompass the large. Although the text relies upon the deluded mind, its intent is to clarify true nature (*tathatā*). The Great Master said:
"If one attains the smallness of the true nature of a mustard seed, it can contain the greatness of Mount Sumeru; if one attains the true nature of Mount Sumeru..."
The greatness of the nature does not obstruct the smallness of a mustard seed. Jingxi said: "Question:

Since true nature is inherently in harmony with real wisdom, how does it relate to external objects such that one speaks of the mutual entry of the large and the small? It is because of the realization of principle. Answer: "Indeed, this true nature pervades the dharma-realm;

those who are deluded perceive internal and external, while those who have awakened realize it is but the One Mind. Furthermore, as for the large and the small being derived from phenomena, [as stated by] Nanyue..."

It is said that if one relies on the meaning of the equality of the substance of the mind (*citta-tattva*) in relation to that [truth], then the characteristics of "great" and "small" have never existed from the beginning.

"Now we explain that there is no mind, no thought, no agent who practices, and no destination reached—this is the inconceivable principle (*tattva*). How does this differ from what you have just stated? Answer: It is not the same as what I have just stated. Question: Some say that the inherent virtues (prakṛti-guṇa) possess both the large and small natures, and that these two natures are, in their very place, a single essence that is inconceivable.
Therefore, the large can accommodate the small, and the small can accommodate the large. However, because the inherent virtues are suited to quiescence, they are difficult to comprehend.
Therefore, one relies upon the phenomena of events to manifest the nature’s virtue of the mutual containment of the large and the small.
To discuss this containment earnestly, it is the nature that contains, not the phenomena. Thus, Jingxi said: "If one uses principle to marvel at phenomena, it is like the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
for example, within a single speck of dust there is a great thousand-fold world-system scroll; a single thought-moment is like a minute particle, and all dharmas are like the scroll."

The analogy of the mustard seed and Mount Sumeru is likewise. How is this statement to be understood? Answer: If one speaks from the perspective of inclusion (*anvaya*), one gains a difference in meaning but loses the identity of the substance (*dravya*).
If one speaks from the perspective of exclusion (*vyatireka*), both meanings are lost; for since the substance of the phenomenon is lost, a difference in meaning cannot be established.

Now, I shall challenge that statement on the basis of their identical substance. Furthermore, the Great Master [Vasubandhu] explained the sūtra by means of the three doors of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*). Regarding this...
Abiding in liberation is the true nature (*dharmatā*). The wisdom capable of abiding therein is real insight (*bhūtaprajñā*). The function that arises from it is skillful means (*upāya*).
If one were to establish this according to other systems, the mutual entry of large and small within phenomena occurs because large and small are mutually accommodated within their nature.
This mutual accommodation of large and small within the nature is precisely the skillful means and liberation of the virtues of the nature (*prakṛtiguṇa*). Why? As Jingxi asked:

The true nature (tathatā) is inherently conjoined with actual wisdom; what concern does it have with external objects? Yet you say that the mutual inclusion of the large and the small occurs through acceding to the principle.
Answer: Indeed, this true nature pervades the entire dharma-realm. Those who are deluded perceive it as internal and external, whereas those who have awakened realize it is but the one mind.

Furthermore, regarding the mutual containment of the large and the small within phenomenal events, this is due to the liberation of the true nature (*tathatā-vimokṣa*) among the three liberations. If it were otherwise...
It is said that one should attain liberation through skillful means within the nature itself. Furthermore, one should not ask how external objects are related [to consciousness].
From this, it is known that the essence of both the Great and the Small is fundamentally a matter of fact; because the true nature is attained, the Great and the Small are mutually inclusive.

It is not that "great" and "small" are themselves the nature (*dharmatā*). Question: Even so, according to this text, great and small are not the nature; why then does the text say, "The principle is entrusted to phenomena"?

If one says that phenomena are interfused, why speak of them as "extraordinary phenomena"? Answer: One should know that within a single thought-moment, there are volumes of sutras as numerous as motes of dust.
From the perspective of true nature (*tathatā*), all of these are phenomena. However, it is simply because those [sages] point to the motes of dust and the sutras as metaphors.

Therefore, a single thought-moment of all dharmas is precisely what constitutes the Dharma. Yet, as for how a single deluded thought can encompass all dharmas, it is because one has attained true nature that such encompassing is possible.
For this reason, when comparing the mindfulness of dharmas to sensory objects and conventional scriptures, it is termed "principle" (*li*).

Thus, by employing metaphors of phenomena to clarify the principle of the Dharma, how much more so when discussing the marvelous methods of the immediate identity [of phenomenon and principle] and the ultimate, perfect meaning. Question: If you do not permit...

Regarding the principle that the large and the small are mutually inclusive: if one asks why it is said that in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* the principle (*li*) excels the phenomenon (*shi*), and why Jingxi says that "restraining the mind to follow the principle is nothing other than the nature of mind" (*xinxing*), the answer is as follows: This is because the ancient masters explained the inconceivable (*buziyi*) solely in terms of phenomenal characteristics (*shixiang*).

The present school, however, explains the inconceivable by way of the arising of these phenomenal functions precisely because of the realization of the principle. This is intended to distinguish [the two].

The ancients spoke only in terms of phenomena; therefore, we now specifically speak in terms of principle (*li*). This does not mean that there are no phenomena, but rather that we speak of "approximating the realization of principle" and "arising from principle to manifest function.
Thus, it is said that principle is superior to phenomena. As for the statement that "restraining the mind according to principle is none other than the nature of mind," it means this.

All phenomena, whether large or small, are none other than true nature (*dharmatā*). Because they are not otherwise, the large and the small are mutually inclusive. Sentient beings are deluded regarding this;

they perceive only the distinctions between internal and external, large and small. Now that they have awakened to it, they see that these large and small, internal and external, are all but the one mind.
It is in relation to delusion that we speak of "the nature of mind" (*cittaprakṛti*); in reality, the nature of mind is itself both internal and external. If...

If it is not "this," why say it is not "non-existence"? Furthermore, if one were to follow other teachings that speak of "non-existence" as the nature of mind, one would have to lead through three types of liberation before seeing that the qualities of nature possess both small and large dimensions in mutual inclusion.

Moreover, this particular passage specifically points to the liberation of true nature as being "not non-existent" in its nature of mind. Thus, we know that the essence of the skillful means is both internal and external. Second, this...

Third, the correct analysis of the metaphorical meaning based on the dream and awakening of ordinary beings, which has three parts: first, that length and brevity are not real; second, "If one awakens... and below, where there is a distinction between principle and phenomena;

third, "If [one]... and below, which is based solely on the mind being signless. Regarding the first part, it relies exclusively on the fact that [the dream state] is not integrated. Regarding the second part, "If one awakens... and below, it concerns the integration of the mind and the integration of phenomena.
Regarding the third part, "If... and below, it relies exclusively on the mind being without marks.

From "Third, regarding the correct [nature]" onwards, there are two parts: first, showing the essential meaning by focusing on the substance of the mind; second, the mutual inclusion because the merit returns to the one mind as its substance.

Regarding the first, there are two sections: first, the direct explanation; second, the reverse clarification from "If this... onwards. Regarding the second, from "Furthermore, although... onwards, there is mutual inclusion because the merit returns to the mind without increase or decrease.

The second section, "Therefore, below," generally distinguishes between the principles and meanings of the Dharma by differentiating between ordinary beings and sages. This has two parts: first, the realization and awakening of all Buddhas;

second, [the explanation of] the mutual inclusion of the long and the short. Regarding the first, there are two sub-sections: first, the mutual inclusion of the long and the short; second, "Furthermore, below," which develops the short into the long.

Now, as for the difference between these two meanings—the mutual inclusion of the long and the short versus developing the short into the long—it is because the principle of mutual inclusion requires that both the long and the short coexist before they can be mutually included.
Regarding the meaning of "mutual manifestation" (*xiāng yǎn*): sometimes it merely means manifesting the short as long, or manifesting the long as short.

Furthermore, "mutual inclusion" (*xiāng shè*) refers to the mutual identity of both characteristic (*xiàng*) and essence (*tǐ*). Manifesting the short as long is the case where the characteristic is distinct while the essence is identical, such as when seven days are manifested as a *kalpa*.
The text for this appears in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. The present text states that the dharma of dependent origination is merely empty and lacks substantial reality. This is...
As for the statement that "the appearance of one kalpa is established by following the mind, and the appearance of seven days is extinguished by following the mind," some may say:
"If the essence of the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination) dharma is eternally abiding, why do you now say it is extinguished by following the mind? Others may say:

"As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states, 'sentient beings call it one kalpa'; here, we speak of its extinction based on what sentient beings call it. How could the essence of the dharma be such [as they perceive]?"
Now, if you say that "repaying" (xie) is spoken of in reference to sentient beings, the present text states: "The Sage well understands the dharma of dependent origination;
it is merely empty and without reality, entirely created by the mind, and perishes as it follows the mind. Is this not to say that [retribution] perishes according to the mind of the Sage?
Yet the Sage has no mind of his own; he takes sentient beings as his mind. Since this mind is thus active in its functioning, therefore—
There is arising and ceasing; yet there are those who say it is not so. Now I ask: regarding the dharma of dependent origination, is it solely real, or is it solely illusory?
If one says it is real, why say it is solely illusory? Why say it manifests illusory appearances based on conceptualization (*saṃjñā*)?

Question: The Perfect Sage’s arousal of function responds without premeditation; why then speak of "appearances"? Answer: The functional aspect of the Dharma-body fundamentally belongs to the realm of phenomena (*vastu*). As for its essence...

The essence of the Dharma fundamentally belongs to the nature (*xing*). Because it functions by being identical to that nature, when spoken of from the perspective of nature, it is said to be "without deliberation," "without conditions," and "immovable.
When spoken of from the perspective of function, it is said to "accord with circumstances," to "act for the sake of things," and to "discriminate.
What is now called "form" (*xiàng*), "arising" (*chéng*), or "passing away" (*xiè*) is spoken of by the Sage from the perspective of function.

Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "What sentient beings call one kalpa, [the Buddha] calls seven days. This is spoken from the perspective of the Sage regarding the nature (*dharmatā*) of things.

Second, as for ordinary, inferior beings—those deluded commoners who, within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), falsely cling to phenomena as being real—two meanings must be understood.

First, because they perceive the nature of the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) as having a fixed form, they take what is empty and insubstantial to be substantial and concrete; therefore, [it is said that] they do not...
Fusion. Second, because ignorance, deluded emotions, and attachments take what is luminous and empty to be substantial images, they do not fuse.
If the latter condition did not exist, then from the stage of Equal Enlightenment downward, there would be no defiled or obstructed emotions to be severed.
The third section clarifies the meaning of how the subduing of afflictions and the receiving of retribution differ. It consists of three parts: first, the presentation of the headings;

second, the detailed explanation following the questions; and third, the conclusion of the detailed explanation. Regarding the first part—the subduing of afflictions and the receiving of retribution explained separately—there are three sections.

First, the detailed explanation of subduing afflictions, which consists of two rounds of question and answer. The first question uses principle (*xing*) to challenge phenomena (*shi*); the second question uses phenomena to challenge principle. This is the first answer.
This is answered directly by engaging with the matter itself. Because it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the *dharmadhātu*, phenomena that are defiled are extinguished by phenomena that are pure.

The subsequent answer is fourfold: first, a general response; second, "as above" and so forth, which refers back to what was stated previously; third, "therefore" and so forth, which is the formal response; and fourth, [the section] divided into two: first, the object of treatment (*pratipakṣya*);

second, "if one cultivates" and so forth, which concerns the remedy (*pratipakṣa*). Each of these sections further contains two parts: first, the dual existence according to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second, ...
However, the "function" (*vṛtti*) mentioned below refers to its pervasive activity; in both passages, the term "function" specifically denotes the activity arising from the object.
Therefore, while this function may be present in one case and absent in another, the nature capable of giving rise to it is fully possessed in both the cultivated and the uncultivated states.
The fourth point is the citation of scriptural evidence from below; this refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. The text has two parts: first, the citation of the scripture;

second, from "As for the Dharma... onwards, the explanation of its meaning. In the present passage, the exposition unfolds by using the refutation of phenomena (*dharma*) to reveal principle (*tattva*);

thus, illness is taken as the phenomenon and the Dharma as the nature. Furthermore, when the lower fascicle states, "Illness lies in the clinging mind, not in the great function," it is refuting emotional attachment to reveal the phenomenon itself. Therefore...
Taking "illness" as the subjective emotion (*qing*) and "Dharma" as the objective function (*yong*). It is not only Nanyue who understands these two directions;

indeed, the Great Master [Zhiyi] and Jingxi [Zhanran] also both held these two views, as shall be clarified below. However, regarding the differences between this "illness" and "Dharma," one must properly understand their underlying intent.

This is because while the subjective emotion that grasps remains the same, the objective Dharma that is grasped is twofold: first, the Dharma of phenomena (*shifa*); [the second being the Dharma of principle].
Second is the Dharma of Principle (*li-fa*). The substance of the Dharma of phenomena (*shi-fa*) is coarse; the substance of the Dharma of principle is subtle and wondrous.
Thus, Jingxi said: "When the mind is coarse, the object is coarse; when the mind is coarse, the object is subtle. Speaking from the perspective of the essential nature of dharmas:

the objects of provisional phenomena (*shi-quan*) are coarse, while the objects of ultimate principle (*li-shi*) are subtle and wondrous. Furthermore, since the phenomena that are grasped are coarse, the mind that grasps them is likewise coarse. Since those...

This is the coarse [level]. Therefore, one knows that the phenomena of objective things (*vastu-dharma*) obtain their existence through the emotions (*citta*), and thus share the same substance as those emotions;

for this reason, both are termed "illness. Consequently, the sublime principle is pointed out and designated as "Dharma" (*dharma*). Thus, although the Dharma and the grasping emotion differ in terms of the object and the subject, their delusive substance is the same.
One cannot be preserved while the other is extinguished; because they are viewed from the perspective of their own nature, both are termed "illness," and both are...

That which is to be destroyed is itself the basis; therefore, both are termed "dharmas. Since both are that which is manifested, they share the same logical principle. Question: In the *Anxin lun* (Treatise on Settling the Mind), it says:

"In reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing, yet deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) calls this 'arising' and 'ceasing. Does this mean one merely eliminates deluded conceptualization while still retaining arising and ceasing as the essence?

Or does it mean that deluded conceptualization causes arising and ceasing to become non-existent? Answer: There is no difference here. (Regarding "no difference": the subjective grasping and the object...)

All phenomena pertaining to conditioned activities are of a delusive nature; they exist together when present and cease together when absent. Therefore, it is said that there is no distinction between them. In this passage, the objective phenomena and the subjective mind are not differentiated (though people generally know this). One must thoroughly understand its underlying intent.

If discussed solely in terms of principle, there is neither arising nor nature (for the single, equal nature is neither phenomenon nor principle). If viewed from the perspective of the merit of the fruit, then nature does not obstruct arising (and principle does not obstruct phenomena).

If viewed from the perspective of sentient beings, they merely give rise to delusion regarding their nature (deluding themselves regarding principle within phenomena). When the sage observes the ordinary person, he sees that what arises is nothing but nature (phenomena are precisely principle).
Now, speaking from the standpoint of returning from delusion to awakening, we cause one to leave arising and return to nature (leaving phenomena to return to principle is exactly the same as this).

In the present text, the "dharma" (phenomenon) is eliminated while the "principle" (li) is not; this is because, in principle, the dharma is not eliminated, whereas in practice, the dharma is eliminated. To see [the dharma] as non-arising in nature: if one perceives the "name" of the principle, that name is obtained through contrast;
yet the essence of the principle is such that its self-nature is manifest. Since this rational nature is the nature of equality, it is neither nature nor arising, neither phenomenon nor principle.

In the preceding passage, the grasped phenomenal dharma and the grasping emotion were not distinguished and were both termed "arising"; this is precisely the same as in the present text, where both are termed "illness. These two points—
The object grasped (*grāhya*) and the subject that grasps (*grāhaka*) are explained as being distinct categories, with three points of difference:
First, the mind that initiates [the action] is the subject (*citta*), while the arising of greed and hatred, along with their karmic retributions, constitutes the object (*dharma*).

Second, the mind of erroneous attachment is the subject, and the object so grasped is the object. For instance, the dharmas of greed and hatred are inherently afflictions; yet, through erroneous attachment—
This constitutes a fault. Furthermore, it is like taking phenomena that are fundamentally provisional (*upāya*) and erroneously grasping them as real.

Thirdly, it is because one takes the mind that is incapable of knowing as "sentiment" (*qing*), and takes the objects that are not known as "phenomena" (*fa*). Just as phenomena are fundamentally identical to principle (*li*), because one does not know their suchness, it is termed "sentiment";
and because one takes the grasped phenomenal objects as "phenomena. However, that which gives rise to erroneous attachment does not know these three.

The names for "sentiment" (*qing*) and "phenomenon" (*shi*) are mutually interchangeable; however, because one wishes to differentiate them so that their characteristics may be made manifest, each takes a single name to illustrate its specific meaning.
Now, regarding these three meanings, sentiment is taken as the "affliction" (*bing*) and phenomena as the "Dharma" (*fa*).

As for the statement, "only remove the affliction, not the Dharma," there are two different senses in which the Dharma is not removed. First, it does not mean that the phenomena of the objective world are not to be removed.
Because when emotional attachments are removed, phenomena (*dharma*) necessarily vanish; it is like treating an eye disease, where the floating hairs (*keśoṇḍuka*) disappear of their own accord.

Thus, one need not remove the phenomena themselves, for those phenomena depart naturally. Second, from the perspective of emotion, one speaks of "separation," while from the perspective of phenomena, one speaks of "identity.

Therefore, one merely removes emotion and does not remove the phenomena themselves. As Jingxi said: "Regarding what is called 'merely removing the illness,' 'illness' refers to the attachment to provisional [teachings] as..."
The "real" refers to all provisional dharmas. If the affliction of clinging to the provisional is removed, then these very provisional dharmas are the real.

Therefore, one removes the affliction but does not remove the dharma. This is consistent with the following passage, where it says the affliction lies in the clinging mind and not in the great function.

As the Wise One said: "For example, fire is burning. If touching it causes the pain of being burned, one avoids touching it out of caution; this is removing the affliction without [removing the fire]."

"One may eliminate fire. Furthermore, Jingxi said: "If one merely breaks through the illness of attachment, what dharma is there to eliminate? The dharmas of the three paths are fundamentally the three virtues;
therefore, all the aforementioned passages describe the detachment of the mind and the identity of dharmas. If one speaks only of identity, the mind itself is not separate [from them].
As Jingxi said: 'If a sage perceives the ordinary, what arises is nothing but nature.'"

Question: Based on the principles of phenomena discussed above, there are three cases: when both the sentient being and the phenomenon are distinct; when both the sentient being and the phenomenon are identical;

and when the sentient being is distinct while the phenomenon is identical. Since the sentient being and the phenomenon are already one, how can these three distinctions exist? Answer: Each follows its own established tenet (*siddhānta*) and possesses its own underlying principle.

The phrase "separated from both emotion and phenomena" (*qingfa ju li*) serves as an antidote to the erroneous views of those who hold to [dualistic] calculations. Because one now does not give rise to the emotions of the nine realms, one is thereby separated from the causal and resultant phenomena of the nine realms;
hence it is said, "separated from arising and returning to the nature. Furthermore, it is said that this is explained in terms of an antidote to refute past calculations.

The phrase "emotion and phenomena are identical" (*qingfa ju ji*) refers to the vision of reality as it truly is (*yathābhūta*). Moreover, when a single Buddha attains enlightenment, the dharma-realm...

There is nothing that is not the Buddha’s environment and its inhabitants. For instance, the causes and effects of the hells, as well as the karmic actions created through emotional attachments, are entirely the realm realized by the Tathāgata.
This is because they accord with principle; in truth, one sees that these emotions and these phenomena are none other than the nature itself.
Therefore, it is said that "arising is precisely the nature," and it is further said that "if one sees the dharma-nature, one sees that the dharma-nature is purely all dharmas."

If this were not the intended meaning, how could it be said that "realizing the Way does not sever phenomena"? To say that "sentiment departs and phenomena are identical" refers to turning away from delusion by means of what is immediate and essential.
One should know that everything arises from the mind’s discrimination; now, simply by departing from sentiment, phenomena naturally become identical [to reality].
Therefore, it is said: "If one merely opens up the state of mind, there is nothing that does not transform."

Question: If one is necessarily separated from both the sentient being and the phenomena, how does this differ from [the concept of] "separation" (*bie*)? Answer: This is discussed in terms of "identity" (*ji*) while positing "separation," yet it is not a definitive separation;
therefore, it differs from "separation. However, regarding the meaning of positing "separation" based on "identity," the distinction is in fact difficult to discern.

I shall now clarify this by means of the analogy of ice and water. For example, if one points to ice and says it is water, there is no need to melt the ice; this is the meaning of "identity," which refers to the relationship between the characteristic (*xiang*) and the essence (*ti*).
"Identity" (*ji*) means "immediacy. It refers to ice being water while it is melting within the ice. This is the meaning of discussing "separation" based on identity.
Thus, the characteristic of ice must be separated from the substance of water for there to be identity; this is the identity of the substance through their mutual separation.
Question: Some may say that the meaning of discussing identity and separation is not like this. For example, ice is water; yet there are those who do not know it and say that ice is not water.
Now, pointing out that ice is water is a discussion of identity. Not knowing that the mind has ceased is a discussion of separation.
Therefore, we know that as soon as the essence of the Dharma is realized, biased emotions naturally depart. How is this to be understood? Now I ask: does this state of ignorance necessarily depart?
If it does not necessarily depart, let me clarify this with an analogy. Since ice is nothing other than water, yet they are conventionally distinguished;
if the ignorant mind likewise departs of its own accord, is it not then a definitive departure? If you say it is a definitive departure, then now—
Question: Since the state of ignorance is that which must be abandoned, one must point to perfect wisdom (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*) as that which is capable of abandoning it.

Furthermore, when discussing abandonment within the context of the Perfect [Teaching], can there be a fixed abandonment? One should know that within the Perfect [Teaching], the mind has no fixed abandonment.

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "That which is well-severed is called 'non-abandonment abandonment'; that which is not well-severed is called 'fixed abandonment'. Again, regarding the phenomena of the objective realm (*dharma-vastu*)...

"Immediacy" (ji) means that because [the Dharma] arises from the entirety of nature, the Dharma is immediate. Now, according to your perspective, does it arise from the entirety of nature, or does it arise outside of nature?
If it arises outside of nature, then the substance of nature would not be pervasive and the endowment of nature would not be complete.

If it arises from the entirety of nature, why is it that while the Dharma is immediate, sentient beings are fixed in separation? Someone might say: "Although it arises from the entirety of nature, they do not know it. Now I ask them: only...
Is this not still a matter of [discerning] the nature? One should seek it through inquiry rather than contention.

Furthermore, if you ask whether the nature is coarse, and if it were definitively separate and not identical [to the phenomenon], then one should not say that "the coarse is identical to the subtle. If you say that the dharma-body of the coarse is identical [to the subtle], [then...]
The essence of the Dharma belongs to the sublime. This, in turn, establishes that the sublime is itself the sublime. To speak in this manner may seem paradoxical. Why?
Because everyone merely sees that the finger pointing at white is white, yet in reality, they have not seen that the finger pointing at black is white.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "It is like bees making honey; although they gather from many flowers, if they do not exclude the excrement, the honey will ultimately not be formed. Therefore—
Know that all excrement is but the seed of honey; this metaphorical text is identical to the current distinction between black and white. Let the wise examine it closely.
As for the claim that one must detach from emotions, this is based on the teachings of the scholars of Siming.

Now, let us further clarify this by means of what Siming himself recounted regarding his lifelong attainments. Siming said: "Without stirring the thoughts of emotion, the wondrous nature of the original source is restored."
This is truly the perfect proclamation of the wise. Day and night I have relied upon it as my seat and my staff;
day and night I have upheld it as my bosom companion and my compass. For over forty years, my resolve has been singular.

Is this not because Siming, through his very nature, attained what was to be realized? Therefore, those who speak of it today describe it as the innate, wondrous nature—neither negating nor manifesting, yet perhaps negating.
...and manifest it. Alternatively, there is only refutation and only manifestation. As for that which both refutes and manifests:
it manifests because the reality of phenomena (dharma) and things (vastu) are both identical to their nature; it refutes because the reality of phenomena and things arise from their own essence.

Because there is nothing external to this refutation other than nature, it is "only refutation. Because there is nothing external to this manifestation other than reality, it is "only manifestation. As it is said:
Regarding this, as for the statement that "only by negating is there manifestation, yet both negation and manifestation are indeterminate":

the merit [of this] lies in the fact that all are of an equal, single nature, fundamentally neither negated nor manifested. Even this state of being neither negated nor manifested is merely a name derived from its relation to its opposite.

If the essence of its self-nature were manifest, then whether it is negated or revealed, whether it is merely negated or merely revealed, or neither negated nor revealed—all such states would be beyond the reach of conceptual thought.
Question: Previously, you distinguished between identity and separation; although the principle is clear, why is it that the metaphors used do not fully accord with the meaning? Furthermore—

Ice is identical to water. Since one does not know this, it is appropriate that [the mind] must be separated [from its objects]. How can one see this ignorant mind and yet claim it is identical [to the enlightened mind]?
Answer: As for ice being identical to water, ice and water are identical because their substance (*tattva*) is the same.

Regarding the mind that did not know ice was identical to water and the present mind that knows ice is identical to water, since the substance of the mind (*citta-tattva*) is the same, [the former] ignorance...
The mind is itself suchness; because one knows the mind, it is also suchness. From the perspective of the object known (*jñeya*), ignorance is itself water;
from the perspective of the subject that knows (*jñātṛ*), ignorance is itself knowledge. This analogy must be thoroughly investigated by each person for themselves. Question:

Of the three meanings mentioned above, why is there no instance where phenomena are separated from emotion and are themselves suchness? Answer: There is indeed this meaning as well. It is because, by pointing to the emotion of grasping, its very nature is itself suchness. Its...
The dharmas grasped as real vanish of their own accord. Nevertheless, the path of refutation and revelation is the essential gateway to attaining Buddhahood.
This has been transmitted from Nanyue to Zhiyi and down to Jingxi; that later followers hold differing views is due to variations in how they comprehend the principle of the Truths (*satya*).
I shall now briefly evaluate this. Although our school speaks of the Three Truths, the conventional truth of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) is absolute.
It is without form or appearance. Now, I shall evaluate this: All explanations of the principle of nature ultimately converge upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Why is this?

If one speaks of the existence of the conventional, yet there is no appearance, then how could that which is without form or appearance not be empty? Thus we know that although conventional names exist, the conventional substance does not.
Although our school discusses the three truths (*trisatya*), because the characteristics of the nature-merit (*prakṛti-guṇa*) cannot be obliterated, they remain present. Now, I shall evaluate this.

He said: "In principle, all discourse on the nature of reality ultimately returns to conventional matters. Why is this? If one says there is an 'emptiness' within emptiness, how could its nature allow for characteristics not to perish?
Since the place where characteristics do not perish is indeed the conventional, we know that although there is the name 'emptiness,' there is no substantial essence of emptiness.
If one takes the extinction of deluded emotions to be emptiness, then even the conventional truth involves the extinction of deluded emotions."
If one claims that the manifestation of the qualities of nature consists solely of emptiness, it results in the non-existence of the conventional.

If you say that when discussing nature itself, nature also possesses emptiness—then, setting aside the discussion of nature itself, for what phenomenon is this emptiness intended? If it is the emptiness of conventional phenomena, [then nature is not empty].
In this case, conventional characteristics can be empty. If they could not be empty, then there would be only the name "emptiness" without the substance of emptiness.
Yet, this [second] view conversely renders the dharma-substance of the dharma-realm ultimately non-empty.

It is precisely because the two schools differ in their realization of principle that their methods of refutation and revelation likewise differ. The first school’s refutation of characteristics to return to emptiness is the refutation of phenomena.

The first school elucidates principle (*li*). Next, the second school refutes attachment to return to the Dharma; this is precisely "refuting attachment to manifest the characteristics. When explained according to their terminology, it is said that both the facts (*shi*) and the principle are manifested.

However, when discussing the ultimate point of return, since the essence of the Dharma and its phenomenal characteristics are not empty, this actually constitutes "refuting attachment to manifest the facts.
Now, how could these two schools not know that when the Shanjia (Tiantai) school speaks of the truth of reality (*di-li*), it is "one yet three" and "three yet one"?
Furthermore, when establishing the categories of meaning (*arthamukha*) by means of this path, it is for the most part based upon the "three" as the fundamental principle.
As for those who argue through refutation and revelation, do they not know that the essential nature of the *dharmadhātu* is neither refuted nor revealed, yet it is both refuted and revealed?

Moreover, when establishing the categories of meaning by means of this path, it is for the most part based upon "refuting and revealing" as the fundamental principle. As for those two schools themselves...
The Way attained is not what I know. What I do know is that the principle of the perfect fusion of the Three in One, as expounded by Tiantai, derives its efficacy from this "One.
As one who has the misfortune of instructing disciples, whenever I establish a gateway of doctrinal meaning, I take this "One" as the fundamental basis.
Yet, this "One" is neither phenomenon nor principle; it is both phenomenon and principle, and yet it is solely phenomenon and solely principle. It is through this "One" that all is empty.

Because it is the Middle Way, the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is signless (*animitta*). Because it is one with this [Middle Way] yet is conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), the dharma-realm has signs (*sanimitta*).

Because it is one with this [Middle Way] yet is merely phenomena (*dharma-mātra*), the dharma-realm has only signs. Because it is one with this [Middle Way] yet is solely emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the dharma-realm has only signlessness.
Therefore, it is neither with signs nor without signs; it is the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is signless, and it is that which has only signs.

It is simply signless; all such things are beyond the reach of conceptual thought. In the treatise, the refutation and manifestation are fundamentally established through that which is neither refuting nor manifesting.
Thus, there is that which is neither refuting nor manifesting yet refutes and manifests, as well as that which merely refutes and merely manifests.
These instances of refutation and manifestation based on that which is neither refuting nor manifesting do not exceed two meanings: first, the manifestation of the essence through one's own practice.

Second is the transformative function for others. Within the context of one’s own practice, because this [function] neither refutes nor manifests, it is discussed in terms of "sameness and difference" regarding the deluded and the awakened, and as "refutation and manifestation" regarding the emotional and the cognitive.
From the perspective of that which is deluded and that which is awakened, it is discussed in terms of "phenomena and principle" regarding the essence of dharmas, and as "refutation and manifestation.
Furthermore, regarding the refutation and manifestation of the essence of dharmas, there are two aspects: either the phenomena of the two deaths are what is to be refuted, and emptiness is...

The two principles within [the middle] are that which is revealed. However, this refutation and revelation depend upon whether one emphasizes identity or distinction. If one emphasizes identity, there is no refutation; if one emphasizes distinction, there is refutation.
It is like saying that "that which is not the path is itself the Buddha-path. If one discusses it in terms of identity, the fact of it being a non-path is not refuted;
if one discusses it in terms of distinction, the fact of it being a non-path is then refuted. Since it is a single nature, it is not refuted.
It does not mean that the entire whole is manifested as this phenomenon; therefore, when it is negated, it is not a negation [of the whole].

Since the principle that, by virtue of its single nature, it is neither negated nor manifested as the entire whole is thus established, when it is manifested, it is not a manifestation [of the whole].
Consequently, one returns to the state of being neither negated nor manifested. Thus, both negation and manifestation may be termed "inconceivable" when discussing their negation and manifestation.

Furthermore, regarding the refutation of difference and the manifestation of identity: the cognition of difference is that which is to be refuted, while the wisdom of identity is that which is to be manifested.
This refutation and manifestation are discussed in terms of both identity and separation. If one discusses identity, there is no refutation; if one discusses separation, it constitutes a refutation.

This is like the deluded cognition that does not know that phenomena are identical to principle, contrasted with the awakened wisdom that knows that phenomena are identical to principle. If one were to discuss identity, this would be [the state of] that deluded cognition.
This is precisely wisdom. If it were merely ignorance, deluded sentiment would not be broken. However, when one speaks of transcendence, deluded sentiment is then broken.
Since the single nature is neither broken nor revealed, yet its entire substance constitutes this deluded sentiment, the point of its breaking is itself no breaking.
Since the single nature is neither broken nor revealed, yet its entire substance constitutes this awakened wisdom, the point of its revelation is itself no revelation. Thus, in this regard:
Returning to the point, neither the refutation nor the manifestation is ultimately established; therefore, both the refutation and the manifestation are termed "inconceivable.

Regarding the discussion of refutation and manifestation, there are two aspects to the function of manifesting for the sake of transforming others. First, concerning emotional intellect (*citta-jñāna*):

the deluded mind that clings to emptiness and thus cannot discern the illness or recognize the medicine is what is to be refuted; whereas the mind that does not cling to emptiness and is able to discern the illness and recognize the medicine is what is manifested.
The awakening to wisdom through medicine is that which is revealed. Second, regarding the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*):

the empty and quiescent phenomena grasped as real are that which is negated, while mundane affairs, both internal and external, are that which is revealed. Furthermore, this negation and revelation are discussed in terms of both identity and difference.

Thus, it is not that [the essence] is not destroyed; rather, it is through detachment that one discusses its destruction. This is no different from the previous examples of non-destruction and non-manifestation, which can be understood accordingly.
Nevertheless, for the sake of easy understanding, I first explain the manifestation of the essence through self-cultivation, followed by the manifestation of function through transforming others.

In reality, both essence and function—destruction and manifestation—are fully contained within a single mind. A person who understands in this way is difficult to find; only such a person of destruction and manifestation may truly be so named.

This is for the purpose of refuting and revealing within the Perfect [Teaching]. Now, for the first time, one understands that phenomena are themselves principle and that emotions are themselves wisdom;
yet this reaches its ultimate consummation only at the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Because "being identical" is the ultimate, "separation" is the exhaustion of the source.

This identity and this separation are fundamentally but a single nature; therefore, they ultimately result in being neither identical nor separate. However, this is neither a refutation nor a revelation; it is directly, while refuting, [revealing].
This reveals the Middle Assembly. Thus, both the deconstructing and the revealing—whether it be solely deconstructing or solely revealing—are all inconceivable.

For example, the single nature directly encompasses the three assemblies of Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle; this one [nature] is thus present within each of these three. Therefore, these Three Truths are all perfectly marvelous.
Furthermore, this "one" is not a fixed one, for this one is itself both circular and square.

Question: Do the two aspects of the essence of phenomena—sentience and wisdom—serve to negate and reveal [the truth]? Answer: The very fact that the essence of phenomena is such is itself the principle (*li*).

The mind that does not know [this] spontaneously becomes knowing. Question: Regarding the manifestation of function for the sake of transforming others, why is there no distinction between sentience and wisdom? Answer:

Furthermore, to demonstrate one aspect, this may be made clear as follows: previously, in the context of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), it was only stated that there is a state of ignorance regarding the conventional nature of emptiness, without saying that this gives rise to erroneous attachments.
Now, in the context of transforming others (*parārtha*), it is only stated that this gives rise to erroneous attachments, without stating the ignorance itself.

If one applies this analogy to the agent, then the state of ignorance regarding the conventional nature of emptiness is what is to be refuted; the wisdom that knows the conventional nature of emptiness is what is to be [upheld].

[The text] clarifies that, regarding phenomena and principle, the deluded attachments that can arise are what is to be negated (*prahātavya*), while the wisdom that can give rise to understanding regarding phenomena and principle is what is to be revealed (*prakāśya*).

Question: In the preceding treatise, the negation and revelation were limited to negating the three delusions and revealing the three truths; there was no mention of a "negation and revelation" consisting of the simultaneous extinction of [delusion] and the illumination [of truth].

Question: What is meant by this? Answer: Since it is said that in the ultimate sense there is neither destruction nor manifestation, is it not the case that both destruction and manifestation are entirely lost?
Furthermore, as for the loss of manifestation, this refers to the loss of the three—emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

This is because the three delusions of ignorance and the dharma-nature of the three truths are fundamentally without names or designations. Therefore, the destruction of the three delusions is in fact no destruction, and the manifestation of the three truths is in fact no manifestation.
Why is it that there is neither refutation nor manifestation? It is simply because the names "delusion" and "truth" are fundamentally non-existent.
Thus, Jingxi said: "It is like the nature of moisture, which originally has no two names; two names are provisionally established to instruct the deluded.

Furthermore, the place where names do not exist is not limited to the disappearance of the names of the three delusions; therefore, the names of the three truths also disappear. Does this disappearance not constitute refutation?

Therefore, the meaning established here is that all instances within the Perfect and Sudden teaching where it speaks of "perishing" (*wang*) or "shattering" (*po*) refer to realizing the essence itself.

That there is no hearing, perishing, shattering, alarm, stagnation, severance, or extinction—this is precisely what is meant by the single true nature being devoid of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Question: If one uses the three thousandfold world (sanzen) to break through and manifest this [reality], what is its meaning? Answer: Because there is nothing that is not subsumed within it, breaking through manifests;
yet it is neither "breaking through" nor "manifesting," for both "only breaking through" and "only manifesting" are themselves the three thousandfold world.

As it is said: "If something were not subsumed within the three thousandfold world, it would not be pervasive; because there is nothing to which it does not reach, it reaches the three truths (sandi) of the principle of wisdom. Thus, the three thousandfold world [is realized].

It is that which is manifested. As it is said, "When the three thousand [realms] are realized as fruition, they are all termed eternal and blissful," the three thousand realms are what is to be broken when one proceeds toward the three delusions of sentient beings.
As it is said, "The three thousand [realms] existing in principle are collectively named the unconditioned," when the realization of non-secularity is achieved, one penetrates both directions.
First, regarding the realization of the essence through one's own practice, this is that which is to be broken, as it is said, "Because of the disappearance of purity and impurity..."

Emptiness is the middle. The function of manifesting transformation for others is what is revealed. As it is said: "The three thousand worlds of transformation for others go forth according to things;

based on the single nature, the entire reality constitutes these three thousand. Therefore, where there is destruction, there is no destruction; where there is manifestation, there is no manifestation.
Thus, the three thousand ultimately converge upon the wondrous Dharma that is neither destroyed nor manifested. This is like the wondrous realm emerging from the pointing finger.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The *Commentary on the Essential Perfection of the Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā Method*, Volume Three.
The *Commentary on the Essential Perfection of the Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā Method*, Volume Four.
Recorded by Shi Liao Ran of Dongye Bailian. Part Two:
Distinguishing the Receiving of Retribution. There are two layers of question and answer. The intent of the first question is as follows:

Since both phenomena (*dharma*) and nature (*dharmatā*) exist within a single mind as the causes for the six realms of existence, why do these causes not simultaneously induce their respective retributions? The answer is twofold. First:
Ordinary beings do not obtain the three [results]. First is the general answer that they do not obtain them; second, from "Why? onwards, is the explanation of the underlying meaning;
third, from "Only... onwards, is the formal answer. They may only possess the causes, but the fruits cannot be simultaneous. Nevertheless, the principle of cause and fruit is in fact not at variance.

What is now called "possessing the causes" is spoken of in terms of activity; because they are accumulated in succession, they are said to be "possessed. If one discusses the actual creation of causes...
In reality, there is both sequence and simultaneity. Because of this sequence, retribution does not manifest simultaneously; yet, because their nature is fused, it can be fully present all at once.

For sentient beings, the principle follows the phenomena, and thus they are close to them; for this reason, the reception of retribution cannot manifest instantaneously. For the Buddhas, the phenomena follow the principle, and thus they are close to it;
for this reason, the physical bodies (rūpakāya) manifest universally at one time. Question: Can the Bodhisattvas of the partial teachings [also] manifest [them] at one time?
Within [the mirror] the six realms of existence also appear. Is this not consistent with reason and direct? Answer:
In truth, it arises from attaining a small portion of the principle of nature (li-xing), yet they do not know it and merely call it "supernatural power" (shentong). As Jingxi said by way of analogy:

"That those of external paths can reach distant matters by listening to the sound of a dead bone is truly because all phenomena are fundamentally inherent within form; thus, the practitioners of external paths obtain a small portion of this, remaining in the dark."
Based on their original nature, they do not know [the workings of] the mind.
Second, "Furthermore, if below..."—it should be understood that for a bodhisattva who may thus employ those [means], there are two fundamental bases for the arising of such employment.

First, the phenomenon (*vastu*); second, the nature (*dharmatā*). Regarding the phenomenon: prior to attaining the Way, while within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one undergoes immeasurable bodies and performs immeasurable karmas.

Now that the fruit has been attained, by the power of compassion and vows, one relies upon past karma as the basis for transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-viniyoga*). The Great Master cites Nanyue, who said:

"One awaits the destruction of afflictions and entry into the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); then, from the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-bhūmi*), one re-enters birth and death."

To repay sentient beings—this is precisely the power of compassionate vows. By employing that nature of past karma, the inherently present nature of evil manifests as the Universal Form Body (*sāmbhogakāya*).
Because the shallow does not encompass the deep and is partial, it gives rise to functional activity. One merely knows that compassion and vows support and complete prior karma.

The deep can encompass the shallow; being perfect and real, it relies upon the fundamental nature. Thus, while not obstructing reliance on karma, one also realizes that this karma is nothing other than [the manifestation of the Buddha-nature].

This is the nature [of the question]. The intent of the subsequent inquiry is as follows: regarding the difficulty of reconciling the individual retribution of a single person with the collective retribution of the ten realms, it should also follow that all ordinary beings and sages receive their retribution sequentially and in a fixed order.

For instance, if one person first receives a human body and subsequently receives a Buddha-body, why not cause all sentient beings to likewise first receive a human body and subsequently receive a Buddha-body? Why is this not so?

Therefore, there are those who simultaneously receive human bodies and those who receive Buddha-bodies. Thus it is said that one should not assume that within a single moment there can be many ordinary beings and sages.

Furthermore, why not allow one person to first receive the retribution of being an ordinary being or a sage, and then allow another person to receive the retribution of being an ordinary being or a sage?
In this way, all ordinary beings and sages would receive their retribution in succession. Therefore, it is said that [this is] not the case.
At one time, there were many ordinary beings and sages.
[The Master] answered in three parts. First, he refuted their calculation. The questioner’s correct calculation was that because the mind is the single substance, it cannot receive many bodies.

Now, [the Master] first refutes this by saying it is not due to the mind being the single substance. Furthermore, fearing they might shift their calculation, [he addresses the point]: "Because the mind is the single substance, it is able [to receive many bodies]."

Because it undergoes many bodies, it is also refuted by saying that it does not arise from a single mind. If one were to state an objection without first refuting the opponent’s position, the subsequent text would say:
"That worldly and supramundane matters are established all arises from the nature of the mind; such is the principle.

Now, if one claims [the self] arises from the mind, this is precisely the calculation of a single self-nature (*svabhāva*). Once that calculation has been refuted, how could there be any further objection to saying that [it arises] from [the mind]?

Because this single mind is the essence, there are differences in the retribution received. Furthermore, because it arises from the essence of the nature (*dharmatā*), it is said that [retribution] does not depend on anything else.

This is truly because the essence of the equal nature is neither many nor one, and is neither sacred nor profane. All the differing retributions received by the profane and the sacred do not belong to the essence of the mind;
they arise from the functional activity of the nature. Therefore, it is said that all [retribution] proceeds from this, for this essence of the nature is fully endowed with all things.

In the Dharma, there are cases where the retribution experienced differs according to whether it is collective or individual; this principle exists entirely due to the nature and function [of phenomena].

Second, "but the Dharma" below indicates that this is *dharmatā* (the natural order of things): within the *dharmadhātu*, by its very nature, there is both the collective aspect of many people and the distinct aspect of a single person.
Because there is a totality, although they share the same mind as their substance, it does not preclude the simultaneous existence of many bodies.

Because there is a distinction, although they likewise share the same mind as their substance, it does not preclude the simultaneous absence of many bodies. As for what is called "the nature of things" (*dharmatā*):
It is so. This means that the dharma does not construct itself; it is simply such as it is. It is what is called "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*).

If one further clings to the notion that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is "dharma-as-it-is," this becomes a calculation of spontaneity that falls under the category of causelessness (*ahetutva*), and must be refuted in the same manner as before.

Furthermore, in the present context, we speak of the dharma-realm being "dharma-as-it-is" because we are following its functional nature (*śakti-vṛtti*). To state it in general terms: it is "dharma-as-it-is" because we are following its essential substance (*svabhāva-tattva*).

It is not because a single mind constitutes the essence that there are differences in receiving various retributions; rather, because they arise from the functional activity of the nature (*dharmatā*), it is the very nature of the *dharmadhātu* to possess both the universal and the particular.
Therefore, one receives various retributions—whether many or one. Whether [the distinction] arises or does not arise, it is all the inherent nature of the *dharmadhātu*.

As for the third point, "if... as below," this reveals that the nature is perfectly complete. This is because the phenomena of receiving retributions earlier or later properly belong to the stage of birth (*jāti*).
Extinction. The characteristics of the emotional mind are also inherently complete within its nature.

Third, a further analysis of the two methods for treating delusions. First, the questioner maintains that the single mind constitutes the essence; therefore, defilement and purity exclude one another.

Since sentient beings and Buddhas share the same single mind, the purity of a Buddha must necessarily eliminate the defilement of a sentient being. If this were so, sentient beings would have no need for cultivation. This is the principle.

"Is it by uniting with *dharmatā* that one attains the Way? He replied in three parts. First, he refuted their calculation. Their calculation holds that the mind alone is the substance, and that defilement and purity exclude one another.

He refuted this, saying it is not so. Fearing they might then calculate otherwise, [he considered] that the defilement of sentient beings and the purity of the Buddhas both have the single mind as their substance, yet the two do not exclude one another;
he likewise refuted this, saying it is not so. Furthermore, fearing they might then calculate otherwise, [he considered] that since it is not due to the single mind...
It must be because the minds of ordinary beings and Buddhas are distinct that they do not negate one another. Now, this is also refuted by stating that it does not arise from separate minds.

However, for those who reckon that [the mind] has separate minds as its substance, both the reckoner and the object of reckoning are entirely false. For those who reckon that it has a single mind as its substance, their clinging attachment is what is false.
We merely refute such clinging and reckonings; we do not mean to refute the fundamental substance of the minds of ordinary beings and sages. Both are merely dharmas...

Regarding the statement that "being free from all characteristics is the meaning of quiescence": [The text continues with the question: "Since all characteristics are non-existent, how can one speak of being 'free from them'? [The text continues with the answer: "Because there is nothing to be abandoned, it is called 'free from characteristics. This is the meaning of quiescence. Regarding the phrase "being free from all characteristics is the meaning of quiescence": [the commentary follows].
The essence of equality is neither with marks nor without marks. It is called "without marks" (animitta) because it is contrasted with function;
however, the term "without marks" is used in opposition to "with marks. "Without marks" pertains to principle (li), while "with marks" pertains to phenomena (shi).

One must distinguish these according to five meanings so that various texts do not become confused. If one considers them in terms of faults and virtues, within the three truths there are no marks of the three paths. If...
Regarding cultivation and nature: the three truths of the nature-merit possess no marks of the three truths of cultivated merit.

Regarding essence and function: within emptiness and the ultimate (śūnyatā), there are no marks of conventional function. Regarding the middle and the extremes: the Middle Way possesses no marks of the two extremes.
Regarding non-apprehension and illumination: the single nature possesses no marks of the three truths. In the present text, "being free from all marks" refers precisely to the essence.

Regarding "function": because the essence of emptiness is devoid of the characteristics of phenomenal function, if one considers it in terms of the extinction of illumination, this very emptiness would still constitute a characteristic of existence, which is likewise something to be abandoned.
If the meaning of "function" refers to the essence possessing both the two functions of opposition and compliance, then there are five aspects to essence and function as well.

Now, essence is emptiness and function is conventional reality. If one considers them in terms of their non-existence and illumination, then that emptiness within essence is still subsumed under function.
To cultivate the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) is itself self-benefit; to cultivate the practice of *vipaśyanā* (insight) is itself the benefit of others.

The meaning [of "self" and "other"] has distinct pairings. First, regarding self and other: here, we follow the discourse on the pairing of essence and function, taking "self" as referring to oneself and "other" as referring to others.

If they were discussed individually, this essence and function—when realized through one's own cultivation and realization—are nothing other than self-benefit; when used to cause others to awaken and enter [the truth], they are nothing other than benefit for others.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The King’s body gathers and transforms beings, manifesting universally in all gates. Thus, the true essence responds [to conditions].

Their function all belongs to altruism. Second, regarding the distinction between cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*): here, we follow the discourse on their essence, taking cessation as the essence and insight as the function.
If they were discussed individually, however, both the essence and the function each possess their own cessation and insight.
The second section has two parts. First is the question: "One cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to eliminate birth and death. Now, the question specifically concerns *vipaśyanā*.

As for what is called *śamatha*, it follows along [with the former] and thus leads to further wandering. This is a challenge based on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) regarding their concomitance.

Whatever marks (*lakṣaṇa*) exist, their substance is birth and death. For instance, even the subtle dust within the *niṣyanda-rūpa-kāya* (recompense body) would have no basis if it were separated from the *karma-vijñāna*.

[The Master] said: "I see it. This doubt arises because we are currently discussing the substance (*dharmatā*) of phenomena. If one follows the full range of its expressive distinctions, this characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which belongs to the Buddha;
and that which belongs to the Buddha is nothing other than the nature (*prakṛti*). Thus, the defiled substance is identical to the pure; the characteristic-substance is identical to the self.

By taking the pure as defiled, it is defiled all day long yet is not defiled; by the extinction [of attachment] to characteristics, it is a characteristic all day long yet is not a characteristic. Therefore...

This characteristic is the great function of the Buddha. Why, then, would one harbor doubts regarding the life-and-death cycle of the Dharma-body? Therefore, the meaning of the response in the text below does not go beyond this point.
As for the statement in the answer, "One merely removes the illness but does not remove the Dharma," the *Tongzhizhe* (The One of Equal Wisdom) says:
Fire can burn people; however, for one who has attained spiritual arts (*dharmavidyā*), there is no obstruction in entering or exiting it, and thus there is no need to extinguish the fire.

Therefore, while the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) cause ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to suffer exhaustion, they constitute the Buddha-work (*buddhakārya*) for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*) and their three bases: first, the presentation of the headings; second, the explanation, which itself consists of three parts.

First, the explanation of the essential nature of what they rely upon, which has two sections: first, the headings; second, the explanation, which has two parts. First, the question; second, the answer, which has two parts. First, the general answer;

second, the formal explanation of this meaning, which has three sections. First, the cessation (*śamatha*), which has four parts. First, the explanation: [the stage of] hearing the teaching by means of the mind.

That "consciousness can know names and meanings" refers generally to the function of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in initiating contemplation. Within the single nature of Perfect Enlightenment, both knowing and not-knowing are inherent;
this very [duality] acts as karma that further perfumes the enlightened nature. When the nature is entirely unaware, it manifests as the environment of dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).

The knowledge of the totality of nature manifests as the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*). This knowledge—whether it knows or does not know—is, in its thorough penetration to the source of returning to nature, nothing other than awakening (*bodhi*).

However, because it follows from phenomena, the secondary retribution (*adhipati-niṣyanda*) is "not-knowing," while the primary retribution is "knowing. Within this primary retribution, there is the form of one of the aggregates (*skandha*).

The mind consists of the four aggregates; the mind possesses cognition, whereas form lacks cognition. Regarding the mind of the four aggregates, delusion constitutes non-cognition, while awakening constitutes cognition.
This distinction between cognition and non-cognition pertains to the sensory objects and forms; it is not that cognition alone exists. It is by virtue of this [distinction] that one knows.

To know while following ignorance and to establish knowledge through views is called delusion. To know that one follows the teacher’s instruction rather than knowing through [independent] knowledge is called awakening.
This merit arises from the aggregate of mental consciousness; based on this knowledge, one may follow the teacher’s instructions and inquire about the stages of cultivation and realization.
The consciousness hears the teaching and gives rise to the understanding that there are no external objects;

this is the stage of "names" (*nāma*). Second, from "hearing this" onwards is the stage of "cultivation. In contrast to the aforementioned understanding gained through hearing, cultivation is practice (*caryā*). However, this practice does not depart from understanding;
even upon reaching ultimate realization, it remains this very understanding. When distinguished according to the stages, it may also be said that this is the stage of "practice" (*caryā-bhūmi*).

The understanding of the path and the understanding of the realization are not different in their essence; therefore, the understanding of the initial mind and the understanding of the stage of fruition are neither two nor distinct.

Now, when it is said that one "increases the nature of understanding" through cultivation, and later that one "attains the perfect clarity of the nature of understanding," we know that both practice and realization are also termed "understanding.
As for the term "expedient means," in the context of the dialectic between cultivation and nature, whatever involves entering through cultivation is so named.

Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): when contrasted with "understanding through practice" (*adhimukti-caryā*), the consciousness that takes objects as its conditions is termed "expedient means. However, the meaning of this "expedient means" extends throughout all practices.
If one distinguishes between the five types of repentance and the dream-king [vision], these are specifically the expedient means for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Vaipulya* sūtras.

When contrasted with the "true" [stage], that which resides in the positions of the outer and inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is called "expedient means. In the present text, it applies generally to all; specifically, it pertains to both the cultivated and the innate, as well as the distinctions according to stages. [This is] the permeation (*vāsanā*).

Regarding the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*) encompasses four types: first, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); second, non-objectifying wisdom (*nirviṣayajñāna*);
third, the fundamental consciousness; and fourth, the true mind (*bhūtamanas*). When divided by way of phenomena and principle, the true mind is the principle, while the other three are phenomena.

When divided by way of the real and the false, the mental consciousness and the fundamental consciousness are false, while the other two are real. When divided by way of subject and object, the mental consciousness and wisdom are...
The former is the agent, while the latter two are the objects. To summarize: it is simply said that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
"Able to know" refers to the wisdom free from objects (*anālambana-jñāna*), which subsumes the absence of external dust. The "store-consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*) is the basis;

"basis" refers to the true mind (*tathatā-citta*), which subsumes the essence of reality. Specifically, this means that the wisdom free from objects perfumes the true mind. Question: Why not simply say "wisdom free from objects"?
Question: This wisdom permeates the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). Answer: When the mind first gives rise to wisdom, it must necessarily rely upon the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*);

yet, while the true [mind] has no fixed location, it pervades all eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭa-vijñāna*). Question: In the Mahāyāna, these are explained as the six and eight consciousnesses; why, then, do you not say that it relies upon its fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*)?

The True [Nature] has no location of its own, yet it pervades all things. Why, then, do you not say that it perfumes the six consciousnesses? Answer: The mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is associated with the "Small" [Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras], as it refers to active manifestation (*pravṛtti*);
the eighth consciousness is associated with the "Great" [Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras], as it is the repository of latent seeds (*ālaya*).

Third, the long-term realization through cultivation. "Cultivating for a long time until it permeates the mind" refers to the stage beginning from contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) up to the stage of semblance.

"The nature of understanding becomes perfectly luminous and illuminates its own essence" means that the entire nature gives rise to wisdom; realizing that wisdom is the nature, once wisdom is luminous, the nature itself is illuminated.
"The mental consciousness immediately ceases" means that the four abidings (*catur-vāsanā*) have perished. If one takes up the "dust-like sands" [of phenomena], this also applies to both cases.
Delusion. At that time, when the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is transformed into non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it is indeed luminous and clear.

Beginning from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) up to the ultimate stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), the principle of destroying delusion throughout the perfect stages (*pariniṣpanna-avasthā*) applies both horizontally and vertically.

According to the phrase "at this time" used here, it must encompass these two aspects. If "this time" refers to the end of a preceding matter and the beginning of a succeeding matter, then it represents the vertical sense. If...
"To be 'at that very time' means to be simultaneous. Question: How does the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) pertain to both types of delusion?

Answer: The meaning of mental consciousness has both general and specific aspects. Thus, its general application is twofold: first, it applies generally to the two delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the dust-and-sand (*rajas-tuṣa*) afflictions.
As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "This mind further has five names; namely, [it includes] the two coarse [delusions]... and so forth.
