This constitutes the first of the three points of the initial argument. It cannot be without mindfulness; it cannot be without those subsequent moments of mindfulness that follow upon the preceding ones. This is what is meant.

1. There is. Second, furthermore, "below" refers to existence (*bhava*), which is precisely mindfulness (*smṛti*). Third, furthermore, "below" refers to existence, which is precisely deluded thought (*vikalpa*).

The text says, "and yet not mindful"; this is precisely ignorance-deluded thought (*avidyā-vikalpa*). What is meant by "and yet not mindful"? This phrase may also give rise to the following passage on the analogy.
2. "For example, below" is the analogy. 3. "This also, below" is the application (*upanaya*). Regarding "both mind and object are dark": it is not...

One should practice non-recollection. There is only deluded recollection directed toward external objects; now, by giving rise to a mind of aversion toward this deluded recollection, one ceases to recollect what has come before.

While the state of constant recollection involves only a single layer of ignorance within the objective realm, by now practicing non-recollection, one adds another layer of the darkness of ignorance upon the mind itself. Therefore, it is said that both mind and object are [obscured].

[The Master] said, "Darkness. [The student] asked, "If one does not think, one does not think of external objects (*viṣaya*). How can this be called 'not thinking of thinking'? [The Master] answered, "When one thinks of external objects, there is 'thinking.
Now, by not thinking of objects, one has already lost the thought that previously directed itself toward external objects.

Because the object of thought is lost, one does not think of external objects; because the subject who thinks is lost, one does not think of thinking. It is simply through this loss that [the state is attained]."
The wisdom of non-dust still belongs to the category of forgetfulness. Although it is called "non-recollection," it is actually a recollection of non-recollection;

therefore, it is now refuted. Furthermore, when one recollects the external objects of the past, there is only the mind that is deluded regarding those objects—a layer of the darkness of ignorance upon the mind.
Now, by again not recollecting those past objects, one adds another layer of ignorance upon the objects themselves; hence, it is called "mind and object."
Both are obscure.

Second, "Furthermore, below," [the text] refutes both "non-attention" and "attention" by means of the analysis of mental attention (*manasikāra*). First, the refutation of these two. First, the refutation of non-attention.
Second, "If one attends," etc., the refutation of attention. Second, "But, below," [the text] exposes the delusions of others. First, it exposes the initial practice for oneself.
Precious Two. First, attaining cessation through causal binding. Second, "Therefore, below," due to delusive jewels. Second, "From 'below,' etc.," refuting habitual cultivation as realization.
First, habitual cultivation as realization. Second, "But not, below," refuting delusion according to its meaning.
Third, first, delusion regarding movement; second, "Furthermore, not, below," delusion residing in affliction; third, "Again, not, below," delusion regarding status. Third, although so.
[The previous section] below permits [the use of] skillful means (*upāya*).

Regarding the second major chapter, which clarifies the objects of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: these are explained through provisional designations (*prajñapti*) within that which is beyond names and numbers.

Whether they are extensive or concise, they all accord with the capacities of sentient beings (*yathā-yoga*). Since the sūtras and śāstras predominantly clarify three dharmas, these three natures (*trisvabhāva*) subsume them all.
All phenomena are exhaustively encompassed without exception. Thus, the *Treatise on the Three Natures* states: "All dharmas do not transcend the three natures.
Now, based on this, the objects of observation for śamatha and vipaśyanā are demonstrated. These observed objects do not exceed two meanings.
First is the delusive object that is observed and from which one must be detached; second is the true object that is observed and revealed through its manifestation.

The nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is also called the "universally imputed" (*parikalpita*); it belongs to the categories of views and afflictions, and constitutes the delusive object. The nature of ultimate reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is also called the "perfected" (*pariniṣpanna*).

This belongs to emptiness; it is the true realm (*tathatā*). That which is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) belongs to ignorance; it is likewise a delusive realm. Therefore, the treatise states:
"The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) refers to the self-nature of all phenomena as manifested by names and conventions, namely, the semblance of objects and consciousness.

The dependent nature refers to the manifestation of the essence of phenomena based upon causes and conditions, namely, the portion of the disturbed consciousness. It depends upon the internal faculties..."

Because it arises conditioned by internal objects, its true nature (*tathatā*) refers to the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*). Furthermore, since the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) belongs to the eight consciousnesses and contains both the defiled and the pure, it encompasses both the real and the delusive.

However, as the states of reality and delusion correspond to the actual practice of cultivation that follows, these objective realms are equivalent in meaning to the stage of "opening and understanding" (*kaijie*);
thus, they may be shown to be identical to what is perceived by the eye of wisdom in the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
This is the realm of knowing. Question: That is the true realm; why is it now said to be permeated by delusion? Answer:
Those three truths are actually taught as the three truths within the delusory realms of the three paths arising from conditions; the underlying intent is the same as here.

Furthermore, this current section shares the same structural characteristics as what follows, and its meaning is analogous to the principle of "correct cultivation" (*samyak-pratipatti*) in the *Mohe Zhiguan*. For in that [text], correct cultivation first...
It clarifies that the object of contemplation is identical to the present realm. Next, it clarifies that the contemplating subject is identical to the present essence and form. Question:

How can the object of contemplation in that text encompass both the real and the false? Answer: That passage cites the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s text on "the mind creating," which encompasses the creation of the ten realms.

How could this not include the true nature of the Buddha and the nine realms of falsehood? If one were to separate the false to reveal the real, then both the real and the false would belong to the sphere of conceptual thought (*cintya*). Both are...
That which is to be abandoned. If the delusive were itself the real, then both the real and the delusive would be inconceivable, and both would be what is manifested.
However, regarding the names of the two natures—*parikalpita* (the imagined) and *paratantra* (the dependent)—the textual expressions are manifold and their systematic classification is not easy.

For now, I shall first distinguish these two natures by way of whether the mental objects (*dharma*) have an essence or lack an essence. As for the *parikalpita-svabhāva*, it is the grasping subject—the deluded mind—which lacks intrinsic nature.
Regarding the substance (*tattva*): the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the substance of the falsely defiled objects that are grasped as real. As the treatise states:

"The dependent nature has a substantial reality distinct from the non-substantiality of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). It further states: "The very substance of the dependent nature is affliction (*kleśa*) and karma;

the imagined nature is able to perfume [the mind] and give rise to grasping. The above discussion has analyzed the natures (*svabhāva*) by pairing them in groups of six and eight. If they are discussed individually:

Each is distinguished according to cause and effect to define the two natures. Within the six consciousnesses, the secondary afflictions and karmic actions that act as perfuming agents constitute the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
With respect to the objects of the six realms that serve as the basis for perfuming, these constitute the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
Since these objects arise based on the perfuming agents, the imagined nature serves as the very basis for the dependent nature, as clarified below in the section on the defiled dependent nature.

For example, when the eight consciousnesses are in a state of non-awakening, they immediately move. The perfuming causes of defilement belong to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), while the transformation of objective realms belongs to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
Therefore, the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* states: "Because the ālayavijñāna arises based on karma, it is called 'dependent.

Thus far, this has been explained solely in terms of deluded consciousness. However, if one considers the relationship between the true and the deluded in a comprehensive sense, there should be three meanings. The first is:
In terms of the fruit, it is explained vertically as the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature); in terms of the cause, it is explained horizontally as the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

Therefore, the objects of the six realms depending upon the eight consciousnesses are called the dependent nature; the objective spheres of the evolving and manifesting [consciousnesses] depending upon the true essence are called the dependent nature.
First, taking the perfuming cause of ignorance (*avidyā*) as the defiled cause and designating the grasping subject as the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Second, without distinguishing between cause and effect, designating it as the nature of discrimination based solely on delusive defilement. Both are equally based upon the true essence and are thus called the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

As stated in the following passage: "The first is the pure portion, which refers to the True [Essence] within defilement; this is termed the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The second is the impure [portion]."
[The first] division refers to the seeds of the habitual tendencies of defiled dharmas and their results as false appearances; this is the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The non-duality of the union of these two natures is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Thirdly, the name "dependent" does not apply solely to the delusory but extends to the true as well, whereas the name "discrimination" applies only to the fruit. As the subsequent text states: "The essence of the mind is equanimous, and this is called..."
Regarding reality (*tattva*): the essence of mind is that which is bound by and follows both defilement and purity; thus, these two dharmas are called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

The manifested false appearances are called the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Furthermore, the *paratantra* name is applied either based on defilement and purity, or solely to the eight consciousnesses.

This is because the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) lacks an intrinsic substance and exists in dependence upon others. As stated in the *Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna*: "In dependence on defilement, it is like earth... [The text continues: "...in dependence on..."
It is pure like gold; therefore, it is called "dependent" (*paratantra*). Furthermore, when this is viewed in relation to that, it is termed "dependent";

when that is viewed in relation to this, it is termed "other-dependent" (*paratantra*). This is identical to what the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa* states: "It serves as the basis for both the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures.

However, the aforementioned analysis of the imagined and dependent natures pertains to defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*). As for pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*), they are fully detailed as follows:
Explanation.
The explanation of the text is divided into three parts. First is the heading. Regarding the statement in the topical outline, "the three natures" (*trisvabhāva*):

they may be called the "three non-natures" (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*), or the "three existent natures," or simply the "three natures. As for the term "self-nature" (*svabhāva*), it refers to one's own nature (*sva-bhāva*) derived from the established truth (*vyavasthāna-satya*).

Because it has obtained this name, it is also called "having nature" (*sabhāva*); these are briefly termed the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). As for what is called "naturelessness" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), it refers to its own specific nature (*svasvabhāva*);

this name is spoken from the perspective of the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*). The *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* (*Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna*) states: "The three naturelessnesses are called the non-established truth."
The *Śāstra* states that the three natures without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) are precisely the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).

If these three natures were all established truths, then the first two natures would be established conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*), for their essence is actually non-existent yet they are established as existent; thus, the nature of ultimate reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) would itself be an established true truth.
It is by negating the two types of existence and establishing the two types of non-existence that it is named "ultimate reality. Returning to this [point]...

Because its nature is free from both existence and non-existence, it is not established; thus, the three natures of non-being are all non-established. Second, regarding the "explanation" below, the text itself is divided into two parts:

first, a general clarification that the three natures constitute three [categories]; second, the specific exposition. Regarding the initial heading: second, the phrase "that which is spoken of" below indicates this.
As for the text stating "the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness," the seventh is combined with the six and collectively termed "discrimination. For example:

The Great Master points to the sūtras to explain that the consciousness which wanders about in search of food and clothing is called the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness) because it is a consciousness of worldly deluded discrimination.
According to the nature of this discriminating consciousness, it should be the sixth *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (evolving consciousness); yet, it is instead termed the seventh consciousness.
This is entirely consistent with the present text’s treatment of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses together as "discrimination. Question: Discrimination...

Question: What is the difference between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)? Answer: There is the nature of discrimination that is itself discriminating consciousness;

this refers to the six consciousnesses. There is the nature of discrimination that is not discriminating consciousness; this refers to the eight consciousnesses. [The phrase] "This is the third" concludes [the section].
Since the meanings are not uniform, what was explained previously was merely based on the general categories.

Second, regarding the "lower" [section], there is a specific explanation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). This consists of two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "First, distinguishing... which itself contains three sections.

Regarding the first, the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), there is first the indication of its meaning, which has three parts: first, the heading; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "Regarding what was said...";

this itself contains two parts. First, the mind that is both defiled and pure, which has three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "That is to say..."; as for what is called "the pure mind," the name is derived from...

Regarding "attainment through correspondence": the essence and intrinsic nature are manifested. As for the term "attainment through correspondence," it means that in contrast to defilement, it is called purity.

Regarding the manifestation of the essence and nature: the essence of the pure mind is precisely the nature of equality (*samatā*). It is neither defiled nor pure, yet it is capable of being both defiled and pure.

Because this essence—the single nature that is neither defiled nor pure—is termed the "nature of defilement and purity," the two natures of defilement and purity are mutually identical. Since purity is [identical to]...
Because it is defiled, this original nature inherently possesses the function of opposition; yet because defilement is itself purity, its essence further encompasses the function of purity.
Although sentient beings who are undefiled may possess the stains of perfuming, this pure nature renders those perfuming stains fundamentally empty.
Although sentient beings manifest defiled appearances, these defiled appearances are quiescent within this pure nature. If one relies upon this pure nature, it is itself defilement.
Since the nature (*dhātu*) is already manifest as defiled phenomena, it cannot be called pure. Therefore, this defiled nature is itself the pure nature;
it does not correspond with defiled phenomena at all, and thus it is further termed "pure. Third, the phrase "therefore" concludes [the argument].
Second, regarding the section "The Lower [Stage]": the "stainless pure mind" is likewise presented with its definition and conclusion. Within the definition, it says:

"The cessation of defiled perfuming" means that the cultivation of evil mental states has ended. "The dissolution of objective defilement" means that the cultivation of evil dharmas has been destroyed.

"The wise one generally says that cultivation of evil is exhausted" refers to the fulfillment of the wisdom of cultivating goodness. "The manifestation of pure virtues" means the perfection of the dharmas of cultivating goodness. Although...

Regarding the statement that "the function of revealing the purity of the nature through permeation (*vāsanā*) does not involve increase": this is because the dharma revealed by wisdom reveals nothing other than itself, as it is the total revelation of the nature;

how, then, could this be an increase through cultivation? Regarding the statement that "the merit of illuminating the essence by temporarily dispelling the clouds of delusion is fundamentally inherent":

the nature of the wisdom that reveals the dharma is originally natural; in reality, it is not called "wisdom-illumination" only when delusion has departed. Therefore, it is said to be "temporarily dispelled. Thus it is reasoned.

Ultimate non-attainment is none other than the inherent virtue of nature; therefore, it is further termed "pure. The word "further" (*fu*) in the preceding passage contrasts with defilement of phenomena (*shiran*), whereas the word "further" in the present passage contrasts with the purity of cultivation (*xiujing*).
Third, the following section provides a summary. Thus, the distinction between "with stains" and "without stains" arises based on the influence of perfuming (*xun*) and in terms of function (*yong*).

Regarding the phenomena of defilement and purity: fundamentally, there is no distinction between being undefiled and being defiled. The essence of the nature of equality is inherently neither defiled nor pure.
The two questions below provide a detailed analysis. First, the question; second, the answer.

Nevertheless, within ignorance, sentient beings nonetheless possess the luminous nature of the Buddha-dharmas; thus, within the luminosity of that nature, the Buddhas nonetheless possess sentient beings.
The nature of the darkness of ignorance is merely a state of delusion that is overturned by its antidote;

therefore, it is said that the Buddhas have no ignorance. Second, the dependent nature has two parts: first, the heading and enumeration; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "purification.

Regarding the first, the dependent nature of the pure portion, there are three sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "that very [nature]," which should be understood as having one essence but three names. The first is called...

It is neither the nature of defilement nor purity. Second is the nature of defilement and the nature of purity. Third are True Suchness free from obstructions and True Suchness while under obstruction.
If discussed generally, according to their essential substance, both are termed "real nature" (*tathatā*);

yet, because they serve as the basis for false appearances, both belong to the "dependent nature. If discussed specifically, there are two differences: first, taking only the "neither-nor" (the non-dual) as the ultimate truth.

Regarding the nature of reality (*tathatā*): the two natures of defilement and purity belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), just as in this very text the two portions of defilement and purity are the dependent nature.
Second, *tathatā* when free from hindrances is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), whereas *tathatā* while under hindrance is the dependent nature.

Question: Regarding the current passage on the pure dependent nature and the imagined nature, how do they compare—do they agree or differ—with the preceding passage concerning the Buddha’s pure qualities?
Answer: They are identical in substance but different in meaning. In the former, the three natures were discussed in relation to sentient beings and Buddhas;

all dharmas possessed by a Buddha are the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), while those possessed by sentient beings are termed the other two natures. In the present case, however, the three natures are discussed separately for both sentient beings and Buddhas. Sentient beings...
The bases all possess a real nature. In both the reverse and the direct modes of cultivation, each has its respective two [aspects]. The text states:
"Furthermore, because they are named 'dependent' (*paratantra*) upon reaching the state of being perfumed by that pure karma," the meaning of "dependent" has two distinct aspects:
first, the body and the land manifest based on the fundamental nature; therefore, the direct mode points to the pure nature as the basis. Second, the body and the land depend upon...
Pure karma can permeate and manifest [the result]; therefore, it points toward pure karma as the "other. As for the text stating that the three bodies lead to self-benefit and benefit for others:
in contrast to the discussion, the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and the Land of Tranquil Light (Sukhāvatī) as one’s own land constitute self-benefit;

the other Reward-body, the Transformation-body, the Land of Other-Enjoyment, and the Land of Expedient Means and Common Residence constitute benefit for others. When discussed comprehensively, these comprise the three bodies and four lands.
That which the Tathāgata has realized for himself is entirely self-benefit; that he benefits others through this very realization is entirely benefit for others.

There are four points of distinction regarding these three aspects. First, as for the questioner’s inquiry based on the preceding text stating that "the defilement of phenomena is exhausted," there are two intended meanings in the response.

First, regarding self and others: while his own practice does not arise [as a karmic result], his transformation of others does arise; therefore it is said that he manifests for the sake of those who are to be converted.

Second, regarding the provisional and the real: while his real creation does not arise, his provisional creation does arise; therefore it is said that he displays the possession of the three poisons and provisionally undergoes the retribution of suffering.
Question: Does the display of the three poisons constitute his nature or is it a matter of fact? Answer: From the perspective of the Buddha himself, it may be understood as either.
This concerns the matter of applying the name "nature" (*prakṛti*) when speaking to sentient beings. Question: The Great Master Zhiyi stated only that "evil nature is not severed.

Does this not imply that this "nature" is a provisional construct and is not the actual phenomenon? Answer: Regarding the functioning of all Buddhas as discussed by the Wise One (Zhiyi), it is precisely because of evil nature that they give rise to what is called "cultivated evil.
This is for the sake of responding to those who lack faith (*icchantika*); although the Buddha gives rise to cultivation, this cultivation is itself nature and is not defiled by evil.
Therefore, it is given the name "abiding reception. Thus the Wise One said: "Throughout the day one employs it, yet throughout the day one remains unstained. He further said:

"Now it is clarified that even those who have abandoned all [virtue] (icchantika) do not sever their inherent virtuous qualities; when they encounter conditions, these virtues manifest. Likewise, the Buddha does not sever his inherent evil;
when moved by karmic conditions and perfumed by the power of goodness, he enters the Avīci Hell and undergoes all manner of evil deeds to transform sentient beings. Please observe this matter!"

The term is explained by means of its correspondence with *icchantika*. It further states: "The *icchantika* is likewise; though their inherent goodness is not severed, they can still give rise to roots of goodness.
If the Tathāgata’s inherent evil were not severed, he would likewise be able to give rise to evil. Although he gives rise to evil, his mind of liberation remains unstained;
to penetrate the limit of evil is itself the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). It continues: "Even up to this point, it says that the *icchantika* does not realize this."
They are different. Please observe the character "qi" (arise) as well as the phrases "although they arise" and "reaching evil.

From this one knows that it is only because the Buddha can realize that cultivation is identical to nature (*xing*) that he differs from the *icchantika*; it does not mean that he does not give rise to the defilement of performing evil deeds through cultivation. Question:

What is the difference between the Buddha's arising of evil deeds through cultivation and [the arising of such deeds] by ordinary beings? Answer: They are identical in essence but differ in meaning. Because their essence is the same, both are referred to as "deeds" (*shi*).
Because their meanings differ, they are distinct from one another in terms of both identity and difference. Thus, the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:

"If an icchantika can penetrate the fact that cultivated evil is no different from the Tathāgata," this is the intent of the second question-and-answer section: it does not go beyond the conventional designation according to the person, and thus it is called "pure.

However, when analyzed according to the actual substance of the dharma (*dharmatā*), it is truly called "defiled. This is, for example, like how the manifestation of function belongs to the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*) and is likewise so named.

Because they constitute bondage, Jingxi said: "If the six realms manifest as bondage, the realm of the two vehicles manifests as liberation, and the realm of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifests as transformation.

Unless one has realized the inconceivable mastery of the body through the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, how could one manifest these thirty-three bodies? It is neither bondage nor liberation, yet it manifests as bondage and liberation. Its...
This means: does "manifest" (pratyakṣa) not refer to a manifest phenomenon? Therefore, one knows that in its essential nature, it is also a manifest phenomenon of bondage.
However, because this phenomenon is identical to its nature, it is termed "liberation by nature" (prakṛti-vimukti) as a simultaneous designation.

Regarding the third question, since it was previously stated that this is the "pure parikalpita-svabhāva," the answer distinguishes between the two natures based on the basis (*āśraya*) of the entity itself. As for the fourth question, there is none.

The two terms "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*) and "purity" (*vyavadāna*) are similar in name; the two meanings of "ultimate reality" (*pariniṣpanna*) and "dependent nature" (*paratantra*) appear identical. Therefore, this question arises:

since that which is dependent must necessarily have a basis, if one points to ultimate reality, it appears identical to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). In the answer, regarding essence, characteristic, and function:
within the dependent nature, the ultimate reality which serves as the basis is set aside, and only that which depends upon it is taken up; therefore, it is called a "characteristic. Furthermore...
This *paratantra* nature encompasses both the object and the subject. The pure karma is that which is depended upon (*āśraya*), while the body and the land are that which depends (*āśrita*).

Whether subject or object, both are aspects of cultivation. When their function manifests light in response to conditions, they are termed the *parikalpita* nature. This is precisely what was meant by the previous statement that the three bodies and four lands all pervade both self and others.

The second [section] concerns the defiled aspect of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). It consists of three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "That very... (*tat-tu*); and third, the analytical selection (*vicāra*). In the explanation, it says:

"It is merely that which is perfumed by the defiled dharmas of ignorance existing within the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Regarding the *paratantra-svabhāva*, this refers to the manifested object. There are two differences in the perfuming dharmas: the first is the initial, independent non-awakening (*abodhi*). *Note:

This translation assumes the text is a commentary on a Yogācāra treatise, likely from the Chinese tradition, given the terminology such as "分別性" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and "依他性" (*paratantra-svabhāva*). The phrase "獨頭不覺" (*dútóu bùjué*) is a specific technical term for a primary state of non-awakening.*

It acts as the perfuming agent (*bhāvanā*). There is the realm of evolving and manifesting objects. Second, today [we hold that] the ignorance of the six consciousnesses acts as the perfuming agent, and there is the realm of illusory appearances.

However, regarding these two realms perfumed by these agents: if one follows alternative explanations, the realm of evolving and manifesting is outside the realm of illusory appearances, while the realm of illusory appearances is inside.
Furthermore, if one follows deluded attachment, one considers the internal realm to be real. Now, according to the definitive teaching of the Great Vehicle, this internal realm is...
This is a state of empty appearance. Since the manifested realms are already two and not identical, the perfuming agent (*kṣobhaka*) consequently has differences between its root and its branches.

Here, we speak from the perspective of the branches; therefore, the realms of the six paths depend upon the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and because these belong to the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*), they pertain to the six consciousnesses.

The realms of dependence on others outside the triple world, however, pertain to the eighth consciousness. If they were not distinct, the essence of the root and branches of the perfuming ignorance (*avidyā*) would be identical. As for the objects...
All manifested realms are the eight consciousnesses. There are four types of analytical selection (*viniścaya*). First, the questioner asks:

"Since sentient beings possess the function of the pure nature (*viśuddha-dhātu*), how could they be entirely devoid of capacity before it has been perfumed and manifested? The meaning of the answer is this: although one has not yet been perfumed oneself, one is protected by the Buddhas;
because of this protection, one gradually cultivates—how then could this not be functional? If there were no pure nature, why would the Buddhas protect anyone? Thus it is said, "It is the same."

Regarding the "essence" (*tattva*): first, because the pure essence of the Buddha-nature is identical in its arising; if a Buddha, through wisdom, protects the pure nature by utterly severing defiled delusions, he thereby also protects the pure nature of sentient beings.
Second, because all Buddhas possess identical essential expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) that constantly protects sentient beings;

if there are those who have the capacity but do not receive [protection], it is because their karmic offenses are so heavy that they do not receive extraction, even though the Buddha’s power is ever-present. Question:
Those with light [karmic] burdens receive extraction, while those with heavy ones do not. Does this not manifest that the Buddha possesses great power?
If the power of the Buddha-fruit is so great, why does it not extract [the heavy]? Answer: The power of the Buddha is indeed great, yet the circumstances of "departing" and "approaching" differ.

It is not that his power is slight and thus unable to lift the heavy. It is like a worldly scale capable of lifting ten thousand *jin*: if one uses a ten-thousand-*jin* object but does not approach the scale, then even if one were to approach it...
What is meant by "not being lifted"? It is that sentient beings, because their transgressions are heavy, do not respond to the power of the Buddha.
If they were to respond, how could he fail to pull them out? In the third question-and-answer section, the answer is given in terms of self-cultivation (*sva-bhāvanā*).

Therefore, it is said that there is no further capacity [other than this], such as the protection of the Buddha. This implies that this purity also possesses functional power; thus, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, regarding grave offenses, the Buddha—
Sentient beings are especially objects of compassionate mindfulness because they originally possess the nature of purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). Regarding the fourth question and answer:
the meaning of the response is that phenomena do not manifest of themselves but must necessarily be formed through perfuming (*vāsanā*).

If sentient beings were immersed in defilement and entirely lacked the capacity for pure perfuming, while the Buddhas were in a state of purity and possessed the virtue of perfuming defilement—what is called "perfuming defilement" is precisely their compassion and vow (*karuṇā-praṇidhāna*)—then [the teaching] would manifest...
Entering the six realms of existence to manifest the three poisons is precisely this compassionate vow that perfumes and transforms one's nature. Question:

If it arises through the perfuming of the provisional, why is it further said that the evil of one's nature is not severed? Answer: If there were no perfuming by the evil of one's nature, it would not be established. Question:

If it arises based on perfuming, why say it does not require effort, like an image appearing in a mirror? Answer: It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the Dharma-realm; or, it may be explained from the perspective of phenomena.

Discerning principle necessarily relies upon the permeation of compassionate vows to manifest within the nature; or, discerning phenomena through principle does not depend on external conditions, as both arise from the nature.

Whether it be the non-duality of phenomenon and principle, or the simultaneous transcendence of both phenomenon and principle—these various explanations according to conditions are all beyond intellectual calculation.

As the text says: "Therefore, the Great Sage relinquishes [discursive thought] to manifest his knowledge of the capacities [of beings]; this means that the capacity for awakening is not yet ready to be activated.

Regarding the abandonment discussed from the perspective of the Dharma, although it is said that the Buddha abandons [the world] according to the capacity of sentient beings, the merit actually belongs to the abandonment by the capacity responding to the Buddha.
This is, for example, like the terminology of "identity" and "separation" regarding phenomena and principle.

The threefold analysis of the nature of differentiation (parikalpita-svabhāva) consists of four parts: first, the presentation and enumeration; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "That which is spoken of," which itself divides into two sections.
First, the pure nature of differentiation; this has two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "That very [nature]," which further divides into two.

First, the presentation of the essence of the dharma-body, the self-realized essence, which is equal, true, and eternal, wherein names and marks vanish, and it cannot be differentiated as arising for the sake of others. If one speaks...
The essence of self-realized equality is said to be conceptualization itself; how much more so when it is manifested as the six destinies and four modes of birth?
Are not all names and signs conceptualization? The text states that "all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) can know the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) down to the six destinies and four modes of birth";
this takes worldly phenomena as its function. From relying on internal realization to manifesting for those who have not yet heard [the Dharma].

This takes supramundane dharmas as its function. Regarding "the knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*): if it were taken as identical with the path-knowledge (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all [phenomena] (*sarvajñatā*), it would belong to the Middle Way.

However, in the present text, it is specifically situated in the various distinctions of all conventional phenomena. Furthermore, the name "knowledge of all modes" refers to the application of all three knowledges together;
alternatively, it may be based on the essence, which is the wisdom of the Middle Way, as when it is said that the Buddha-eye contemplates the six [realms].

The Path arises. Second, regarding this meaning, there are two parts to the explanation of the term's significance: first, the arising of the objection; second, the formal explanation beginning with "Although...

and so forth. Regarding the first, concerning the response: those who are not defiled by the world and do not exert effort are all said to be "pure" because they follow their inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*).

This very nature of pure, equal enlightenment gives rise to the function of discrimination in accordance with objective phenomena; thus, this supreme function is established from the perspective of the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Second, as for the subsequent section concerning the capacity of the practitioner (*yogin*), "causing others to be purified" means causing sentient beings also to attain this nature.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of discriminating for others," the character *wei* (為) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*). This means that one employs the Buddha’s virtuous functions to effect discrimination on behalf of sentient beings.

The second [section] concerns the three types of defiled discrimination. First is the heading; second, from "That very... onwards, is the explanation. That which is grasped as a false appearance is the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

Grasping the false as real is the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). As the text says, "they arise mutually," this means that because one grasps the imagined nature as real, the dependent nature arises in the form of a false appearance;
conversely, it must be through the dependent nature appearing in a false form that the grasping of the imagined nature as real arises.

Regarding distinct natures: just as ordinary people today give rise to a sense of real attachment toward the sense organs and their objects, performing extremely evil deeds that perfume the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
After the end of their lives, the realm of hell manifests before them. The substance of the hell that manifests has no reality; it is a false appearance.
This arises from a sense of reality producing a false appearance. Although it is a false appearance, it is perceived through the power of deluded attachment.
That hell is a real entity arises from producing a sense of reality from what is ultimately empty. The third question provides a detailed analysis. In the response, it says:
"Although there is no distinct substance that gives rise to one another, emptiness and reality differ. Regarding the phrase "no distinct substance":

first, when the false is contrasted with the true, both the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*) are equally false dharmas; therefore, they have no distinct substance. This is stated from the perspective of the false itself.

The six consciousnesses are the *parikalpita* (imagined nature), while the eight consciousnesses are the *paratantra* (dependent nature). How could they not have distinct entities? Second, if we examine the actual substance of these two natures according to their reality:

the *parikalpita* has no substance, for it clings to the unreal as real; thus, in this sense, there is no distinct entity. However, if one distinguishes their entities according to their designations:
the *parikalpita* takes factual reality as its entity, whereas the *paratantra* takes illusory appearances as its entity. How could they not have distinct entities? Third...

The grasping of the afflictions of seeing and thinking belongs to the nature of parikalpita (imagined nature). The illusory appearances of the six realms belong to the nature of paratantra (dependent nature).

Since this reality and illusion are both deluded dharmas of the six consciousnesses within the realm of desire, they do not possess distinct entities. The grasping of reality by ignorance belongs to the nature of parikalpita.
The illusory appearances of the two lands belong to the nature of paratantra. Since this reality and illusion are both the causes of the eight consciousnesses outside the realm of desire—
Therefore, they do not have distinct entities. If one were to take the grasping subject and the grasped object as being different, how could they not have distinct entities? Question:

It may be that the six consciousnesses grasp the false appearances of the eight consciousnesses as real; however, why do you speak of "false" and "real" respectively for those within the realm and those outside the realm?

Answer: Since the meanings of "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and "without resistance" (*apratigha*) are distinct, they cannot be debated as if they were identical; thus, they are distinguished individually. Question:

If one provisionally distinguishes them by clinging to the void as being real, how does one differentiate between the internal and external boundaries? Answer: We shall now use the analogy of a bright mirror and its reflected image.

If one clings to the brightness as being void while regarding the image as real, this is like that which is outside the boundary. If one clings to the image as being void while regarding the physical form as real, this...

Just as it is within the realm (*dhātu*), it is precisely because those within the realm are deluded regarding the images of the eight consciousnesses that they falsely grasp these empty [images] as substantial forms.

Those outside the realm are deluded regarding the Middle Way; they falsely grasp this luminosity as substantial images. Therefore, the derivative afflictions (*śākhā-kleśa*) merely involve delusion regarding images and belong to the category of delusions concerning phenomena (*vastu-moha*).

Their fundamental [afflictions] arise from delusion regarding luminosity and belong to the category of delusions concerning principle (*tattva-moha*). Once the derivative afflictions are destroyed, [the fundamental ones follow].

To eliminate attachment to reality while remaining seated within the emptiness of images is, from the perspective of that specific stage, called "knowing true emptiness. However, if viewed from the standpoint of the Middle Way, this very emptiness still constitutes an obstruction.

Once the fundamental delusions are shattered, one can eliminate the reality of these images and thereby perceive their luminous emptiness; it is only through this destruction of delusion that one finally exhausts the source and reaches the ultimate.
Without this discernment, the principles of the Dharma will not be clear. In truth, according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are of one essence.
There is a further section below regarding the third watch [of the night]. Once again, two meanings are employed to illustrate the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Regarding the first meaning:

the meaning of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) does not differ from what was stated previously; however, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) differs from what was stated before.

Previously, it was held that the two kinds of false appearances—defiled and pure—depend upon the two kinds of perfuming agents (*vāsana*), which is a case of "the phenomenon depending on the phenomenon. Alternatively, it was held that the false appearance depends on the defiled and pure nature. That is to say...

The fact (the phenomenon) relies upon the principle (the nature). Now, because the essence of the nature relies upon the two types of perfuming agents—defilement and purity—it is the case that the principle relies upon the fact.
As for the text stating that "the fruit of manifested false appearances is called the nature of discrimination," this is also not the same as the former [notion of] discrimination.

The former discrimination clings to the false as real; the present discrimination simply follows from the false appearances. Thus, what was previously the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) becomes the present *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
Because from now on the principle (*nyāya*) is taken as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), phenomena are merely conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Regarding the second meaning:

the text states that within the dependent nature, conceptual construction is established as the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). This is because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) has both general and specific aspects.

Generally, it encompasses the essence and function of the nature, as well as the truth of being obstructed and the truth of emerging from obstruction. Specifically, it refers to the essence of the nature and the truth of emerging from obstruction. Now, based on the preceding text...
If one separately takes the reality that exists within the obstacle as the true nature (dharmatā), then the reality existing within the obstacle belongs to the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).

Consequently, it can be said that there is yet another meaning: namely, taking the reality existing within the obstacle as the true nature. In this case, the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is also not the same as before.
Previously, the causes that perfume through defilement and purity were taken as the basis within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature);

therefore, both the causes that perfume through defilement and purity belong to the *paratantra*. However, the resulting fruits perfumed by defilement and purity are categorized as the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
Regarding the current text, if we speak in terms of defilement and purity, the present section pertains specifically to defilement, whereas the preceding section was general.

If we speak in terms of the perfuming agent (*kṣobhaka*) and the perfumed object (*kṣobhya*), the present section applies generally to both cause and effect as being conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), whereas the preceding section instead constituted the specific [distinction].

As for the statement that "the non-duality of the two natures in their harmonious union is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)," it means that when phenomena depend on principle, the phenomenon is the dependent nature; and when principle depends on phenomena, [the principle is likewise the dependent nature].
Principle is the dependent nature; therefore, in this present passage, the single term "dependent" encompasses both this phenomenon and its principle.
This differs from the preceding passage, where [the dependent] was either distinct as a phenomenon or distinct as a principle.
There are two levels of analytical discrimination (*viniścaya*). The first distinguishes between the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the five sensory consciousnesses;

this, however, does not yet distinguish between the consciousnesses associated with the five sense organs and the sixth mental consciousness—it is only in the second that they are so distinguished. Therefore, there are two layers of discrimination.

As for the initial question and answer, it is because the tenets of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools differ; specifically, within the Hīnayāna, it is admitted that the five sensory consciousnesses can also give rise to the three [mental factors].

[The opponent says: "Therefore, we know that each of the five consciousnesses is individually capable of discerning a single object and giving rise to feeling, perception, and mental formations (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra*).

The Mahāyāna is not like this; thus, the five consciousnesses are only able to apprehend objects without yet initiating discernment. As soon as discernment arises, it belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

[The proponent] now asks: "Consciousness is, by definition, discernment (*vijñapti*). If there is no discernment, how can they be called the 'five consciousnesses'? [The opponent] answers: "It is precisely because of the Mahāyāna [that this is so]."

The five consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) do not arise sequentially; therefore, the locus of discrimination for the five consciousnesses is precisely the mental consciousness.

Question: Although there is no sequence, there must necessarily be distinct characteristics between the five consciousnesses and the mental consciousness in order to be able to say that the five consciousnesses apprehend objects without giving rise to discrimination.
Answer: If one were to distinguish their differences, one could also say that it begins with the eye [consciousness].

When perceiving color-form (*rūpa*), it is distinct from other sensory objects (*viṣaya*). The meaning of "discrimination" (*vijñapti*) is general; each [sense] obtains its respective object, which is also a form of discrimination.

However, this differs from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in that it specifically distinguishes the physical characteristics of the object of color-form—such as blue, yellow, long, short, beautiful, or ugly—and for this reason, it is different from the mental consciousness.
Next, regarding the question and answer: this is also because some within the Hīnayāna school maintain that the mental consciousness is divided into five or six distinct parts. For now, however...

To illustrate this principle by way of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), consider the following: the sensory organ (*indriya*) gives rise to visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which perceives the external object before it and discriminates it as smoke;
this belongs to the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Having perceived the smoke, one then infers the existence of fire.
This refers to the object of inference cognized by the visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*). Although the object of the smoke has ceased, the mental recollection of it persists;
this belongs to the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as it takes as its object a dharma-atom (*dharmāyatana*) that is a past form-atom (*rūpa-dhātu*) fallen away from the sensory field.

Thus, the tenets of this school differ from those of the Mahāyāna in two respects: first, the visual consciousness discriminates the smoke and is also capable of giving rise to the three [subsequent] minds, such as feeling (*vedanā*).

Unlike the Mahāyāna view, where visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) can only apprehend the present sensory object, as soon as a conceptualization arises—such as "this is smoke"—it belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

This was already clarified in the first part of the initial response. Second, the Lesser Vehicle school maintains that the five sensory consciousnesses perceive objects through inference (*anumāna*), whereas the sixth mental consciousness takes past objects as its objective support; therefore, they distinguish between these two types of consciousness as being different.
In the Mahāyāna, the consciousnesses that perceive the five present sense-objects as well as past objects are collectively termed the *manovijñāna*;

it does not distinguish between five and six. This is as answered here now. Question: Why does the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) not follow the Mahāyāna approach, yet instead distinguishes between five and six, stating:

"The five consciousnesses and the five *manovijñānas* do not yet belong to afflictions, as they remain in the state of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)"? Answer: If one speaks from the perspective of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is simply...

There is one consciousness; because its substance follows the sense organs, it is divided into five or six. If this essential meaning is grasped, there is no conflict between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
This is why Jingxi explained both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna together; therefore, he also said:

"If one relies on the Sautrāntika or the Mahāyāna Dharma-lakṣaṇa [Abhidharma], the simultaneous mental consciousness takes as its objects the five present sensory objects as well as past objects. Furthermore, one must know that it is not only the substance of the five consciousnesses that is meant.

It is the same as the sixth [consciousness]. Indeed, the substance of the five consciousnesses is also entirely the same; however, when distinguishing the objects and the mind, one contemplates only the recollection of consciousness (*vijñāna-smṛti*).
When taking them collectively from their essential nature, this constitutes contemplating the five consciousnesses, the five mental factors (*manas*), and the sixth consciousness.

Therefore, none of the various consciousnesses are excluded. Thus, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "Now, first, one contemplates the various consciousnesses as objects, taking them individually according to their respective sense bases. Hence...

Only the sixth consciousness is clearly perceived at its initial attainment; the other five consciousnesses become manifest only as they encounter their respective conditions. Because people are often ignorant of this, they simply say [the sixth is primary].
Third, the preceding section concludes with the following summary.

The third major section, "The Essential Nature and Characteristics of Samatha and Vipaśyanā": What has been presented thus far was the exposition of understanding; now, the actual establishment of practice is undertaken.

"Essential nature" (*ti*) refers to the fundamental substance, while "characteristics" (*zhuang*) refers to the outward appearance. This clarifies that the essential nature and characteristics of *samatha* and *vipaśyanā* are themselves non-objective wisdom (*wu chen zhi*).

Their manifestations are demonstrated by way of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). However, both the School of Names (*Ming zong*) and the School of Characteristics (*Xiang zong*) universally employ these terms for the three natures, each having its own specific interpretation.

Establishing [the teaching] involves departing from distinct categories. Now, following the tradition of the Shanjia school, I shall first set forth the general principles. The ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) cannot be named;
however, because sentient beings have no means to understand the pinnacle of the Dharma-realm, it is provisionally designated as the "Equal Single Nature" (pingdeng yixing).

Thus, Jingxi said: "Fundamentally, this refers to the Single Nature. Yet, even this Single Nature is not something that can be distinguished by number; how much less could it be [described otherwise]?"

Seeking through form: it is perfectly wondrous and inconceivable, lacking nothing. Because of the presence of delusion, although [the nature] is one from the perspective of its essence, it appears diverse from the perspective of delusion.
Delusion takes this nature—which is without marks—as a false mark; this arises from ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the eight consciousnesses and is termed the *paratantra-svabhāva*.

Delusion takes this nature’s false mark as a real mark; this arises from view-delusion and affliction-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa-avidyā*), which are the six consciousnesses and are termed the *parikalpita-svabhāva*.
Distinct natures: the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which consists of the causes and effects of the eight consciousnesses, pertains to matters outside the realm;

the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which consists of the causes and effects of the six consciousnesses, pertains to matters within the realm. Furthermore, being deluded regarding these matters and unable to comprehend them is termed the "dust-and-sand" delusions (*rajas-aṇu-kleśa*).

In terms of the consciousnesses, these actually encompass all six and eight; however, for the duration of a single lifetime, they are categorized as residing in the seventh consciousness. Regarding this single deluded thought, once the delusion...
There are three [obstructions]. How could that which is deluded by them be said to be one? As Jingxi said: "Nature refers to the three obstructions; therefore, it possesses all three.

The delusions of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions) mistake the void for the real, thereby losing the true emptiness. For this reason, the single nature that is the object of delusion is called 'true emptiness.
Because one loses the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through delusion regarding the *paryavasthāna-kleśas* (dust-like afflictions), for this reason, the object of delusion..."
The single nature is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Ignorance deludes this nature, producing illusory appearances and causing one to lose its true aspect.

For this reason, that single nature which is the object of delusion is termed the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). The essence of this nature is not threefold; the "three" are spoken of only in relation to delusion.
That which is able to delude—the delusive objects of the three afflictions—belongs to the two natures of discrimination (*parikalpita*) and dependence (*paratantra*).

That which is deluded by it—the true objects of the three truths—is the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna*). If one points to the three afflictions as being themselves the three truths, this may also be said to mean that "nature" refers to the three afflictions;
therefore, it possesses all three. Furthermore, the substance of the two natures that are able to delude is conventional phenomena, while that which is deluded is the truth.

The substantial entity is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Furthermore, since the former two natures are ignorance, they belong to emptiness and the conventional; the latter, the true reality, corresponds to the Middle Way.

Since one is deluded regarding the nature of the three truths by means of the three afflictions, one should cultivate the non-discriminative wisdom of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to penetrate this delusion and perceive that nature.
This wisdom is itself the nature; yet, although each individual nature exists due to delusion, [it is realized through such wisdom].

Third: This wisdom is also not unitary because its nature is manifold. As Jingxi (Jingci) said: "Cultivation is accomplished based on nature; the accomplishment of the three [wisdoms] is the natural law (*dharmatā*).
By means of this wisdom, one ceases the attachment to the reality of discriminative delusions and perceives true emptiness.

Therefore, this wisdom is devoid of real objects; it is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). By means of this wisdom, one illuminates and comprehends delusion and reality, thereby recognizing that delusion.
[Objection: Therefore, this wisdom belongs to the provisional contemplation within the realm [of the dependent nature]. [Response:

Because this wisdom illuminates that the dependent nature is non-existent yet existent, and because it recognizes its illusory characteristics, this wisdom belongs to the provisional contemplation beyond the realm.
Because this wisdom halts at the characteristics of the illusory marks of the dependent nature, seeing that existence is non-existence, one perceives the Middle Way.
Indeed, this wisdom is thus able to be free from the marks of the dust of ignorance; it is precisely the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).

By means of these three contemplations, one contemplates the two natures and the three delusions, thereby attaining the three truths of reality. Therefore, one cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* regarding the two natures of the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*).
As for cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is because wisdom and views are both extinguished within the present moment.
However, regarding the essence of nature: when the three truths are identical to the one truth, it is termed "stopping" (*śamatha*).

Because the wisdom that illuminates both [aspects] realizes the innate functioning of nature within the present moment, the one truth is identical to the three truths; this is termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). As the Master Zhili said:
"The three truths as one truth in one's own practice is termed 'the real' (*tattva*); the one truth as three truths for the sake of transforming others is termed 'the provisional' (*upāya*). Indeed.

Entering into reality is cessation (*śamatha*); emerging from expedient means is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Although the names and categories of the dharmas employed differ, the path utilized is in truth no different.
It is for this reason that I now record this. Question: Since the three truths are the natural, inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*), why is it said that they exist because of the three delusions?
Answer: The Master Zhiyi says: "In principle, there are truly no names; they are established in opposition to non-existence."

This clarifies that they are designated according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "It is only for the sake of guiding sentient beings that [the Buddha] speaks by means of provisional names (*prajñapti*).
Because it is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, it is called the Middle Way.

It is precisely because this is inherently possessed within the natural, innate nature (*prakṛti*) that, due to the three types of delusion and their concomitant production, three provisional designations are established. Therefore, it can be said that the Three Truths are the natural nature itself.

[The Master] asked: "If the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is such that cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) only distinguish the three truths as being mutually identical in their single essence, should it not follow that the former two natures are not identical with that one?

[The Master] replied: "Although the explanation follows a sequential order, the underlying intent is without before or after. [The Master] asked: "If one wishes to practice this, how does one point to the mind?"
Answer: Since the understanding gained through hearing and study was already opened up in the preceding chapter, how could the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* now follow a different path?

Therefore, the source of both delusion and awakening is the same, being the complete essence of the entire treasury [of the teachings]. Truth and falsehood are non-dual; there is nothing that is not the pure mind. Subject and object are of one suchness, and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) reach the same goal.
If even the observing subject—the contemplation itself—is identical with delusion, how could the observed object—the principle of the truths—be separate or distant from it? This is so.

Therefore, in every speck of dust and every thought-moment, there is nothing that is not the identity of the three and the one. This state is inconceivable right where it is. It is three within one, and one within three;

neither before nor after, neither vertical nor horizontal. This perfect understanding is the reality of the principle of delusion, the reality known through names, the reality practiced in the stage of contemplative action, and even the ultimate reality of the final stage of wondrous enlightenment. It is only that, according to the depth of one's cultivation, there are differences in realization.

They are distinct. If one proceeds from the former two natures to establish the third, then the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) involves cultivating only emptiness and the conventional;

the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) involves cultivating only the conventional and the middle way. Upon reaching the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the triad of emptiness, the conventional, and the middle way is fully and perfectly complete as three-in-one.

Therefore, while the cultivation of the former two natures appears to have distinct superior aspects, the perfected nature is entirely identical with the single mind. If, in every moment of thought, these three aspects are practiced simultaneously...
In study: discrimination is precisely the provisional (parikalpita), cessation is precisely the empty (śūnyatā), and non-duality in its own place is precisely the middle (pariniṣpanna).

Although these three differ, they are but a single thought-moment. Taking this oneness as three, it is termed "contemplation" (vipaśyanā); taking these three as one, it is termed "cessation" (śamatha).

Since this is so for the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), it is likewise for the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva). Thus, one sees that within the one [middle], the three natures are fully present.
The three and the one are entirely one. They are neither three nor one, yet they are both three and one; this is inconceivable.

If it were not so, how would it differ from the stages [of the *bhūmis*] or the [doctrinal] categories? One must not grasp at the provisional while departing from the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*). Question:

Previously, you identified the nature of reality (*tathatā*) as the three truths, as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and as the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*). Why is this? Answer: The "truths" (*satya*) are simply the principle (*li*). Even that principle does not exist.
First, as for why there are three: they are merely designated as three in relation to conditions. Therefore, the Wise One said: "In reality, it is the Single Truth; it is expediently taught as three.
To speak of them as three, their progression and regression differ, and thus there are three vehicles. First, this single nature is what sentient beings are deluded about.
Delusion itself is "existence" (*yu*); existence is called the conventional (*sāṃvṛti*). This existence is distinct from non-existence and is entirely [the ultimate].
Because its nature is existent, this single nature is termed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

If sentient beings were to perceive only its existence without knowing that this existence is entirely constituted by nature, it could merely be called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) and not "truth" (*satya*). Now, because this convention is explained as being precisely that nature, it is called the conventional truth.
Furthermore, in contrast to the delusion regarding existence, it is said that this single nature—the essence of which is fundamentally empty—is the [ultimate] nature. Therefore...

It is called the Truth of Reality (*satyadharma*). Furthermore, in contrast to emptiness and existence, this single nature is taught; since the essence of this nature is neither empty nor existent, it is non-dual in its very locus, and is therefore called the Middle Truth (*madhyasatya*).
However, these three truths are established upon the basis of this single nature; thus the Patriarch said: "Although they are of one substance, three names are established.
The name is realized through the substance, and the substance is identical to the name. Therefore, it can be said that [they are one].
The three are, in fact, one characteristic; in reality, there is no difference between them. Now, we take this principle as our tenet, and thus designate the true nature as the "Three Truths.
Second, previously, when delusion regarding existence was considered from the perspective of its underlying nature, it was termed the "Conventional Truth" (saṃvṛti-satya).

However, if we discuss it from the standpoint of the very essence of that deluded existence, there are further two meanings: first, because this reality is conventional in nature, it is called the Conventional Truth; second, regarding...

The conventional knowledge of conventional phenomena is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Therefore, the single nature (*eka-lakṣaṇa*) exists only nominally within emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Since the conventional is a phenomenon, it pertains to the first two natures; emptiness is the principle, and thus pertains to the true nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Regarding these three, as for the previous designation of the single nature as "emptiness," this refers to ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), which is also spoken of in relation to that upon which emptiness depends. If, however, one speaks from the perspective of its own essence (*svabhāva*), [it is as follows].
This emptiness is not of a single nature; its essence is the illusory appearance of ignorance, which is subsumed under the aforementioned dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Therefore, the single nature is designated solely as the "Middle" (*madhyama*). Thus, the true nature belongs to the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

The commentary on the text is divided into three parts: first, the presentation of the outline; second, the explanation beginning with "First, regarding... (*di chos*); and third, the conclusion beginning with "Next... (*gnyis pa*). The explanation itself consists of two sections:

first, regarding defilement and turbidity; second, regarding purity. The former clarifies that objects of perception accord with delusion regarding reality, which gives rise to the subsequent manifestation of false thoughts.

Therefore, in the [section on] "Actual Nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it was placed first. Now, clarifying that the cultivation of contemplation follows the reversal of delusion and the return to the True, it is presented as a sequential account;

thus, Actual Nature is placed last. Furthermore, these three natures encompass both defiled and pure objects. Now, they are universally applied as the objects of contemplation, because all objects contemplated by ordinary beings do not transcend these three dharmas:
the three defiled natures constitute the dharma of sentient beings (*sattva-dharma*) along with the dharma of the mind (*citta-dharma*). The pure...
The purification of the three natures is itself the Buddha-dharma. These three dharmas do not transcend the internal and the external. Sentient beings and Buddhas belong to the external;

mental phenomena belong to the internal. Furthermore, regarding the two kinds of form—the self and its environment—even these belong to the internal when viewed in relation to sentient beings and Buddhas.

If one regards the environment (niśraya-vipāka) from the perspective of the self, then the environment is external and the self is internal; likewise, regarding the self's own retribution (vipāka), form is external and mind is internal.
However, the object of observation in this context encompasses both the internal and the external.
